131. A 41-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the right arm and face. She had a long flight 2 days ago and has a swollen, tender left calf. A soft systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border, and S2 is widely split and does not vary with respiration. MRI confirms an acute stroke.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Atrial septal defect with paradoxical embolism
   - **A.** Vasculitis of cerebral vessels — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **B.** Paradoxical embolism of a venous thrombus through an atrial septal defect **(Correct)** — Correct. Fixed wide splitting of S2 suggests an atrial septal defect; a DVT can cross the interatrial communication into the systemic circulation.
   - **C.** Cardiac myxoma fragment — Wrong. No positional symptoms or mass described.
   - **D.** Embolism of a left atrial thrombus from atrial fibrillation — Wrong. No irregular rhythm is described.
   - **E.** Atherosclerotic plaque rupture in the carotid artery — Wrong. Unlikely at her age without risk factors, and does not explain the DVT link.
   - **F.** Air embolism from the flight — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - long flight 2 days ago — Venous stasis and deep vein thrombosis.
     - swollen, tender left calf — DVT, the embolic source.
     - widely split and does not vary with respiration — Fixed splitting of S2: atrial septal defect.
     - soft systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border — Increased flow across the pulmonic valve.
   - **Reasoning:** DVT + fixed split S2 + pulmonic flow murmur → ASD → venous clot crosses the atrial septum → arterial (cerebral) embolism.
   - **Teaching point:** "Fixed split = Fixed hole in the atrial wall."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains how she developed a stroke?
   - Page: 301

132. A 32-year-old man who emigrated as an adult has never had medical care. He reports fatigue and dyspnea. His fingers are normal, but his toes are cyanotic and clubbed. Oxygen saturation is 98% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot. A loud P2 is heard; no continuous murmur is present.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Eisenmenger syndrome from PDA
   - **A.** Reversal of flow across a patent ductus arteriosus from pulmonary hypertension **(Correct)** — Correct. Eisenmenger physiology in an uncorrected PDA sends deoxygenated pulmonary artery blood into the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, causing cyanosis and clubbing of the lower extremities only.
   - **B.** Peripheral arterial disease of the legs — Wrong. Would not lower arterial oxygen saturation.
   - **C.** A large ventricular septal defect with right-to-left shunt — Wrong. Would cause cyanosis of both upper and lower extremities.
   - **D.** Transposition of the great arteries — Wrong. Presents in the newborn.
   - **E.** Tetralogy of Fallot — Wrong. Diffuse cyanosis.
   - **F.** Coarctation of the aorta proximal to the left subclavian artery — Wrong. Does not cause cyanosis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - never had medical care — Uncorrected congenital shunt.
     - his toes are cyanotic and clubbed — Differential cyanosis: lower body only.
     - 98% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot — Desaturated blood enters below the left subclavian artery.
     - no continuous murmur is present — The PDA murmur disappears when pulmonary and aortic pressures equalize.
   - **Reasoning:** Untreated PDA → years of L→R flow → pulmonary vascular remodeling → pulmonary hypertension → shunt reverses (Eisenmenger) → deoxygenated blood to lower body → cyanotic, clubbed toes with normal fingers.
   - **Teaching point:** PDA Eisenmenger = "blue toes, pink fingers."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains the differential cyanosis?
   - Page: 301

133. A newborn is cyanotic shortly after birth. His mother took a medication for bipolar disorder throughout pregnancy. Echocardiography shows apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets with atrialization of the right ventricle and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Ebstein anomaly
   - **A.** Carbamazepine — Wrong. Associated with neural tube defects and craniofacial anomalies.
   - **B.** Olanzapine — Wrong. Not associated.
   - **C.** Valproate — Wrong. Associated with neural tube defects.
   - **D.** Quetiapine — Wrong. Not the classic association.
   - **E.** Lamotrigine — Wrong. Not the classic association.
   - **F.** Lithium **(Correct)** — Correct. First-trimester lithium exposure is associated with Ebstein anomaly.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - a medication for bipolar disorder — Lithium is a classic mood stabilizer.
     - apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets — Ebstein anomaly.
     - atrialization of the right ventricle — Part of the RV functions as atrium.
   - **Reasoning:** Maternal mood stabilizer + newborn with downward-displaced tricuspid valve and severe TR → Ebstein anomaly → lithium.
   - **Teaching point:** "Lithium makes the tricuspid Lie low" (Ebstein).
   - **Follow-up:** Which medication did the mother most likely take?
   - Page: 300

134. A 2-day-old boy has cyanosis, a holosystolic murmur and a seizure. Serum calcium is 6.4 mg/dL. Chest radiography shows absence of the thymic shadow. Echocardiography shows a single large vessel arising from both ventricles above a ventricular septal defect.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Persistent truncus arteriosus and 22q11 deletion
   - **A.** Sinus venosus tissue — Wrong. Causes sinus venosus ASD.
   - **B.** Second heart field myocardium only — Wrong. Not the classic answer.
   - **C.** Cardiac jelly of the septum primum — Wrong. Causes ASD.
   - **D.** Neural crest cells **(Correct)** — Correct. 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome) impairs neural crest migration into the truncus and conotruncal ridges, causing persistent truncus arteriosus and other outflow defects, plus 3rd/4th pouch defects (thymic and parathyroid aplasia).
   - **E.** Paraxial mesoderm — Wrong. Forms somites.
   - **F.** Endocardial cushion mesenchyme — Wrong. Causes AV septal defects.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Serum calcium is 6.4 mg/dL — Hypocalcemia from parathyroid aplasia.
     - absence of the thymic shadow — Thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency).
     - a single large vessel arising from both ventricles — Persistent truncus arteriosus.
   - **Reasoning:** Neonatal hypocalcemia + absent thymus + conotruncal defect → 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) → failed neural crest migration → truncus arteriosus failed to divide.
   - **Teaching point:** CATCH-22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, 22q11.
   - **Follow-up:** Abnormal development of which cell population best explains this infant's cardiac defect?
   - Page: 284

135. A newborn girl has upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, a single palmar crease and hypotonia. A murmur is heard, and echocardiography shows a defect involving both the lower atrial septum and the upper ventricular septum with a common atrioventricular valve.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** AV septal defect in Down syndrome
   - **A.** Septum secundum — Wrong. Ostium secundum ASD or PFO.
   - **B.** Ductus arteriosus — Wrong. PDA.
   - **C.** Bulbus cordis only — Wrong. Not specific.
   - **D.** Aorticopulmonary septum — Wrong. Transposition or truncus.
   - **E.** Infundibular septum — Wrong. Tetralogy of Fallot.
   - **F.** Endocardial cushions **(Correct)** — Correct. Atrioventricular septal defects result from failed fusion of the endocardial cushions and are strongly associated with Down syndrome.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, a single palmar crease and hypotonia — Down syndrome.
     - both the lower atrial septum and the upper ventricular septum — The crux of the heart formed by the endocardial cushions.
     - a common atrioventricular valve — Complete AV septal defect.
   - **Reasoning:** Down syndrome phenotype + defect at the heart's crux with common AV valve → AV septal (endocardial cushion) defect.
   - **Teaching point:** Down syndrome "Cushions" the heart badly: endocardial cushion defects.
   - **Follow-up:** Failure of which embryologic structure most likely caused this cardiac defect?
   - Page: 285

136. A 72-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history and hypertension has a pulsatile, nontender epigastric mass. Ultrasonography shows a 5.8-cm infrarenal aortic dilation. He has no symptoms.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Abdominal aortic aneurysm
   - **A.** Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch — Wrong. Takayasu arteritis.
   - **B.** Transmural inflammation with matrix metalloproteinase degradation of elastin and collagen **(Correct)** — Correct. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are associated with atherosclerosis and smoking; inflammation and MMPs weaken the media.
   - **C.** Intimal tear with blood dissecting the media — Wrong. Aortic dissection.
   - **D.** Fibromuscular hyperplasia of the media — Wrong. Fibromuscular dysplasia.
   - **E.** Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum — Wrong. Syphilitic thoracic aortitis.
   - **F.** Cystic medial degeneration from fibrillin defects — Wrong. Typical of thoracic aortic disease in Marfan syndrome.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 50-pack-year smoking history — Smoking is the strongest risk factor for AAA.
     - pulsatile, nontender epigastric mass — AAA on examination.
     - infrarenal aortic dilation — Typical AAA location.
   - **Reasoning:** Elderly male smoker + pulsatile epigastric mass + infrarenal dilation → AAA → atherosclerosis-related inflammation, MMP activity → weakened media.
   - **Teaching point:** AAA = "Aging Arteries from Ash" (smoking); screen men 65–75 who ever smoked.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this lesion?
   - Page: 302

137. A pathologist examines the aorta of a 19-year-old man who died in a motor vehicle collision. He had no known medical problems. There are flat yellow streaks on the intimal surface that do not protrude into the lumen.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Atherosclerosis
   - **A.** Plasma cells producing antibodies — Wrong. Not the hallmark.
   - **B.** Platelet aggregates — Wrong. Form on disrupted plaques.
   - **C.** Smooth muscle cells forming a fibrous cap — Wrong. A later stage (fibrous plaque).
   - **D.** Neutrophils releasing elastase — Wrong. Not the characteristic early event.
   - **E.** Macrophages filled with oxidized LDL (foam cells) **(Correct)** — Correct. Fatty streaks, the earliest visible lesions of atherosclerosis, consist of lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) after endothelial dysfunction and LDL oxidation.
   - **F.** Calcium deposits — Wrong. Occur in advanced plaques.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 19-year-old — Fatty streaks begin in childhood and adolescence.
     - flat yellow streaks on the intimal surface — Fatty streaks.
     - do not protrude into the lumen — Early, nonobstructive lesion.
   - **Reasoning:** Endothelial injury → LDL enters and is oxidized → monocytes enter and become foam cells → fatty streak → later smooth muscle migration and fibrous cap.
   - **Teaching point:** Atherosclerosis order: "Endothelium hurt → Foam → Fibrous cap → Fracture (rupture)."
   - **Follow-up:** The earliest cellular event in the formation of these lesions is accumulation of which of the following in the intima?
   - Page: 303

138. A 36-year-old woman who smokes has had episodes of chest pain at 4 AM that wake her from sleep and last 10 minutes. During one episode, an ECG shows ST elevation in the inferior leads that resolves completely within minutes. Coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries. She also has migraines.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina
   - **A.** Amlodipine **(Correct)** — Correct. Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina is treated with calcium channel blockers (and nitrates); smoking cessation helps.
   - **B.** Clopidogrel — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **C.** Sumatriptan — Wrong. Triptans cause coronary vasospasm and should be avoided.
   - **D.** Aspirin alone — Wrong. Does not prevent vasospasm.
   - **E.** Ergotamine — Wrong. Ergots provoke vasospasm.
   - **F.** Propranolol — Wrong. Nonselective β-blockade leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen vasospasm.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chest pain at 4 AM that wake her from sleep — Resting, early-morning episodes typical of vasospasm.
     - ST elevation in the inferior leads that resolves completely within minutes — Transient transmural ischemia from spasm.
     - normal coronary arteries — No fixed stenosis.
     - She also has migraines — Avoid triptans, which worsen vasospasm.
   - **Reasoning:** Young smoker + nocturnal rest angina + transient ST elevation + normal coronaries → coronary vasospasm → CCBs and nitrates; avoid nonselective β-blockers and triptans.
   - **Teaching point:** Prinzmetal "Prefers Ca channel blockers"; triggers: smoking, cocaine, triptans.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is most appropriate to prevent these episodes?
   - Page: 306

139. A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with chest pain 1 hour after snorting cocaine. He is agitated and diaphoretic. Temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 128/min and blood pressure 176/108 mm Hg. Pupils are dilated. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST elevation. Aspirin is given.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Cocaine-associated chest pain
   - **A.** Succinylcholine — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **B.** Haloperidol — Wrong. Lowers seizure threshold and impairs heat dissipation.
   - **C.** Metoprolol — Wrong. β-blockers are avoided in acute cocaine toxicity because unopposed α-stimulation can worsen hypertension and vasospasm.
   - **D.** Physostigmine — Wrong. Treats anticholinergic toxicity.
   - **E.** Naloxone — Wrong. Reverses opioids, not cocaine.
   - **F.** Lorazepam **(Correct)** — Correct. Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate, blood pressure and agitation; nitrates and calcium channel blockers can be added.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 1 hour after snorting cocaine — Sympathomimetic toxicity.
     - agitated and diaphoretic — Central sympathetic stimulation.
     - Pupils are dilated — Sympathomimetic (vs anticholinergic, which is dry).
   - **Reasoning:** Cocaine → blocks catecholamine reuptake → tachycardia, hypertension, coronary vasospasm → benzodiazepines first, avoid β-blockers.
   - **Teaching point:** Cocaine chest pain: "Benzos Before Blockers (never β first)."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacotherapy?
   - Page: 306

140. A 66-year-old man is treated with a stent for an acute anterior myocardial infarction. Four days later he develops recurrent chest pain with new ST elevation. Cardiac troponin I remains elevated from the initial event.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Cardiac biomarkers
   - **A.** AST — Wrong. Nonspecific.
   - **B.** CK-MB **(Correct)** — Correct. CK-MB rises within hours and returns to normal in 48–72 hours, so a new rise after day 3 indicates reinfarction.
   - **C.** Lactate dehydrogenase — Wrong. Nonspecific and slow.
   - **D.** BNP — Wrong. Reflects ventricular stretch, not infarction.
   - **E.** Troponin I — Wrong. Stays elevated for 7–10 days, so it cannot easily distinguish a new event at day 4.
   - **F.** Myoglobin — Wrong. Very early and nonspecific.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Four days later — Reinfarction window after initial markers peak.
     - troponin I remains elevated from the initial event — Troponin stays high 7–10 days.
     - new ST elevation — Recurrent transmural ischemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Recurrent pain day 4 + troponin already high → need a marker that normalizes quickly → CK-MB re-rise means reinfarction.
   - **Teaching point:** "Troponin Tarries (7–10 days); CK-MB Comes and goes (2–3 days)."
   - **Follow-up:** Which serum marker is most useful to confirm a new (re-)infarction?
   - Page: 309

141. A 61-year-old man had a myocardial infarction 4 weeks ago. He now has fever, pleuritic chest pain that improves when he leans forward, and a three-component friction rub. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. ESR is elevated.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Dressler syndrome
   - **A.** Uremia — Wrong. No renal failure described.
   - **B.** Reinfarction — Wrong. Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression indicates pericarditis.
   - **C.** Ventricular free wall rupture — Wrong. Occurs 3–14 days after MI with tamponade.
   - **D.** Bacterial infection of the pericardium — Wrong. Would be more acute with purulence.
   - **E.** Autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens released by necrosis **(Correct)** — Correct. Dressler syndrome (postcardiac injury syndrome) is an autoimmune fibrinous pericarditis weeks after MI.
   - **F.** Ventricular aneurysm — Wrong. Causes persistent ST elevation, heart failure and thrombi, not fever with a rub.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 4 weeks ago — Dressler syndrome occurs weeks to months after MI.
     - improves when he leans forward — Pericarditis.
     - diffuse ST elevation with PR depression — Pericarditis ECG.
   - **Reasoning:** MI weeks ago → myocardial antigens exposed → autoimmune pericarditis (Dressler) → fever, positional pleuritic pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation → NSAIDs/colchicine.
   - **Teaching point:** Post-MI pericarditis: "early (days) = fibrinous over the infarct; late (weeks) = Dressler, the Delayed autoimmune one."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his current condition?
   - Page: 313

142. A 58-year-old man undergoes successful primary angioplasty 5 hours after the onset of an anterior myocardial infarction. He dies of a ventricular arrhythmia 12 hours later. Microscopic examination of the reperfused myocardium shows hypereosinophilic transverse bands across myocytes and areas of hemorrhage.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Reperfusion injury
   - **A.** Neutrophil-mediated liquefaction — Wrong. Not the explanation for bands.
   - **B.** Viral cytopathic effect — Wrong. Not related.
   - **C.** Amyloid deposition — Wrong. Not related.
   - **D.** Calcium influx after restoration of blood flow causing hypercontraction **(Correct)** — Correct. Reperfusion injury: Ca2+ influx and free radicals cause contraction band necrosis and hemorrhage.
   - **E.** Fibrosis from healing — Wrong. Takes weeks.
   - **F.** Lipofuscin accumulation — Wrong. A wear-and-tear pigment.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 5 hours after the onset — Late reperfusion of injured myocardium.
     - hypereosinophilic transverse bands across myocytes — Contraction bands.
     - areas of hemorrhage — Reperfusion damages microvessels.
   - **Reasoning:** Reperfusion of injured myocardium → Ca2+ influx and oxygen free radicals → hypercontraction → contraction band necrosis and hemorrhage.
   - **Teaching point:** "Reperfusion Restores blood, but brings Calcium and Radicals."
   - **Follow-up:** These findings are most directly caused by which of the following?
   - Page: 308

143. A 45-year-old man who grew up in a rural adobe house in Bolivia has palpitations, dyspnea and severe constipation. Examination shows an enlarged heart with an S3. Barium enema shows a markedly dilated colon, and barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus. ECG shows right bundle branch block.
   - **Domain:** Microbiology
   - **Topic:** Chagas disease
   - **A.** Trypanosoma cruzi **(Correct)** — Correct. Chagas disease, transmitted by the reduviid (kissing) bug, causes dilated cardiomyopathy and destruction of enteric neurons (megacolon, megaesophagus).
   - **B.** Trypanosoma brucei — Wrong. African sleeping sickness.
   - **C.** Toxoplasma gondii — Wrong. Causes encephalitis or chorioretinitis.
   - **D.** Clostridium botulinum — Wrong. Paralytic illness.
   - **E.** Coxsackie B virus — Wrong. Myocarditis without megacolon or megaesophagus.
   - **F.** Leishmania donovani — Wrong. Visceral leishmaniasis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - rural adobe house in Bolivia — Exposure to reduviid bugs living in cracks of mud walls.
     - dilated colon — Megacolon from enteric neuron destruction.
     - dilated esophagus — Megaesophagus (achalasia-like).
   - **Reasoning:** Latin American rural exposure + dilated cardiomyopathy + megacolon + megaesophagus → Chagas disease → Trypanosoma cruzi (treat with benznidazole or nifurtimox).
   - **Teaching point:** "Chagas: Cardiomegaly + Colon + Esophagus — the Kissing bug's 3 big organs."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
   - Page: 155

144. A 52-year-old woman with breast cancer completed chemotherapy 1 year ago. She now has progressive dyspnea, orthopnea and leg edema. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. She received a cumulative high dose of one agent.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Anthracycline cardiotoxicity
   - **A.** Filgrastim — Wrong. Treats neutropenia.
   - **B.** Amifostine — Wrong. Protects kidneys from cisplatin.
   - **C.** Dexrazoxane **(Correct)** — Correct. Anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity is dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy from free radicals; dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, reduces it.
   - **D.** Trastuzumab — Wrong. Itself causes reversible cardiotoxicity.
   - **E.** Leucovorin — Wrong. Rescues normal cells from methotrexate.
   - **F.** Mesna — Wrong. Prevents cyclophosphamide hemorrhagic cystitis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - breast cancer — Anthracyclines are part of many breast cancer regimens.
     - ejection fraction of 30% — Dilated cardiomyopathy.
     - cumulative high dose of one agent — Anthracycline toxicity is cumulative dose-related.
   - **Reasoning:** Breast cancer chemotherapy → high cumulative doxorubicin → free radical myocyte injury → irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy → prevent with dexrazoxane.
   - **Teaching point:** "DOXorubicin breaks the heart; DEXrazoxane DEfends it."
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug could have been given with the chemotherapy to reduce this complication?
   - Page: 447

145. A 48-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder has dyspnea, leg edema and warm extremities. Pulse is 112/min and blood pressure 128/52 mm Hg. He has bounding pulses, an S3 and bilateral crackles. He also has numbness of the feet. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a high cardiac output.
   - **Domain:** Biochemistry
   - **Topic:** Wet beriberi
   - **A.** Niacin (vitamin B3) — Wrong. Pellagra.
   - **B.** Vitamin B12 — Wrong. Causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy but not high-output heart failure.
   - **C.** Folate — Wrong. Megaloblastic anemia.
   - **D.** Vitamin C — Wrong. Scurvy.
   - **E.** Thiamine (vitamin B1) **(Correct)** — Correct. Wet beriberi causes high-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation, plus peripheral neuropathy (dry beriberi).
   - **F.** Vitamin D — Wrong. Osteomalacia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - long-standing alcohol use disorder — Main risk factor for thiamine deficiency in high-income settings.
     - warm extremities — Peripheral vasodilation.
     - 128/52 mm Hg — Wide pulse pressure from low SVR.
     - high cardiac output — High-output heart failure.
   - **Reasoning:** Alcohol → thiamine deficiency → impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase → vasodilation and high-output failure (wet) + neuropathy (dry) → give thiamine.
   - **Teaching point:** Beriberi = "Ber1 Ber1": vitamin B1; wet = "Wet heart."
   - **Follow-up:** Deficiency of which vitamin best explains his heart failure?
   - Page: 64

146. A 62-year-old man has dyspnea and a decrescendo diastolic murmur. Chest radiography shows a calcified, dilated ascending aorta. He had a painless genital ulcer decades ago that was never treated. He also has a positive Romberg sign and pupils that accommodate but do not react to light.
   - **Domain:** Microbiology
   - **Topic:** Syphilitic aortitis
   - **A.** The elastic lamellae from fibrillin defects — Wrong. Marfan syndrome.
   - **B.** The aortic intima with plaque formation — Wrong. Atherosclerosis affects mostly the abdominal aorta.
   - **C.** The aortic valve leaflets from vegetations — Wrong. Endocarditis.
   - **D.** The vasa vasorum of the aorta **(Correct)** — Correct. Tertiary syphilis causes endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum, leading to medial ischemia, "tree bark" aortic wall, ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic regurgitation.
   - **E.** The adventitia from granulomas in the aortic arch branches — Wrong. Takayasu arteritis.
   - **F.** The coronary ostia only — Wrong. Can be involved but are not the primary lesion.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - calcified, dilated ascending aorta — Syphilitic aortitis affects the ascending aorta and arch.
     - painless genital ulcer decades ago that was never treated — Untreated primary syphilis (chancre).
     - positive Romberg sign — Tabes dorsalis.
     - accommodate but do not react to light — Argyll Robertson pupils.
   - **Reasoning:** Untreated syphilis → tertiary stage → endarteritis of vasa vasorum → aortic media ischemia → ascending aortic aneurysm with tree-bark wall → aortic regurgitation; plus tabes and Argyll Robertson pupils.
   - **Teaching point:** Tertiary syphilis "hits the Big Vessels via the small vessels (vasa vasorum)."
   - **Follow-up:** The aortic disease is primarily caused by inflammation of which structure?
   - Page: 319

147. A 25-year-old woman has had fatigue, low-grade fever, night sweats and pain in her left arm when combing her hair for 3 months. The left radial pulse is barely palpable, and blood pressure is 88/60 mm Hg in the left arm and 130/80 mm Hg in the right arm. A bruit is heard over the left subclavian artery. ESR is 70 mm/h.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Takayasu arteritis
   - **A.** Atherosclerotic subclavian stenosis — Wrong. Unlikely at 25 with constitutional symptoms.
   - **B.** Granulomatous inflammation of temporal artery branches in the elderly — Wrong. Giant cell arteritis affects people over 50.
   - **C.** Necrotizing vasculitis of medium arteries associated with hepatitis B — Wrong. Polyarteritis nodosa.
   - **D.** Segmental thrombosing vasculitis of small and medium arteries in a smoker — Wrong. Buerger disease.
   - **E.** IgA immune complex small-vessel vasculitis — Wrong. IgA vasculitis.
   - **F.** Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch and its major branches in a young woman **(Correct)** — Correct. Takayasu arteritis ("pulseless disease") is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis, typically in women under 40.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - fever, night sweats — Constitutional symptoms of vasculitis.
     - pain in her left arm when combing her hair — Arm claudication.
     - 88/60 mm Hg in the left arm and 130/80 mm Hg in the right arm — Asymmetric arm pressures from subclavian stenosis.
     - ESR is 70 mm/h — Active inflammation.
   - **Reasoning:** Young woman + constitutional symptoms + arm claudication + weak pulse + BP difference + bruit → Takayasu arteritis (granulomatous aortic arch vasculitis) → glucocorticoids.
   - **Teaching point:** Takayasu = "Takes away pulses" in young women; giant cell arteritis in the elderly.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best describes this condition?
   - Page: 478

148. A 34-year-old man who smokes two packs of cigarettes daily has painful ulcers on the tips of several fingers and toes and pain in his calves when walking. He has had recurrent tender cordlike nodules along superficial veins of his legs. Angiography shows segmental occlusions of small and medium arteries with corkscrew collaterals.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Thromboangiitis obliterans
   - **A.** Warfarin — Wrong. Not the main therapy.
   - **B.** Complete smoking cessation **(Correct)** — Correct. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is strongly linked to tobacco; stopping smoking is the only proven way to halt progression and avoid amputation.
   - **C.** Plasmapheresis — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **D.** Antibiotics — Wrong. Not infectious.
   - **E.** High-dose glucocorticoids — Wrong. Not effective.
   - **F.** Cyclophosphamide — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - smokes two packs of cigarettes daily — Heavy tobacco exposure.
     - painful ulcers on the tips of several fingers and toes — Distal ischemia.
     - tender cordlike nodules along superficial veins — Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis.
     - corkscrew collaterals — Classic angiographic finding.
   - **Reasoning:** Young heavy smoker + digital ischemia + claudication + superficial thrombophlebitis + segmental occlusions → Buerger disease → smoking cessation.
   - **Teaching point:** Buerger = "Burning tobacco"; quit or lose digits.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most important treatment?
   - Page: 478

149. A 46-year-old man has chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge, hemoptysis and cola-colored urine. Chest CT shows multiple cavitating nodules. Urinalysis shows red cell casts. A nasal biopsy shows necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
   - **A.** Proteinase 3 **(Correct)** — Correct. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) is associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3).
   - **B.** Histones — Wrong. Drug-induced lupus.
   - **C.** Glomerular basement membrane type IV collagen — Wrong. Goodpasture syndrome (no granulomas, no sinus disease).
   - **D.** Myeloperoxidase — Wrong. MPO-ANCA is associated with microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
   - **E.** Centromere — Wrong. Limited scleroderma.
   - **F.** Double-stranded DNA — Wrong. Lupus.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge — Upper respiratory tract involvement.
     - multiple cavitating nodules — Lung involvement.
     - red cell casts — Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
     - necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis — Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
   - **Reasoning:** Upper airway + lung + kidney involvement with necrotizing granulomas → granulomatosis with polyangiitis → c-ANCA (PR3).
   - **Teaching point:** GPA hits "ELK": Ears/nose/throat, Lungs, Kidneys; "c-ANCA = Cytoplasmic = PR3."
   - **Follow-up:** The autoantibody most specific for this disease targets which antigen?
   - Page: 478

150. A 54-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B has fever, weight loss, abdominal pain after meals, new hypertension and painful foot drop. Labs show elevated creatinine; urinalysis has no red cell casts. Chest radiography is normal. Mesenteric angiography shows multiple microaneurysms.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Polyarteritis nodosa
   - **A.** Onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis — Wrong. Malignant hypertension.
   - **B.** Granulomas with giant cells in the aortic arch — Wrong. Takayasu.
   - **C.** Transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium arteries with lesions of different ages **(Correct)** — Correct. Polyarteritis nodosa, associated with hepatitis B, causes segmental transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium arteries (sparing the lungs), with microaneurysms.
   - **D.** Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits — Wrong. IgA vasculitis.
   - **E.** Eosinophil-rich granulomas — Wrong. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
   - **F.** Cholesterol emboli — Wrong. Atheroembolic disease.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chronic hepatitis B — HBV-associated immune complex vasculitis.
     - abdominal pain after meals — Mesenteric ischemia.
     - painful foot drop — Mononeuritis multiplex.
     - Chest radiography is normal — PAN spares the lungs.
     - multiple microaneurysms — "String of pearls" on angiography.
   - **Reasoning:** HBV + constitutional symptoms + renal, GI and nerve ischemia + spared lungs + microaneurysms → polyarteritis nodosa → transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium arteries.
   - **Teaching point:** PAN: "Pearls (aneurysms), No lungs, Hep B."
   - **Follow-up:** Biopsy of an affected artery would most likely show which of the following?
   - Page: 478

151. A 6-year-old boy has a raised, nonblanching rash on his buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain and painful knees. Two weeks ago he had an upper respiratory infection. Platelet count is normal. Urinalysis shows hematuria.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** IgA vasculitis
   - **A.** Medium-vessel vasculitis with coronary aneurysms — Wrong. Kawasaki disease.
   - **B.** Bacterial infection of the joints — Wrong. Septic arthritis.
   - **C.** Antibodies against platelet glycoproteins — Wrong. Immune thrombocytopenia (platelets would be low).
   - **D.** Deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in small vessels **(Correct)** — Correct. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) causes palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and IgA nephropathy-like glomerulonephritis, often after a URI.
   - **E.** Shiga toxin–mediated endothelial injury — Wrong. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (thrombocytopenia).
   - **F.** Deficiency of ADAMTS13 — Wrong. TTP (thrombocytopenia).
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - raised, nonblanching rash on his buttocks and legs — Palpable purpura.
     - colicky abdominal pain — GI vasculitis (risk of intussusception).
     - Platelet count is normal — Purpura is from vasculitis, not thrombocytopenia.
     - hematuria — Renal involvement.
   - **Reasoning:** Child + recent URI + palpable purpura with normal platelets + arthralgia + abdominal pain + hematuria → IgA vasculitis (IgA immune complexes).
   - **Teaching point:** HSP's tetrad: "Purpura, Pain in belly, Polyarthralgia, Pee with blood."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis?
   - Page: 479

152. A 38-year-old woman has episodes in which her fingers turn white, then blue, then red when exposed to cold. She also has tightening skin on her fingers, heartburn and small dilated vessels on her face. Anti-centromere antibodies are positive.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Raynaud phenomenon
   - **A.** Verapamil — Wrong. Non-dihydropyridine; less vascular selective.
   - **B.** Pseudoephedrine — Wrong. A vasoconstrictor.
   - **C.** Methotrexate — Wrong. Not for Raynaud.
   - **D.** Propranolol — Wrong. β-blockers can worsen vasospasm.
   - **E.** Sumatriptan — Wrong. Causes vasoconstriction.
   - **F.** Nifedipine **(Correct)** — Correct. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are first-line for Raynaud phenomenon, here secondary to limited scleroderma (CREST).
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - white, then blue, then red — Triphasic color change of Raynaud phenomenon.
     - tightening skin on her fingers — Sclerodactyly.
     - small dilated vessels on her face — Telangiectasias.
     - Anti-centromere antibodies are positive — Limited scleroderma (CREST).
   - **Reasoning:** Cold-induced triphasic color change + sclerodactyly + esophageal dysmotility + telangiectasia + anti-centromere → CREST with secondary Raynaud → dihydropyridine CCB.
   - **Teaching point:** CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is the first-line treatment for her color changes?
   - Page: 480

153. A 64-year-old man with hypertension started a new antihypertensive drug 2 months ago. He now has an acutely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Serum calcium is 10.7 mg/dL and serum glucose is mildly elevated compared with prior values.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Thiazide adverse effects
   - **A.** Lisinopril — Wrong. ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalemia and cough, not gout.
   - **B.** Losartan — Wrong. Losartan modestly lowers uric acid.
   - **C.** Hydrochlorothiazide **(Correct)** — Correct. Thiazides cause hyperuricemia (gout), hypercalcemia and hyperglycemia, along with hypokalemia and hyponatremia ("hyperGLUC").
   - **D.** Spironolactone — Wrong. Hyperkalemia, gynecomastia.
   - **E.** Hydralazine — Wrong. Drug-induced lupus, reflex tachycardia.
   - **F.** Amlodipine — Wrong. Peripheral edema.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - acutely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint — Podagra (gout).
     - calcium is 10.7 mg/dL — Thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption.
     - glucose is mildly elevated — Thiazide hyperglycemia.
   - **Reasoning:** New antihypertensive + gout + hypercalcemia + hyperglycemia → thiazide → "hyperGLUC" (Glycemia, Lipidemia, Uricemia, Calcemia).
   - **Teaching point:** Thiazides make you "hyperGLUC."
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug was most likely started?
   - Page: 321

154. A 70-year-old woman with hypertension started a new medication 6 weeks ago. Her blood pressure is now controlled, but she has bilateral ankle swelling that does not improve with furosemide. Serum albumin, liver tests and echocardiography are normal.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Calcium channel blocker edema
   - **A.** Metoprolol; reduced cardiac output — Wrong. Not the mechanism with normal echo.
   - **B.** Amlodipine; preferential arteriolar dilation raising capillary hydrostatic pressure **(Correct)** — Correct. Dihydropyridine CCBs dilate precapillary arterioles more than venules, raising capillary pressure; diuretics do not help, but adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB can.
   - **C.** Clonidine; increased aldosterone — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **D.** Hydrochlorothiazide; sodium retention — Wrong. Thiazides cause sodium loss.
   - **E.** Pioglitazone; heart failure — Wrong. Not an antihypertensive here and echo is normal.
   - **F.** Lisinopril; bradykinin-mediated capillary leak — Wrong. ACE inhibitors cause angioedema, not dependent edema.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - started a new medication 6 weeks ago — Drug-related timing.
     - does not improve with furosemide — Not due to volume overload.
     - echocardiography are normal — Not heart failure.
   - **Reasoning:** Antihypertensive + ankle edema resistant to diuretics + normal heart, liver, albumin → dihydropyridine CCB → arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure.
   - **Teaching point:** "Amlodipine: Ankles get big."
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug most likely caused her edema, and by what mechanism?
   - Page: 323

155. A 58-year-old man with resistant hypertension takes several medications, including one that stimulates central α2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow. He runs out of his pills while traveling. Two days later he has headache, tremor, sweating, anxiety and a blood pressure of 210/120 mm Hg.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Clonidine rebound hypertension
   - **A.** Hydrochlorothiazide — Wrong. No rebound syndrome.
   - **B.** Lisinopril — Wrong. No rebound syndrome.
   - **C.** Losartan — Wrong. No rebound.
   - **D.** Amlodipine — Wrong. No significant rebound.
   - **E.** Clonidine **(Correct)** — Correct. Sudden discontinuation causes rebound hypertension and sympathetic overactivity.
   - **F.** Minoxidil — Wrong. Causes hypertrichosis and reflex tachycardia, not rebound.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - stimulates central α2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow — Clonidine mechanism.
     - He runs out of his pills — Abrupt discontinuation.
     - headache, tremor, sweating, anxiety — Sympathetic surge.
   - **Reasoning:** Central α2-agonist stopped abruptly → loss of inhibition → catecholamine surge → rebound hypertensive crisis.
   - **Teaching point:** "Clonidine: Can't stop suddenly."
   - **Follow-up:** Abrupt withdrawal of which drug best explains this?
   - Page: 243

156. A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is switched from an ACE inhibitor to a combination tablet containing an angiotensin receptor blocker and a second drug. His physician tells him to wait 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose before starting it.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Sacubitril-valsartan
   - **A.** Increases natriuretic peptides by inhibiting neprilysin; washout prevents angioedema from combined bradykinin buildup **(Correct)** — Correct. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which degrades ANP, BNP and bradykinin; combining it with an ACE inhibitor greatly raises angioedema risk.
   - **B.** Increases potassium excretion; washout prevents hypokalemia — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **C.** Increases bradykinin by blocking ACE; washout prevents hypotension — Wrong. The second drug is not an ACE inhibitor.
   - **D.** Increases cGMP by inhibiting PDE5; washout prevents priapism — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **E.** Increases aldosterone by blocking renin; washout prevents hyperkalemia — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **F.** Increases cAMP by inhibiting PDE3; washout prevents arrhythmia — Wrong. That is milrinone.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — ARNI improves survival in HFrEF.
     - combination tablet containing an angiotensin receptor blocker and a second drug — Sacubitril-valsartan.
     - wait 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose — Avoid overlap of ACE and neprilysin inhibition.
   - **Reasoning:** Sacubitril blocks neprilysin → ↑ natriuretic peptides (vasodilation, natriuresis) and ↑ bradykinin → with an ACE inhibitor, bradykinin accumulates → angioedema → 36-hour washout.
   - **Teaching point:** "Neprilysin Nibbles natriuretic peptides"; block it and they stay.
   - **Follow-up:** The second drug increases which substances, and why is the washout needed?
   - Page: 324

157. A 64-year-old man with heart failure (ejection fraction 30%) is in sinus rhythm with a resting heart rate of 82/min despite the maximal tolerated dose of a β-blocker. A drug is added that lowers his heart rate without changing blood pressure or contractility. A month later he reports seeing brief flashes of bright light in dim settings.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Ivabradine
   - **A.** L-type Ca2+ channels in the myocardium — Wrong. Would reduce contractility.
   - **B.** Late Na+ current — Wrong. Ranolazine.
   - **C.** The funny current (If) in the SA node **(Correct)** — Correct. Ivabradine blocks HCN channels, slowing phase 4 depolarization in SA nodal cells; luminous phenomena (phosphenes) result from similar channels in the retina.
   - **D.** β1-adrenergic receptors — Wrong. He is already on a maximal β-blocker.
   - **E.** Na+/K+-ATPase — Wrong. Digoxin.
   - **F.** Muscarinic M2 receptors — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - in sinus rhythm — Ivabradine only works in sinus rhythm.
     - lowers his heart rate without changing blood pressure or contractility — Pure SA node rate reduction.
     - brief flashes of bright light in dim settings — Phosphenes (luminous phenomena).
   - **Reasoning:** HFrEF + high resting rate despite β-blocker + pure rate slowing + phosphenes → ivabradine → blocks If (HCN) in the SA node.
   - **Teaching point:** "IVabradine slows the If" — and makes you see stars.
   - **Follow-up:** The added drug acts on which target?
   - Page: 328

158. A 63-year-old man with stable angina uses sublingual nitroglycerin. He takes a medication he did not mention for erectile dysfunction and, 4 hours later, uses nitroglycerin for chest pain. He becomes dizzy and his blood pressure falls to 70/40 mm Hg.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors
   - **A.** Both drugs block L-type Ca2+ channels — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **B.** Both drugs increase cAMP in vascular smooth muscle — Wrong. The pathway is cGMP.
   - **C.** The erectile drug causes bradycardia — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **D.** Nitroglycerin causes methemoglobinemia — Wrong. Not this picture.
   - **E.** Both drugs block α1 receptors — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **F.** Nitrates raise cGMP via NO while the other drug blocks cGMP breakdown, causing excessive vasodilation **(Correct)** — Correct. PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) potentiate nitrate-induced cGMP accumulation; the combination is contraindicated.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - a medication he did not mention for erectile dysfunction — PDE5 inhibitor.
     - 4 hours later — Within the interaction window.
     - blood pressure falls to 70/40 mm Hg — Severe hypotension.
   - **Reasoning:** Nitrate → NO → guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP; PDE5 inhibitor → ↓ cGMP breakdown → massive vasodilation → hypotension.
   - **Teaching point:** "Nitrates + 'nafils' = never" (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil).
   - **Follow-up:** Which mechanism explains the severe hypotension?
   - Page: 322

159. A 52-year-old man under spinal anesthesia becomes hypotensive (82/50 mm Hg) with a heart rate of 88/min. An intravenous drug is given. Within a minute, blood pressure rises to 128/80 mm Hg, and his heart rate falls to 58/min.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** α1-agonists and the baroreceptor reflex
   - **A.** Dopamine at a low dose — Wrong. Renal vasodilation; does not cause reflex bradycardia.
   - **B.** Isoproterenol — Wrong. A β-agonist that increases heart rate and can lower blood pressure.
   - **C.** Atropine — Wrong. Increases heart rate.
   - **D.** Phenylephrine **(Correct)** — Correct. A pure α1-agonist raises SVR and blood pressure; baroreceptors respond with a reflex fall in heart rate.
   - **E.** Dobutamine — Wrong. Increases heart rate and contractility.
   - **F.** Epinephrine at a high dose — Wrong. Raises both blood pressure and heart rate.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - under spinal anesthesia — Sympathectomy-related vasodilation.
     - blood pressure rises to 128/80 mm Hg — Vasoconstriction.
     - heart rate falls to 58/min — Reflex bradycardia via the baroreceptor reflex.
   - **Reasoning:** Pure α1-agonist → ↑ SVR → ↑ BP → baroreceptors fire more → ↑ vagal tone → reflex bradycardia.
   - **Teaching point:** "Phenylephrine Pushes pressure up, Pulls rate down."
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug was most likely given?
   - Page: 241

160. A 74-year-old man has exertional dyspnea. ECG shows a wide QRS complex (160 ms) with a broad, notched R wave in leads I and V6. On auscultation, the two components of S2 are heard more distinctly during expiration and merge into a single sound during inspiration.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Splitting of S2
   - **A.** Delayed closure of the aortic valve from left bundle branch block **(Correct)** — Correct. Late LV activation delays A2 so that P2 comes first; inspiration delays P2 toward A2, narrowing the split (paradoxical splitting). Aortic stenosis can do the same.
   - **B.** Pulmonary hypertension with a loud P2 — Wrong. Causes a loud P2 but not paradoxical splitting.
   - **C.** Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve from right bundle branch block — Wrong. RBBB causes wide splitting that widens further with inspiration.
   - **D.** Early closure of the aortic valve from mitral regurgitation — Wrong. Widens the normal split.
   - **E.** Equal right and left atrial pressures from an atrial septal defect — Wrong. Causes fixed splitting.
   - **F.** Normal physiologic splitting — Wrong. Normally the split widens with inspiration.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - broad, notched R wave in leads I and V6 — Left bundle branch block.
     - heard more distinctly during expiration — The split is widest in expiration: reversed from normal.
     - merge into a single sound during inspiration — Inspiratory delay of P2 closes the reversed gap.
   - **Reasoning:** LBBB → delayed LV contraction → A2 after P2 → inspiration delays P2 toward A2 → split narrows on inspiration (paradoxical).
   - **Teaching point:** "Paradoxical = Problems on the left (LBBB, aortic stenosis); Wide = Right bundle; Fixed = atrial hole."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains this pattern of S2 splitting?
   - Page: 293

## Endocrine 1

Source: `mock-endocrine-1.json`

161. A 58-year-old woman has had two kidney stones in a year, constipation, fatigue and low mood. She takes no supplements or diuretics. Serum phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase is mildly elevated and creatinine is normal. 24-hour urine calcium is high. Her serum calcium and intact PTH are plotted on the nomogram shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Primary hyperparathyroidism
   - **A.** Milk-alkali syndrome — Wrong. PTH suppressed, alkalosis, renal failure.
   - **B.** Squamous cell carcinoma secreting PTHrP — Wrong. Intact PTH would be suppressed.
   - **C.** Vitamin D intoxication — Wrong. PTH would be suppressed.
   - **D.** Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia — Wrong. Urine calcium would be low.
   - **E.** Parathyroid adenoma **(Correct)** — Correct. High calcium with inappropriately high PTH, low phosphate and hypercalciuria is primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single adenoma.
   - **F.** Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease — Wrong. Calcium would be low or normal, phosphate high, creatinine abnormal.
   - **G.** Sarcoidosis — Wrong. Calcitriol-mediated, PTH suppressed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - two kidney stones in a year, constipation, fatigue and low mood — Stones, groans and psychiatric overtones.
     - She takes no supplements or diuretics — Excludes calcium/vitamin D excess and thiazides.
     - Serum phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL — PTH causes renal phosphate wasting.
     - 24-hour urine calcium is high — Distinguishes from FHH.
   - **Reasoning:** Hypercalcemia + high PTH (plot) + low phosphate + hypercalciuria + normal kidneys → primary hyperparathyroidism → adenoma.
   - **Teaching point:** High Ca with a "not-low" PTH = parathyroid problem; high Ca with low PTH = everything else.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?

162. A 36-year-old man has had polyuria (8 L/day) and intense thirst since undergoing transsphenoidal resection of a craniopharyngioma 1 week ago. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L. A supervised water deprivation test is performed; the results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Central diabetes insipidus
   - **A.** Hydrochlorothiazide — Wrong. Used for nephrogenic DI.
   - **B.** Water restriction — Wrong. Treats primary polydipsia; dangerous here.
   - **C.** Desmopressin **(Correct)** — Correct. Failure to concentrate urine with deprivation but a >50% rise after desmopressin indicates central DI; replace ADH with desmopressin.
   - **D.** Tolvaptan — Wrong. An ADH antagonist for SIADH.
   - **E.** Lithium — Wrong. Causes nephrogenic DI.
   - **F.** Demeclocycline — Wrong. Used for SIADH.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - transsphenoidal resection of a craniopharyngioma — Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary.
     - Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L — Free water loss.
     - polyuria (8 L/day) and intense thirst — Large-volume dilute urine.
   - **Reasoning:** Pituitary surgery + polyuria + hypernatremia + no rise in urine osmolality with deprivation + large rise after desmopressin → central DI → desmopressin.
   - **Teaching point:** Desmopressin "Delivers" in central DI; in nephrogenic DI it "Doesn't."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

163. A 59-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history has rapidly progressive weakness, edema, hypertension and darkening of his skin over 2 months. Serum K+ is 2.6 mEq/L and glucose is 260 mg/dL. He has no striae or central obesity. Endocrine test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Ectopic ACTH syndrome
   - **A.** Measure plasma metanephrines — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **B.** CT of the chest **(Correct)** — Correct. ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome that does not suppress and does not respond to CRH suggests ectopic ACTH, classically small cell lung cancer in a smoker.
   - **C.** CT of the adrenal glands — Wrong. ACTH is high, so the source is not adrenal.
   - **D.** MRI of the pituitary — Wrong. A pituitary source would usually suppress with high-dose dexamethasone and respond to CRH.
   - **E.** Start prednisone — Wrong. He already has cortisol excess.
   - **F.** Bilateral adrenalectomy immediately — Wrong. Find the source first.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 45-pack-year smoking history — Risk factor for small cell lung cancer.
     - rapidly progressive weakness, edema, hypertension and darkening of his skin — Very high ACTH and cortisol develop quickly; MSH-like pigmentation.
     - K+ is 2.6 mEq/L — Massive cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors.
     - He has no striae or central obesity — Too rapid for classic Cushingoid features.
   - **Reasoning:** Smoker + rapid hypercortisolism with hypokalemia and pigmentation + very high ACTH + no suppression, no CRH response → ectopic ACTH → small cell lung cancer → CT chest.
   - **Teaching point:** High ACTH: "pituitary listens (suppresses with high-dose dex, responds to CRH), ectopic ignores."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

164. A 26-year-old nurse has had palpitations, heat intolerance and a 7-kg weight loss for 2 months. Pulse is 112/min. The thyroid is not enlarged or tender. There is no exophthalmos. Her test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Exogenous thyrotoxicosis
   - **A.** Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis — Wrong. Painful gland, high ESR and high thyroglobulin.
   - **B.** Painless (silent) thyroiditis — Wrong. Low uptake, but thyroglobulin is high from gland destruction.
   - **C.** Toxic multinodular goiter — Wrong. Nodular gland with patchy high uptake.
   - **D.** Graves disease — Wrong. RAIU would be high and diffuse.
   - **E.** Struma ovarii — Wrong. Low neck uptake but thyroglobulin is not suppressed.
   - **F.** Surreptitious intake of levothyroxine **(Correct)** — Correct. Thyrotoxicosis with low iodine uptake and low thyroglobulin means hormone is coming from outside the gland; the gland is suppressed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 26-year-old nurse — Health worker with access to medications.
     - The thyroid is not enlarged or tender — Not Graves goiter or painful thyroiditis.
     - 7-kg weight loss — Possible motive (weight loss).
   - **Reasoning:** Thyrotoxicosis + low RAIU (gland not making hormone) + low thyroglobulin (gland not releasing stored hormone) → exogenous thyroid hormone.
   - **Teaching point:** Low uptake + low thyroglobulin = "Took it" (pills); low uptake + high thyroglobulin = "Torn" gland (thyroiditis).
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely cause?

165. A 24-year-old woman is evaluated after her father and aunt developed thyroid cancer. Her family pedigree is shown (she is the arrow, III-2; shaded symbols indicate medullary thyroid carcinoma; the aunt II-4 also had episodic hypertension from an adrenal tumor). Her serum calcitonin is mildly elevated.
   - **Domain:** Genetics
   - **Topic:** MEN2 and medullary thyroid carcinoma
   - **A.** RET; prophylactic total thyroidectomy **(Correct)** — Correct. Autosomal dominant medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma is MEN2 (RET proto-oncogene); carriers need prophylactic thyroidectomy.
   - **B.** BRAF; radioactive iodine — Wrong. Somatic mutation in papillary carcinoma.
   - **C.** APC; colectomy — Wrong. Familial adenomatous polyposis.
   - **D.** NF1; observation — Wrong. Not associated with medullary carcinoma.
   - **E.** MEN1; parathyroidectomy — Wrong. MEN1 does not include medullary thyroid carcinoma.
   - **F.** VHL; annual renal MRI only — Wrong. VHL causes pheochromocytoma but not medullary carcinoma.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - father and aunt developed thyroid cancer — Familial thyroid cancer across generations.
     - episodic hypertension from an adrenal tumor — Pheochromocytoma.
     - serum calcitonin is mildly elevated — C-cell hyperplasia or early medullary carcinoma.
   - **Reasoning:** Vertical transmission (autosomal dominant) of medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma → MEN2 → RET mutation → prophylactic thyroidectomy.
   - **Teaching point:** "RET = REmove Thyroid."

166. A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes injects insulin twice daily. He wakes at 3 AM sweating and shaky several times a week; fingerstick glucose is 48 mg/dL at those times. His morning glucose is then 240 mg/dL. Plasma insulin profiles after a subcutaneous dose of three preparations are shown; he takes curve 2 at 10 PM.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Insulin preparations
   - **A.** Glargine — Wrong. Long acting with a flat profile (curve 3).
   - **B.** Degludec — Wrong. Very long acting, flat.
   - **C.** Regular — Wrong. Short acting: peaks at 2–4 hours.
   - **D.** NPH **(Correct)** — Correct. Intermediate-acting NPH peaks about 4–10 hours after injection; a bedtime dose peaks around 2–4 AM, causing nocturnal hypoglycemia (and rebound morning hyperglycemia, the Somogyi effect).
   - **E.** Detemir — Wrong. Long acting.
   - **F.** Lispro — Wrong. Rapid acting (curve 1): peaks within 1 hour.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - wakes at 3 AM sweating and shaky — Nocturnal hypoglycemia.
     - morning glucose is then 240 mg/dL — Rebound hyperglycemia after hypoglycemia (Somogyi effect).
     - he takes curve 2 at 10 PM — A peak 4–6 hours after bedtime.
   - **Reasoning:** Bedtime intermediate insulin peaking at 4–6 h → 2–4 AM hypoglycemia → counter-regulatory rebound → high fasting glucose → curve 2 is NPH (fix: move NPH earlier or switch to glargine).
   - **Teaching point:** Insulin "speeds": Lispro = sprint (1 h), Regular = jog, NPH = hill (peak 6 h), Glargine = flat road.
   - **Follow-up:** Which insulin does curve 2 represent?

167. In a physiology experiment, healthy volunteers receive glucose either orally or as an intravenous infusion adjusted so that plasma glucose concentrations are identical in both conditions. Plasma insulin responses are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Incretin effect
   - **A.** Metformin — Wrong. Reduces hepatic glucose output.
   - **B.** Acarbose — Wrong. Slows carbohydrate absorption.
   - **C.** Glipizide — Wrong. Acts directly on β-cell K+ channels regardless of route.
   - **D.** Pioglitazone — Wrong. Increases insulin sensitivity.
   - **E.** Liraglutide **(Correct)** — Correct. The incretin effect: gut hormones (GLP-1 from L cells, GIP from K cells) amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion after oral intake; GLP-1 agonists mimic it.
   - **F.** Canagliflozin — Wrong. Causes glucosuria.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - plasma glucose concentrations are identical in both conditions — Isolates the effect of the route of glucose delivery.
     - either orally or as an intravenous infusion — Only oral glucose triggers gut hormone release.
     - healthy volunteers — Normal β cells, so the difference reflects physiology, not disease.
   - **Reasoning:** Same plasma glucose, more insulin after oral intake → gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) potentiate β-cell response → GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors exploit this.
   - **Teaching point:** "Incretins = INtestine inCREases INsulin."
   - **Follow-up:** The difference between the curves is mainly due to hormones that are mimicked or prolonged by which drug?

168. A 9-day-old infant with ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds) is brought in with vomiting and lethargy. Blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. Her laboratory results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
   - **A.** Aromatase — Wrong. Virilization without adrenal crisis.
   - **B.** 21-hydroxylase **(Correct)** — Correct. Salt-wasting CAH: ↓ aldosterone and cortisol (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, hypoglycemia), ↑ 17-hydroxyprogesterone, ↑ renin and androgen excess virilizing a 46,XX infant.
   - **C.** 11β-hydroxylase — Wrong. Causes hypertension with low renin.
   - **D.** 17α-hydroxylase — Wrong. Causes hypertension and lack of sex steroids (no virilization).
   - **E.** 5α-reductase — Wrong. Affects 46,XY genital development.
   - **F.** Cholesterol desmolase — Wrong. All steroids low; no virilization.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds) — Prenatal androgen excess in a 46,XX infant.
     - Blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg — Salt wasting.
     - vomiting and lethargy — Adrenal crisis in the second week of life.
   - **Reasoning:** Virilized XX + salt wasting + hyperkalemia + high 17-OHP + high renin → 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
   - **Teaching point:** "Ends in 1 (21, 11) virilizes; starts with 1 (17, 11) is hypertensive"; 21 is the salt waster.
   - **Follow-up:** Which enzyme is deficient?
