260. A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Colonoscopy shows only one other polyp. His father had colon cancer at 48 and his paternal aunt had endometrial cancer at 50. Tumor histology shows microsatellite instability.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Lynch syndrome
   - **A.** Nonhomologous end joining — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Homologous recombination — Wrong. BRCA.
   - **C.** DNA mismatch repair **(Correct)** — Correct. Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): autosomal dominant mismatch repair defect with microsatellite instability, right-sided colon cancer and endometrial and ovarian cancers.
   - **D.** Nucleotide excision repair — Wrong. Xeroderma pigmentosum.
   - **E.** Base excision repair — Wrong. Not the classic answer.
   - **F.** APC/β-catenin pathway — Wrong. FAP and sporadic tumors.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - ascending colon — Lynch tends to be proximal.
     - only one other polyp — Not a polyposis syndrome.
     - paternal aunt had endometrial cancer — Extracolonic Lynch cancers.
     - microsatellite instability — Mismatch repair defect.
   - **Reasoning:** Early, right-sided colon cancer + few polyps + family endometrial cancer + MSI → Lynch → mismatch repair defect.
   - **Teaching point:** Lynch "3-2-1" rule: 3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 under 50.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following processes is most likely defective?
   - Page: 395

261. A 15-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain. Examination shows dark brown macules on his lips, buccal mucosa and fingers. Endoscopy shows multiple polyps in the jejunum; biopsy shows branching smooth muscle with normal-appearing mucosa.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
   - **A.** Breast, pancreatic and gastrointestinal cancers **(Correct)** — Correct. Peutz-Jeghers: autosomal dominant (STK11), hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation, increased risk of breast, colorectal, gastric, small bowel and pancreatic cancers.
   - **B.** Osteomas and desmoid tumors — Wrong. Gardner syndrome.
   - **C.** Medulloblastoma — Wrong. Turcot syndrome.
   - **D.** Hepatoblastoma only — Wrong. FAP.
   - **E.** No increased cancer risk — Wrong. The risk is increased.
   - **F.** Endometrial cancer only — Wrong. Lynch.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - dark brown macules on his lips, buccal mucosa and fingers — Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation.
     - recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain — Intussusception from polyps.
     - branching smooth muscle — Hamartomatous polyp.
   - **Reasoning:** Mucocutaneous pigmentation + hamartomatous small bowel polyps → Peutz-Jeghers → cancer risk.
   - **Teaching point:** Peutz-Jeghers: freckles on the lips + hamartomas in the gut.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is this patient at increased risk for?
   - Page: 394

262. A 50-year-old man has fatigue, joint pain in his second and third metacarpophalangeal joints and erectile dysfunction. His skin is bronze. Glucose is 210 mg/dL. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated. His iron studies are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hemochromatosis
   - **A.** Iron deficiency anemia — Wrong. Opposite disorder.
   - **B.** Kidney failure — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **C.** Small bowel lymphoma — Wrong. Celiac.
   - **D.** Hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis **(Correct)** — Correct. Hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE, C282Y) causes iron deposition, cirrhosis and HCC; also restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
   - **E.** Lung cancer — Wrong. Not linked.
   - **F.** Hemorrhagic stroke — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - second and third metacarpophalangeal joints — Arthropathy typical of hemochromatosis.
     - His skin is bronze — Skin pigmentation.
     - Glucose is 210 mg/dL — Pancreatic iron deposition ("bronze diabetes").
     - erectile dysfunction — Pituitary iron → hypogonadism.
   - **Reasoning:** Bronze skin + diabetes + MCP arthropathy + hypogonadism + very high transferrin saturation and ferritin, low TIBC (table) → hemochromatosis → cirrhosis/HCC.
   - **Teaching point:** Hemochromatosis: high ferritin, high iron, high saturation, LOW TIBC.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely cause of death if this condition is untreated?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       "head": [

         "Reference"
       ],

           "240 µg/dL",
           "60–160"
         ],
         [
           "TIBC",

         ],
         [
           "Transferrin saturation",
           "88%",
           "20–50%"
         ],
         [
           "Ferritin",
           "2,100 ng/mL",
           "20–250"
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Iron studies
   - Page: 402

263. A 17-year-old boy has a tremor, slurred speech and declining school performance. He has become irritable. Examination shows a golden-brown ring at the edge of the cornea. ALT is 120 U/L. Serum ceruloplasmin is low and 24-hour urine copper is high.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Wilson disease
   - **A.** Mitochondrial inheritance — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Autosomal dominant, HFE — Wrong. HFE is recessive and causes hemochromatosis.
   - **C.** Autosomal recessive, SERPINA1 — Wrong. Codominant α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
   - **D.** Autosomal dominant, APC — Wrong. FAP.
   - **E.** X-linked recessive, ATP7A — Wrong. Menkes disease.
   - **F.** Autosomal recessive, ATP7B **(Correct)** — Correct. Wilson disease: defective hepatocyte copper transporter impairs biliary excretion and incorporation into ceruloplasmin.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - golden-brown ring at the edge of the cornea — Kayser-Fleischer ring.
     - tremor, slurred speech — Basal ganglia copper deposits.
     - irritable — Psychiatric changes.
     - Serum ceruloplasmin is low — Copper is not incorporated.
   - **Reasoning:** Young patient + liver injury + movement disorder + KF ring + low ceruloplasmin + high urine copper → Wilson disease → ATP7B, recessive.
   - **Teaching point:** Wilson = ATP7B on chromosome 13 — "Wilson's Copper Trouble (7B)."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the inheritance and defective gene?
   - Page: 402

264. A 48-year-old woman has severe itching and fatigue for 1 year. She also has dry eyes and dry mouth. Examination shows xanthelasmas. Alkaline phosphatase is 610 U/L. Ultrasound shows a normal extrahepatic biliary tree. Antimitochondrial antibodies are positive.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Primary biliary cholangitis
   - **A.** Macrovesicular steatosis — Wrong. MASLD or alcohol.
   - **B.** Lymphocytic infiltration and granulomatous destruction of intralobular bile ducts **(Correct)** — Correct. Primary biliary cholangitis.
   - **C.** Centrilobular congestion — Wrong. Budd-Chiari or heart failure.
   - **D.** Periportal PAS-positive globules — Wrong. α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
   - **E.** Concentric "onion skin" fibrosis of extrahepatic ducts — Wrong. PSC.
   - **F.** Interface hepatitis with plasma cells — Wrong. Autoimmune hepatitis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - severe itching — Cholestatic pruritus.
     - dry eyes and dry mouth — Sjögren association.
     - xanthelasmas — Hypercholesterolemia from cholestasis.
     - normal extrahepatic biliary tree — Small intrahepatic ducts are affected.
     - Antimitochondrial antibodies are positive — Specific for PBC.
   - **Reasoning:** Middle-aged woman + pruritus + cholestasis + normal extrahepatic ducts + AMA → PBC → granulomatous destruction of intralobular ducts.
   - **Teaching point:** PBC: "Primary Biliary = Small ducts; AMA; woman." Treat with ursodiol.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely pathologic finding?
   - Page: 402

265. A 32-year-old woman with polycythemia vera has had abdominal pain and swelling for 3 weeks. The liver is enlarged and tender, and there is shifting dullness. There is no jugular venous distension. Doppler ultrasound shows absent flow in the hepatic veins.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Budd-Chiari syndrome
   - **A.** Periportal fibrosis — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **B.** Granulomas — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **C.** Bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules only — Wrong. A late finding.
   - **D.** Ballooning degeneration with Mallory bodies — Wrong. Alcoholic hepatitis.
   - **E.** Centrilobular congestion and necrosis **(Correct)** — Correct. Budd-Chiari syndrome: hepatic venous outflow obstruction causes centrilobular congestion ("nutmeg liver").
   - **F.** Ground-glass hepatocytes — Wrong. Hepatitis B.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - polycythemia vera — Hypercoagulable state.
     - liver is enlarged and tender — Congestive hepatomegaly.
     - shifting dullness — Ascites.
     - no jugular venous distension — Distinguishes from right heart failure.
     - absent flow in the hepatic veins — Hepatic vein thrombosis.
   - **Reasoning:** Hypercoagulable state + painful hepatomegaly + ascites + no JVD + hepatic vein occlusion → Budd-Chiari → centrilobular congestion.
   - **Teaching point:** Nutmeg liver without JVD = Budd-Chiari; with JVD = right heart failure.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following would most likely be seen on liver biopsy?
   - Page: 397

266. A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 16 hours after taking an unknown number of tablets in a suicide attempt. She has nausea and right upper quadrant tenderness. Her test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure
   - **A.** Inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase — Wrong. Fomepizole.
   - **B.** Chelates the drug in the gut — Wrong. Activated charcoal adsorbs drugs but is too late at 16 hours.
   - **C.** Replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI **(Correct)** — Correct. Acetaminophen overdose: NAPQI depletes glutathione and causes centrilobular necrosis; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione.
   - **D.** Alkalinizes the urine — Wrong. Salicylates.
   - **E.** Competitively blocks opioid receptors — Wrong. Naloxone.
   - **F.** Binds Fab fragments to the drug — Wrong. Digoxin.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 16 hours after taking an unknown number of tablets — Time to plot on the nomogram.
     - right upper quadrant tenderness — Hepatic injury.
     - nausea — Early symptom.
   - **Reasoning:** Overdose + level above the treatment line + transaminases in the thousands + high INR (table) → acetaminophen toxicity → N-acetylcysteine.
   - **Teaching point:** Acetaminophen → NAPQI → needs glutathione → NAC gives "N-A-C = Not A Corpse."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the mechanism of the antidote that should be given?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       "head": [

         "Result",
         "Reference"
       ],
       "rows": [
         [
           "Serum drug level at 16 hours",
           "110 µg/mL",
           "Treatment threshold at 16 hours ≈ 40"
         ],
         [
           "ALT",

           "7–56"
         ],
         [
           "AST",
           "3,410 U/L",
           "10–40"
         ],

         ],
         [
           "Salicylate level",

           ""
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Laboratory results
   - Page: 397

267. A 7-year-old boy has repeated vomiting and becomes confused 5 days after recovering from chickenpox. His mother gave him a pain reliever for his fever. He develops seizures. Serum ammonia and liver enzymes are elevated; glucose is 48 mg/dL.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Reye syndrome
   - **A.** Codeine — Wrong. Not linked.
   - **B.** Aspirin **(Correct)** — Correct. Reye syndrome: aspirin in children with viral illness (VZV, influenza) causes mitochondrial injury, microvesicular steatosis and encephalopathy.
   - **C.** Diphenhydramine — Wrong. Not linked.
   - **D.** Acetaminophen — Wrong. Safe for fever in children.
   - **E.** Ibuprofen — Wrong. Not linked.
   - **F.** Valacyclovir — Wrong. Not linked.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 5 days after recovering from chickenpox — Viral trigger (VZV, influenza).
     - a pain reliever for his fever — The causative drug.
     - Serum ammonia and liver enzymes are elevated — Hepatic dysfunction.
     - glucose is 48 mg/dL — Hypoglycemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Child + recent VZV + aspirin + vomiting, encephalopathy, high ammonia, hypoglycemia → Reye syndrome.
   - **Teaching point:** Aspirin is avoided in children except for Kawasaki disease.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug did he most likely receive?
   - Page: 398

268. A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis becomes confused and sleepy 2 days after an episode of upper GI bleeding. Examination shows flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. There is no focal deficit. Head CT is normal.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Hepatic encephalopathy
   - **A.** Haloperidol — Wrong. Not a treatment.
   - **B.** Furosemide — Wrong. Can precipitate encephalopathy.
   - **C.** Loperamide — Wrong. Constipation worsens encephalopathy.
   - **D.** High-protein diet — Wrong. Increases ammonia load.
   - **E.** Lactulose **(Correct)** — Correct. Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose is converted by colonic bacteria to acids that trap ammonia as NH4+; rifaximin is added for recurrence.
   - **F.** Lorazepam — Wrong. Worsens encephalopathy.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - alcohol-related cirrhosis — Liver failure and portosystemic shunting.
     - after an episode of upper GI bleeding — Blood in the gut is a protein load.
     - flapping tremor — Asterixis.
     - Head CT is normal — Excludes structural causes.
   - **Reasoning:** Cirrhosis + GI bleed (protein load) + confusion + asterixis → hepatic encephalopathy → lactulose.
   - **Teaching point:** Ammonia goes up with GI bleeds, infection, constipation, diuretics, sedatives.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
   - Page: 399

269. A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis from hepatitis C has increasing abdominal girth, fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness. She is confused. Diagnostic paracentesis results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
   - **A.** Escherichia coli **(Correct)** — Correct. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is usually caused by gram-negative organisms such as E. coli and Klebsiella; ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ confirm it.
   - **B.** Staphylococcus aureus — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **C.** Bacteroides fragilis — Wrong. Polymicrobial anaerobes suggest secondary peritonitis.
   - **D.** Enterococcus faecalis — Wrong. Gram-positive.
   - **E.** Mycobacterium tuberculosis — Wrong. Low SAAG and lymphocytes.
   - **F.** Candida albicans — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - cirrhosis from hepatitis C — Portal hypertension with ascites.
     - fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness — Peritonitis.
     - She is confused — SBP often worsens encephalopathy.
   - **Reasoning:** Cirrhotic ascites + fever + SAAG 1.8 (portal hypertension) + PMN ≥250 + gram-negative rods (table) → SBP → E. coli.
   - **Teaching point:** SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension; ascitic PMN ≥250 = SBP.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely organism?

     ```json
         ]
       ]
     ```

   - Page: 397

270. Two brothers aged 20 and 24 are evaluated for jaundice. Both are otherwise well with normal liver enzymes, normal complete blood counts and no hemolysis. Brother 2 has noticed dark urine. Their test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Hereditary hyperbilirubinemias
   - **A.** Hepatic storage defect without pigment — Wrong. Rotor syndrome has no black liver.
   - **B.** Increased hemolysis — Wrong. No hemolysis.
   - **C.** Absent UDP-glucuronosyltransferase — Wrong. Crigler-Najjar type I; severe in infancy.
   - **D.** Defective hepatocyte excretion of conjugated bilirubin **(Correct)** — Correct. Dubin-Johnson syndrome: conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from defective canalicular excretion (MRP2), with a black liver.
   - **E.** Mildly decreased UDP-glucuronosyltransferase — Wrong. Gilbert syndrome (Brother 1).
   - **F.** Obstruction of the common bile duct — Wrong. Enzymes would be cholestatic and abnormal.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - normal liver enzymes — Benign inherited disorder.
     - no hemolysis — Excludes overproduction.
     - Brother 2 has noticed dark urine — Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and appears in urine.
   - **Reasoning:** Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + urine bilirubin + normal enzymes + black liver (table) → Dubin-Johnson → defective excretion.
   - **Teaching point:** Dubin-Johnson = Dark liver; Rotor = Regular liver.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most likely defect in Brother 2?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       ],

           "4.2 mg/dL"
         ],

         ],

         ],
         [
           "Urine bilirubin",
           "Absent",

         ]

     ```
     Comparison of the two brothers
   - Page: 401

271. A 3-day-old boy has severe jaundice that has worsened despite phototherapy. Total bilirubin is 28 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated. There is no hemolysis. He develops lethargy, poor feeding and arching of the back.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Crigler-Najjar syndrome
   - **A.** Gilbert syndrome — Wrong. Mild and benign.
   - **B.** Physiologic jaundice — Wrong. Not this severe or refractory.
   - **C.** Breast milk jaundice — Wrong. Milder, later onset.
   - **D.** Biliary atresia — Wrong. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
   - **E.** Dubin-Johnson syndrome — Wrong. Conjugated.
   - **F.** Absent UDP-glucuronosyltransferase **(Correct)** — Correct. Crigler-Najjar type I presents early with very high unconjugated bilirubin and kernicterus.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - worsened despite phototherapy — Severe enzyme deficiency.
     - almost all unconjugated — Conjugation failure.
     - arching of the back — Kernicterus (opisthotonus).
     - There is no hemolysis — Excludes overproduction.
   - **Reasoning:** Neonate + very high unconjugated bilirubin + no hemolysis + kernicterus → Crigler-Najjar type I → absent UGT.
   - **Teaching point:** Type II responds to phenobarbital; type I does not.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely cause?
   - Page: 401

272. A 5-week-old girl has jaundice that began at 2 weeks of age. She is feeding well and gaining weight. Her stools are pale and her urine is dark. Total bilirubin is 7.8 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 5.9 mg/dL. GGT is markedly elevated. Ultrasound shows an absent gallbladder.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Biliary atresia
   - **A.** Exchange transfusion — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **B.** Stop breastfeeding — Wrong. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated.
   - **C.** Phototherapy — Wrong. Not useful in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
   - **D.** Hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai procedure) **(Correct)** — Correct. Biliary atresia: fibro-obliterative destruction of extrahepatic bile ducts; early Kasai procedure, with liver transplant if it fails.
   - **E.** Phenobarbital — Wrong. Crigler-Najjar type II.
   - **F.** Observation — Wrong. Delay worsens outcome.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - began at 2 weeks of age — Persistent jaundice after 2 weeks.
     - Her stools are pale and her urine is dark — Biliary obstruction.
     - direct fraction of 5.9 mg/dL — Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
     - absent gallbladder — Extrahepatic biliary atresia.
   - **Reasoning:** Infant + persistent conjugated jaundice + acholic stools + high GGT + absent gallbladder → biliary atresia → Kasai.
   - **Teaching point:** Biliary atresia is the most common reason for pediatric liver transplantation.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
   - Page: 401

273. A 68-year-old woman has fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. She becomes confused and her blood pressure falls to 84/50 mmHg. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a dilated common bile duct.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acute cholangitis
   - **A.** Elective cholecystectomy in 6 weeks — Wrong. Delay is dangerous.
   - **B.** Urgent ERCP with biliary drainage **(Correct)** — Correct. Acute cholangitis with Reynolds pentad needs urgent decompression.
   - **C.** Shock wave lithotripsy — Wrong. Not used.
   - **D.** Ursodiol — Wrong. Not for acute disease.
   - **E.** Percutaneous liver biopsy — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **F.** Total parenteral nutrition only — Wrong. Not definitive.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain — Charcot triad.
     - She becomes confused and her blood pressure falls — Reynolds pentad.
     - dilated common bile duct — Biliary obstruction.
   - **Reasoning:** Charcot triad + confusion + hypotension (Reynolds) + dilated CBD → ascending cholangitis → urgent ERCP.
   - **Teaching point:** Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain. Add shock and confusion = Reynolds pentad.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment after resuscitation and antibiotics?
   - Page: 403

274. An 80-year-old woman has had vomiting and abdominal distension for 3 days. She has a history of recurrent biliary colic. Abdominal x-ray shows dilated small bowel loops and air in the biliary tree. A rounded opacity is seen in the right lower quadrant.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Gallstone ileus
   - **A.** Emphysematous cholecystitis — Wrong. Gas in the gallbladder wall without obstruction.
   - **B.** Sigmoid volvulus — Wrong. Coffee bean sign.
   - **C.** Gallstone ileus **(Correct)** — Correct. Fistula between the gallbladder and the GI tract lets a stone enter and obstruct, often at the ileocecal valve; air in the biliary tree.
   - **D.** Ogilvie syndrome — Wrong. Colonic dilation.
   - **E.** Acute cholangitis — Wrong. Fever and jaundice.
   - **F.** Intussusception — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - recurrent biliary colic — Gallstone disease.
     - air in the biliary tree — Pneumobilia from a fistula.
     - dilated small bowel loops — Small bowel obstruction.
     - right lower quadrant — Stone impacted at the ileocecal valve.
   - **Reasoning:** Elderly + gallstones + small bowel obstruction + pneumobilia + RLQ stone → gallstone ileus.
   - **Teaching point:** Rigler triad: small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic gallstone.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 403

275. A 36-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back for 12 hours. He does not drink alcohol and has no gallstones on ultrasound. He has eruptive xanthomas on his buttocks. His test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acute pancreatitis
   - **A.** Mumps — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **B.** Gallstones — Wrong. Ultrasound shows none.
   - **C.** Scorpion sting — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **D.** Hypercalcemia — Wrong. Calcium is normal.
   - **E.** Alcohol — Wrong. He does not drink.
   - **F.** Hypertriglyceridemia **(Correct)** — Correct. Triglycerides >1000 mg/dL cause acute pancreatitis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - epigastric pain radiating to the back — Pancreatitis.
     - eruptive xanthomas on his buttocks — Very high triglycerides.
     - no gallstones on ultrasound — Excludes the most common cause.
     - does not drink alcohol — Excludes the second most common cause.
   - **Reasoning:** Epigastric pain to the back + lipase >3× normal + TG 2,400 (table) + eruptive xanthomas → hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis.
   - **Teaching point:** GET SMASHED: Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcemia/Hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, Drugs.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acute condition?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
     {
       "type": "table",
       "head": [
         "Test",
         "Result",
         "Reference"
       ],
       "rows": [
         [
           "Lipase",
           "1,450 U/L",
           "<60"
         ],
         [
           "Triglycerides",
           "2,400 mg/dL",
           "<150"
         ],
         [
           "Calcium",
           "8.6 mg/dL",
           "8.4–10.2"
         ],
         [
           "Glucose",
           "318 mg/dL",
           "70–100"
         ],
         [
           "Serum sample",
           "Milky, lipemic",
           ""
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Laboratory results
   - Page: 404

276. A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has weight loss, dark urine, pale stools and itching. Examination shows jaundice and a nontender, palpable gallbladder. He had redness and tenderness in his left calf last month, followed by similar findings in his right arm. CA 19-9 is elevated.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Pancreatic adenocarcinoma
   - **A.** Hepatocellular carcinoma — Wrong. Not with a palpable gallbladder.
   - **B.** Choledocholithiasis — Wrong. Painful; gallbladder usually fibrotic.
   - **C.** Chronic pancreatitis — Wrong. Pain and calcifications.
   - **D.** Primary biliary cholangitis — Wrong. Middle-aged women.
   - **E.** Pancreatic adenocarcinoma of the head **(Correct)** — Correct. Painless jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and elevated CA 19-9.
   - **F.** Acute cholecystitis — Wrong. Tender gallbladder with fever.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - smoked for 40 years — Strongest modifiable risk factor.
     - nontender, palpable gallbladder — Courvoisier sign.
     - redness and tenderness in his left calf last month, followed by similar findings in his right arm — Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome).
     - CA 19-9 is elevated — Tumor marker.
   - **Reasoning:** Older smoker + painless obstructive jaundice + Courvoisier sign + migratory thrombophlebitis + CA 19-9 → pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.
   - **Teaching point:** Courvoisier: a palpable nontender gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be stones.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 405

277. A 38-year-old man who has never smoked has worsening shortness of breath. Chest CT shows panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes. He also has elevated liver enzymes and mild hepatomegaly. Liver biopsy shows periodic acid-Schiff–positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** α1-antitrypsin deficiency
   - **A.** Accumulation of misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum **(Correct)** — Correct. α1-antitrypsin deficiency: misfolded protein aggregates in hepatocytes cause cirrhosis; lack of circulating enzyme inhibitor causes panacinar emphysema.
   - **B.** Autoimmune destruction of bile ducts — Wrong. PBC.
   - **C.** Fat accumulation from insulin resistance — Wrong. MASLD.
   - **D.** Copper accumulation — Wrong. Wilson disease.
   - **E.** Iron deposition — Wrong. Hemochromatosis.
   - **F.** Glycogen storage — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - never smoked — Emphysema in a nonsmoker points to an inherited cause.
     - panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes — α1-antitrypsin pattern.
     - periodic acid-Schiff–positive, diastase-resistant globules — Retained α1-antitrypsin.
     - elevated liver enzymes and mild hepatomegaly — Liver involvement.
   - **Reasoning:** Young nonsmoker + lower-lobe panacinar emphysema + liver disease + PAS-positive globules → α1-antitrypsin deficiency → misfolded protein in hepatocyte ER.
   - **Teaching point:** Lungs suffer from too little enzyme inhibitor; the liver suffers from too much retained protein.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains the liver findings?
   - Page: 400

278. A 58-year-old man from a region where hepatitis B is common has cirrhosis. He has new right upper quadrant pain, weight loss and worsening ascites. Serum α-fetoprotein is 1,850 ng/mL. CT shows a liver mass with arterial-phase enhancement and washout on delayed images.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hepatocellular carcinoma
   - **A.** Direct invasion of the stomach — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **B.** No spread; benign lesion — Wrong. AFP and imaging indicate malignancy.
   - **C.** Peritoneal seeding before any liver growth — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **D.** Invasion of the portal and hepatic veins **(Correct)** — Correct. Hepatocellular carcinoma spreads hematogenously and invades the portal or hepatic veins, which can cause Budd-Chiari syndrome.
   - **E.** Spread to the ovaries — Wrong. Gastric (Krukenberg).
   - **F.** Early lymphatic spread to supraclavicular nodes — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - where hepatitis B is common — The leading cause worldwide.
     - cirrhosis — Major risk factor.
     - α-fetoprotein is 1,850 ng/mL — Tumor marker.
     - arterial-phase enhancement and washout — Typical imaging.
   - **Reasoning:** HBV cirrhosis + rising AFP + arterial-enhancing mass with washout → HCC → vascular invasion.
   - **Teaching point:** HCC: diagnose by imaging plus AFP in cirrhosis; biopsy often not needed.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is most likely to occur as this tumor spreads?
   - Page: 400

279. A 70-year-old woman has left lower quadrant pain, fever and constipation for 2 days. She eats a low-fiber diet. Temperature is 38.5°C and there is tenderness in the left lower quadrant. White blood cell count is 15,800/mm³. CT shows fat stranding around the sigmoid colon with multiple outpouchings.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Diverticulitis
   - **A.** Abdominal x-ray for free air — Wrong. Can be done.
   - **B.** Colonoscopy **(Correct)** — Correct. Diverticulitis: colonoscopy is avoided acutely because of perforation risk; it is done after recovery to exclude cancer.
   - **C.** CT of the abdomen with contrast — Wrong. The preferred test.
   - **D.** Urinalysis — Wrong. Reasonable.
   - **E.** Complete blood count — Wrong. Routine.
   - **F.** Blood cultures — Wrong. Reasonable if septic.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - left lower quadrant pain, fever — "Left-sided appendicitis".
     - low-fiber diet — Risk factor for diverticulosis.
     - multiple outpouchings — Diverticula.
     - fat stranding around the sigmoid colon — Inflammation.
   - **Reasoning:** Elderly + LLQ pain + fever + leukocytosis + sigmoid diverticula with stranding → diverticulitis → avoid colonoscopy acutely.
   - **Teaching point:** Diverticulosis bleeds painlessly; diverticulitis hurts and causes fever.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate test to avoid during the acute episode?
   - Page: 390

280. A 4-week-old firstborn boy has projectile, nonbilious vomiting after every feed for 1 week. He seems hungry immediately after vomiting. An olive-shaped mass is felt in the epigastrium. His mother was given erythromycin for a chest infection when he was 1 week old.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
   - **A.** Normal electrolytes — Wrong. Vomiting causes abnormalities.
   - **B.** Anion gap metabolic acidosis — Wrong. Not expected early.
   - **C.** Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis **(Correct)** — Correct. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: loss of gastric HCl causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia.
   - **D.** Respiratory alkalosis with hyponatremia — Wrong. Not expected.
   - **E.** Respiratory acidosis — Wrong. Not expected.
   - **F.** Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia — Wrong. Not expected with vomiting.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - projectile, nonbilious vomiting — Obstruction proximal to the ampulla.
     - firstborn boy — Risk factor.
     - olive-shaped mass — Hypertrophied pylorus.
     - erythromycin — Macrolide exposure is a risk factor.
   - **Reasoning:** Infant aged 2–6 weeks + projectile nonbilious vomiting + olive mass → pyloric stenosis → hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
   - **Teaching point:** Vomiting = loss of acid = alkalosis; diarrhea = loss of base = acidosis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following acid-base and electrolyte findings is most likely?
   - Page: 366

## Gastrointestinal 2

Source: `mock-gastrointestinal-2.json`

281. A 38-year-old man vomited repeatedly after a night of binge drinking. On the last few episodes he vomited bright red blood. He is now comfortable. Pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. There is no crepitus or chest pain. Hemoglobin is 13.6 g/dL. Endoscopy shows a longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Mallory-Weiss syndrome
   - **A.** Dieulafoy lesion — Wrong. A large submucosal artery, not a tear.
   - **B.** Mallory-Weiss syndrome **(Correct)** — Correct. Partial-thickness, longitudinal laceration at the GE junction from severe vomiting; painless hematemesis, usually self-limited.
   - **C.** Esophageal adenocarcinoma — Wrong. Mass lesion.
   - **D.** Esophageal varices — Wrong. Dilated submucosal veins in cirrhosis.
   - **E.** Boerhaave syndrome — Wrong. Transmural rupture with mediastinitis.
   - **F.** Peptic ulcer disease — Wrong. Ulcer seen.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - vomited repeatedly after a night of binge drinking — Alcohol and severe vomiting are classic triggers.
     - There is no crepitus or chest pain — Argues against transmural rupture.
     - longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction — Partial-thickness laceration.
     - He is now comfortable — Bleeding is usually self-limited.
   - **Reasoning:** Binge drinking + retching → hematemesis + GE junction mucosal tear, no mediastinitis → Mallory-Weiss.
   - **Teaching point:** Mallory-Weiss = mucosa; Boerhaave = burst through all layers.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 384

282. A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large amount of bright red blood. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg. He has spider angiomas, palmar erythema and splenomegaly. Two large-bore IV lines are placed and blood transfusion is started.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Esophageal varices and octreotide
   - **A.** Vitamin K — Wrong. Does not stop variceal bleeding.
   - **B.** Nitroglycerin alone — Wrong. Not first line.
   - **C.** Misoprostol — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **D.** Octreotide **(Correct)** — Correct. A somatostatin analog that inhibits splanchnic vasodilatory hormones and reduces portal pressure in acute variceal bleeding.
   - **E.** Lactulose — Wrong. Prevents encephalopathy, does not stop bleeding.
   - **F.** Pantoprazole alone — Wrong. Does not lower portal pressure.
   - **G.** Propranolol IV — Wrong. Nonselective β-blockers are used for prophylaxis, not active bleeding with shock.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - alcohol-related cirrhosis — Portal hypertension.
     - spider angiomas, palmar erythema and splenomegaly — Stigmata of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension.
     - vomits a large amount of bright red blood — Variceal hemorrhage.
     - Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg — Hemodynamic instability.
   - **Reasoning:** Cirrhosis + massive hematemesis + portal hypertension → variceal bleed → octreotide + endoscopic banding.
   - **Teaching point:** Octreotide treats bleeds; propranolol prevents them.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug should be started to reduce portal blood flow while awaiting endoscopy?
   - Page: 407

283. A 45-year-old woman has episodes of severe chest pain that occur while eating and sometimes wake her at night. She has intermittent dysphagia for both solids and liquids. Cardiac stress testing is normal. A barium swallow shows a "corkscrew" esophagus. Esophageal manometry is shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Distal esophageal spasm
   - **A.** Distal esophageal spasm **(Correct)** — Correct. Simultaneous, uncoordinated, high-amplitude contractions instead of a peristaltic wave cause chest pain and a corkscrew esophagus.
   - **B.** Scleroderma esophagus — Wrong. Weak, low-amplitude contractions.
   - **C.** Eosinophilic esophagitis — Wrong. Rings and furrows.
   - **D.** Angina pectoris — Wrong. Stress test normal.
   - **E.** Achalasia — Wrong. Nonrelaxing LES with bird's beak.
   - **F.** Zenker diverticulum — Wrong. Pharyngeal pouch.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - severe chest pain that occur while eating — Spasm mimics angina.
     - dysphagia for both solids and liquids — Motility disorder.
     - Cardiac stress testing is normal — Cardiac cause excluded.
     - "corkscrew" esophagus — Barium appearance of spasm.
   - **Reasoning:** Chest pain with swallowing + normal cardiac workup + corkscrew esophagus + simultaneous high-pressure contractions (figure) → distal esophageal spasm.
   - **Teaching point:** Normal peristalsis is sequential (staggered peaks); spasm fires all levels at once.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

   - Page: 384

284. A 72-year-old man has bad breath, a gurgling sound in his neck when he swallows and regurgitation of food he ate days earlier. He has had several episodes of aspiration pneumonia. Barium swallow shows a pouch arising posteriorly just above the upper esophageal sphincter.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Zenker diverticulum
   - **A.** Hiatal hernia — Wrong. Stomach above the diaphragm.
   - **B.** True diverticulum of the midesophagus from traction — Wrong. Midesophageal traction diverticula involve all layers.
   - **C.** Esophageal web — Wrong. A membrane, not a pouch.
   - **D.** Congenital vitelline duct remnant — Wrong. Meckel.
   - **E.** False diverticulum through the Killian triangle **(Correct)** — Correct. Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal false (pulsion) diverticulum herniating through the Killian triangle above the cricopharyngeus.
   - **F.** Epiphrenic true diverticulum — Wrong. Distal.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bad breath — Halitosis from retained food.
     - regurgitation of food he ate days earlier — Food retention in the pouch.
     - just above the upper esophageal sphincter — Killian triangle location.
     - aspiration pneumonia — Overflow into the airway.
   - **Reasoning:** Elderly + halitosis + gurgling + regurgitation of old food + posterior pouch above the UES → Zenker → false diverticulum through Killian triangle.
   - **Teaching point:** Zenker = False (only mucosa and submucosa); Meckel = True (all layers).
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best describes this lesion?
   - Page: 391

285. A 49-year-old woman has heartburn and difficulty swallowing. She has thickened, tight skin on her fingers and face, color changes of her fingers in the cold and small dilated vessels on her face. Esophageal manometry shows absent peristalsis in the distal esophagus and very low LES pressure.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Scleroderma esophageal dysmotility
   - **A.** Skeletal muscle inflammation — Wrong. Polymyositis affects the upper (skeletal muscle) esophagus.
   - **B.** Loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons — Wrong. Achalasia; high LES pressure.
   - **C.** Simultaneous high-pressure contractions — Wrong. Distal esophageal spasm.
   - **D.** Esophageal web — Wrong. Plummer-Vinson.
   - **E.** Eosinophilic infiltration — Wrong. Eosinophilic esophagitis.
   - **F.** Atrophy and fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle **(Correct)** — Correct. Scleroderma (CREST) causes smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis, low LES pressure, poor peristalsis and reflux.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - thickened, tight skin on her fingers and face — Sclerodactyly.
     - color changes of her fingers in the cold — Raynaud phenomenon.
     - small dilated vessels on her face — Telangiectasias.
     - very low LES pressure — Distinguishes from achalasia.
   - **Reasoning:** CREST features + reflux + absent distal peristalsis + low LES pressure → scleroderma → smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis.
   - **Teaching point:** Achalasia: LES too tight. Scleroderma: LES too loose.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains her esophageal findings?
   - Page: 384

286. A 64-year-old man from Japan has early satiety, epigastric pain and a 9-kg weight loss. Examination shows a hard, enlarged lymph node above the left clavicle. Endoscopy shows a thickened, rigid stomach wall without a discrete mass. Biopsy shows cells with mucin pushing the nucleus to the side.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Gastric cancer
   - **A.** Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma — Wrong. Usually a discrete ulcerated mass.
   - **B.** Gastric carcinoid — Wrong. Neuroendocrine cells.
   - **C.** Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma **(Correct)** — Correct. Signet ring cells infiltrating the wall cause linitis plastica; spread to the Virchow node.
   - **D.** Gastric MALT lymphoma — Wrong. Lymphocytes, not signet ring cells.
   - **E.** Gastrointestinal stromal tumor — Wrong. Spindle cell tumor.
   - **F.** Ménétrier disease — Wrong. Giant rugae, benign.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - from Japan — High incidence of gastric cancer.
     - hard, enlarged lymph node above the left clavicle — Virchow node.
     - thickened, rigid stomach wall — Linitis plastica.
     - mucin pushing the nucleus to the side — Signet ring cells.
   - **Reasoning:** Weight loss + early satiety + Virchow node + rigid stomach + signet ring cells → diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma.
   - **Teaching point:** Diffuse type: signet rings and leather bottle; spreads to Virchow, Sister Mary Joseph and Krukenberg.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 386

287. A 30-year-old man is admitted with second- and third-degree burns over 45% of his body surface area. On day 4 he has hematemesis and a falling hemoglobin. Endoscopy shows multiple shallow erosions in the stomach and duodenum.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acute gastritis (Curling ulcer)
   - **A.** Increased vagal stimulation and acid production — Wrong. Cushing ulcer after brain injury.
   - **B.** Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells — Wrong. Chronic autoimmune gastritis.
   - **C.** H. pylori infection — Wrong. Chronic gastritis.
   - **D.** Hypovolemia causing mucosal ischemia **(Correct)** — Correct. Curling ulcer: acute gastritis after burns from hypovolemia and decreased mucosal blood flow.
   - **E.** Bile reflux — Wrong. Not the mechanism here.
   - **F.** Gastrinoma — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - burns over 45% of his body surface area — Major burns.
     - multiple shallow erosions — Acute erosive gastritis.
     - On day 4 — Stress-related mucosal injury.
   - **Reasoning:** Severe burns → hypovolemia → mucosal ischemia → acute erosive gastritis (Curling ulcer).
   - **Teaching point:** "Burned by the Curling iron"; "Always Cushion the brain."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the mechanism of his lesions?
   - Page: 386

288. A 58-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has fatigue, tingling in her feet and loss of position sense. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL with an MCV of 118 fL. Serum gastrin is markedly elevated. Antibodies to intrinsic factor are present.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Chronic autoimmune gastritis
   - **A.** Cardia only — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Duodenal bulb — Wrong. Not in the stomach.
   - **C.** Body and fundus **(Correct)** — Correct. Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells in the body and fundus, causing achlorhydria, high gastrin and B12 deficiency.
   - **D.** Antrum — Wrong. H. pylori gastritis mainly affects the antrum.
   - **E.** Lesser curvature only — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Pylorus — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Hashimoto thyroiditis — Associated autoimmune disease.
     - loss of position sense — Dorsal column involvement from B12 deficiency.
     - MCV of 118 fL — Megaloblastic anemia.
     - Serum gastrin is markedly elevated — Achlorhydria removes negative feedback.
     - Antibodies to intrinsic factor — Pernicious anemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Autoimmune disease + megaloblastic anemia + neuropathy + high gastrin + anti-IF → autoimmune gastritis → parietal cells in body/fundus.
   - **Teaching point:** Type A (Autoimmune) = body; type B (Bacterial) = antrum.
   - **Follow-up:** Which region of the stomach is most affected?
   - Page: 386

289. A 67-year-old woman with osteoarthritis takes naproxen several times a day. She has had burning epigastric pain for 2 months that becomes worse soon after meals, and she has lost weight because she is afraid to eat. H. pylori testing is negative.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Gastric ulcer
   - **A.** Increased vagal acid secretion — Wrong. Cushing ulcer.
   - **B.** Acid hypersecretion from a gastrinoma — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **C.** Bile acid deficiency — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Increased gastrin release — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **E.** Parietal cell autoimmunity — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Decreased prostaglandin synthesis reducing mucosal protection **(Correct)** — Correct. NSAIDs inhibit COX and reduce prostaglandins, decreasing mucus and bicarbonate and causing gastric ulcers.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - takes naproxen several times a day — NSAID use.
     - worse soon after meals — Gastric (not duodenal) ulcer pattern.
     - afraid to eat — Weight loss with gastric ulcers.
     - H. pylori testing is negative — Points to the NSAID.
   - **Reasoning:** Chronic NSAID use + pain worse with meals + weight loss → gastric ulcer → reduced prostaglandin-mediated protection.
   - **Teaching point:** Gastric ulcer: pain Greater with meals; Duodenal ulcer: Decreases with meals.
   - **Follow-up:** Which mechanism best explains her condition?
   - Page: 387

290. A 46-year-old woman had a partial gastrectomy 3 months ago. About 20 minutes after meals she has cramping, diarrhea, sweating, palpitations and lightheadedness. About 2 hours after meals she becomes shaky and confused. Her plasma glucose after a meal is shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Dumping syndrome
   - **A.** Vitamin B12 deficiency — Wrong. A late complication, but not this.
   - **B.** Adrenal insufficiency — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **C.** Bacterial overgrowth — Wrong. Bloating and diarrhea, not hypoglycemia.
   - **D.** Insulinoma — Wrong. Fasting hypoglycemia.
   - **E.** Excess insulin release after rapid glucose absorption **(Correct)** — Correct. Dumping syndrome: hyperosmolar food enters the small bowel quickly (early fluid shift symptoms); the glucose spike causes excessive insulin and late hypoglycemia.
   - **F.** Bile acid malabsorption — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - partial gastrectomy 3 months ago — Loss of pyloric control of emptying.
     - About 20 minutes after meals — Early dumping from fluid shifts.
     - About 2 hours after meals — Late dumping from reactive hypoglycemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Gastric surgery → rapid emptying of hyperosmolar food → early fluid shifts + glucose spike then excess insulin → late hypoglycemia (figure).
   - **Teaching point:** Early dumping = fluid shift; late dumping = insulin overshoot.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains her late symptoms?

291. A 35-year-old man returned 6 months ago from a 2-year stay in rural India. He has chronic diarrhea, weight loss and fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Stool studies for ova and parasites are negative. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative. Small bowel biopsy shows villous blunting throughout the small intestine.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Tropical sprue
   - **A.** Gluten-free diet — Wrong. Celiac serology is negative.
   - **B.** Tetracycline and folic acid **(Correct)** — Correct. Tropical sprue responds to antibiotics and folate.
   - **C.** Pancreatic enzymes — Wrong. Not pancreatic insufficiency.
   - **D.** Lactase supplements — Wrong. Lactose intolerance.
   - **E.** Metronidazole only — Wrong. Giardia; stools negative.
   - **F.** Corticosteroids — Wrong. Not first line.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 2-year stay in rural India — Residence in the tropics.
     - MCV of 112 fL — Folate and B12 deficiency.
     - Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative — Excludes celiac.
     - throughout the small intestine — Unlike celiac, which is mainly proximal.
   - **Reasoning:** Tropics + malabsorption + megaloblastic anemia + negative celiac serology → tropical sprue → antibiotics and folate.
   - **Teaching point:** Tropical sprue = celiac-like biopsy + travel history + negative serology.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
   - Page: 388

292. A 28-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis has 12 bloody bowel movements daily. She now has fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension and tenderness. Abdominal x-ray shows a transverse colon diameter of 8 cm. She recently started loperamide.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Ulcerative colitis and toxic megacolon
   - **A.** Colonic perforation **(Correct)** — Correct. Toxic megacolon can perforate; avoid antimotility drugs and treat urgently.
   - **B.** Strictures — Wrong. Crohn disease.
   - **C.** Iron deficiency — Wrong. Not the immediate risk.
   - **D.** Colorectal adenocarcinoma — Wrong. A long-term risk.
   - **E.** Fistula formation — Wrong. Crohn disease.
   - **F.** Primary sclerosing cholangitis — Wrong. A long-term association.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 12 bloody bowel movements daily — Severe ulcerative colitis.
     - fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension — Systemic toxicity.
     - transverse colon diameter of 8 cm — Colonic dilation (>6 cm).
     - recently started loperamide — Antimotility drugs can precipitate toxic megacolon.
   - **Reasoning:** Severe UC + systemic toxicity + colon >6 cm (antimotility drug) → toxic megacolon → perforation risk.
   - **Teaching point:** Never give antimotility drugs in severe colitis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most serious immediate risk of her condition?
   - Page: 389

293. A 64-year-old woman has had watery, nonbloody diarrhea 6 to 8 times a day for 4 months. She takes sertraline and omeprazole. Colonoscopy shows normal-appearing mucosa. Biopsy shows a thickened subepithelial collagen band.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Microscopic colitis
   - **A.** Irritable bowel syndrome — Wrong. Biopsy would be normal.
   - **B.** Celiac disease — Wrong. Small bowel.
   - **C.** Crohn disease — Wrong. Visible lesions.
   - **D.** Ulcerative colitis — Wrong. Visible inflammation.
   - **E.** Ischemic colitis — Wrong. Hematochezia.
   - **F.** Microscopic (collagenous) colitis **(Correct)** — Correct. Chronic watery diarrhea in older women with normal-appearing mucosa; collagenous or lymphocytic subtypes on biopsy.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - watery, nonbloody diarrhea — Chronic secretory diarrhea.
     - sertraline and omeprazole — Drugs associated with microscopic colitis.
     - normal-appearing mucosa — Diagnosis needs biopsy.
     - thickened subepithelial collagen band — Collagenous colitis.
   - **Reasoning:** Older woman + chronic watery diarrhea + PPI/SSRI + normal colonoscopy + collagen band → microscopic colitis.
   - **Teaching point:** Microscopic colitis: "it looks normal until you look under the microscope."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 389

294. A 19-year-old man has had pain for 18 hours that began around the umbilicus and moved to the right lower quadrant. He has nausea and anorexia. Temperature is 38.1°C. Pressing on the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant. White blood cell count is 14,200/mm³.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Appendicitis
   - **A.** S2 — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** T5 — Wrong. Epigastric.
   - **C.** C4 — Wrong. Diaphragmatic referral to the shoulder.
   - **D.** T10 **(Correct)** — Correct. Midgut visceral pain is referred to the umbilicus (T10); once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed, pain localizes to McBurney point.
   - **E.** T12 — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** L1 — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - began around the umbilicus — Visceral midgut pain.
     - moved to the right lower quadrant — Parietal peritoneal irritation.
     - Pressing on the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant — Rovsing sign.
     - nausea and anorexia — Classic accompanying symptoms.
   - **Reasoning:** Periumbilical pain migrating to the RLQ + fever + Rovsing sign → appendicitis; visceral pain referred to T10.
   - **Teaching point:** Appendix pain starts at the belly button (T10) and settles at McBurney point.
   - **Follow-up:** The initial periumbilical pain is carried by visceral afferent fibers entering the spinal cord at which level?
   - Page: 390

295. A newborn girl has bilious vomiting within hours of her first feed. She has a flat facial profile, upslanting eyes and a single palmar crease. Her mother had polyhydramnios. Abdominal x-ray shows two large gas bubbles in the upper abdomen with no distal bowel gas.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Duodenal atresia
   - **A.** Hypertrophy of pyloric muscle — Wrong. Nonbilious vomiting at weeks.
   - **B.** Failure of lateral fold closure — Wrong. Gastroschisis or omphalocele.
   - **C.** Malrotation with Ladd bands — Wrong. Some distal gas usually.
   - **D.** Vascular accident in the jejunum — Wrong. Jejunal atresia; "apple peel."
   - **E.** Failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize **(Correct)** — Correct. Duodenal atresia: "double bubble," associated with Down syndrome.
   - **F.** Failure of neural crest migration — Wrong. Hirschsprung.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bilious vomiting within hours of her first feed — Obstruction distal to the ampulla.
     - flat facial profile, upslanting eyes and a single palmar crease — Down syndrome.
     - polyhydramnios — Fetus cannot swallow and absorb amniotic fluid.
     - two large gas bubbles — Double bubble sign.
   - **Reasoning:** Neonate + bilious vomiting + Down syndrome + polyhydramnios + double bubble → duodenal atresia → failed recanalization.
   - **Teaching point:** Duodenal atresia = failed recanalization; jejunal/ileal atresia = vascular accident.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains this condition?
   - Page: 366

296. A newborn boy has bowel protruding through a defect to the right of a normal umbilical cord. The bowel is not covered by a membrane. His mother is 19 years old and smoked during pregnancy.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Gastroschisis
   - **A.** It results from failure of lateral fold closure and is usually not associated with chromosomal abnormalities **(Correct)** — Correct. Gastroschisis: uncovered bowel lateral to the umbilicus, associated with young maternal age and smoking.
   - **B.** It results from failed recanalization — Wrong. Duodenal atresia.
   - **C.** It is caused by failure of neural crest migration — Wrong. Hirschsprung.
   - **D.** It is a defect of the diaphragm — Wrong. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
   - **E.** It is covered by peritoneum and is often associated with trisomies — Wrong. Describes omphalocele.
   - **F.** It results from persistent herniation of midgut through the umbilical ring — Wrong. Omphalocele.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - to the right of a normal umbilical cord — Paraumbilical defect.
     - not covered by a membrane — Gastroschisis is uncovered.
     - 19 years old and smoked during pregnancy — Risk factors.
   - **Reasoning:** Uncovered bowel beside a normal cord + young, smoking mother → gastroschisis → lateral fold closure failure.
   - **Teaching point:** Gastroschisis = "extrudes" uncovered; omphalocele = "sealed" in peritoneum.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best describes this defect compared with the alternative diagnosis?
   - Page: 366

297. A 3-week-old girl suddenly develops bilious vomiting and is irritable. She was feeding well before. The abdomen is mildly distended. Upper GI contrast study shows the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the midline with a "corkscrew" appearance of the proximal small bowel.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Malrotation and midgut volvulus
   - **A.** Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis — Wrong. Nonbilious vomiting.
   - **B.** Malrotation of the midgut **(Correct)** — Correct. Abnormal rotation leaves the bowel on a narrow mesentery prone to midgut volvulus; Ladd bands may also obstruct.
   - **C.** Meckel diverticulum — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **D.** Duodenal atresia — Wrong. Present from birth.
   - **E.** Hirschsprung disease — Wrong. Delayed meconium.
   - **F.** Annular pancreas — Wrong. Duodenal narrowing without a corkscrew.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - suddenly develops bilious vomiting — Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency.
     - She was feeding well before — Acquired obstruction.
     - to the right of the midline — Abnormal DJ junction location.
     - "corkscrew" appearance — Midgut volvulus.
   - **Reasoning:** Infant + new bilious vomiting + malpositioned DJ junction + corkscrew → malrotation with midgut volvulus.
   - **Teaching point:** Bilious vomiting in an infant = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely underlying anomaly?
   - Page: 392

298. A boy born at 28 weeks' gestation is fed formula in the neonatal intensive care unit. On day 10 he develops feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and bloody stools. Abdominal x-ray shows bubbly gas within the bowel wall.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Necrotizing enterocolitis
   - **A.** Hirschsprung disease — Wrong. Delayed meconium.
   - **B.** Duodenal atresia — Wrong. Double bubble.
   - **C.** Necrotizing enterocolitis **(Correct)** — Correct. Premature, formula-fed infants develop intestinal necrosis, usually in the terminal ileum and proximal colon, with pneumatosis intestinalis.
   - **D.** Malrotation — Wrong. Corkscrew.
   - **E.** Meconium ileus — Wrong. Cystic fibrosis.
   - **F.** Intussusception — Wrong. Older infants.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - born at 28 weeks' gestation — Prematurity.
     - fed formula — Formula feeding is a risk factor.
     - bloody stools — Mucosal necrosis.
     - bubbly gas within the bowel wall — Pneumatosis intestinalis.
   - **Reasoning:** Premature + formula-fed + distension + bloody stools + pneumatosis → NEC.
   - **Teaching point:** Pneumatosis in a preemie = NEC.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 393

299. A 67-year-old man is admitted with fever. Blood cultures grow a gram-positive coccus that is nonhemolytic, grows in bile and hydrolyzes esculin, but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the aortic valve. He has mild iron deficiency anemia.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Colorectal cancer
   - **A.** Colonoscopy **(Correct)** — Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) bacteremia or endocarditis is associated with colorectal cancer.
   - **B.** Liver biopsy — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **C.** Bone marrow biopsy — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **D.** Dental examination — Wrong. Viridans streptococci.
   - **E.** Chest CT — Wrong. Not the first step.
   - **F.** Urine culture — Wrong. Enterococcus.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - grows in bile and hydrolyzes esculin, but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl — Group D streptococcus (not Enterococcus).
     - vegetation on the aortic valve — Endocarditis.
     - mild iron deficiency anemia — Occult GI blood loss.
   - **Reasoning:** S. gallolyticus endocarditis + iron deficiency → colorectal cancer → colonoscopy.
   - **Teaching point:** S. bovis in the blood → look in the colon.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
   - Page: 395

300. A 71-year-old woman had an episode of hypotension during cardiac bypass surgery yesterday. Today she has crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea. Colonoscopy shows edematous, ulcerated mucosa at the splenic flexure with a sharp transition to normal mucosa.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Colonic ischemia
   - **A.** It is drained by the portal vein only — Wrong. Not relevant.
   - **B.** It lacks a muscularis propria — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** It has the highest bacterial load — Wrong. Not the reason.
   - **D.** It is supplied only by the celiac trunk — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** It is a watershed area between the SMA and IMA territories **(Correct)** — Correct. Colonic ischemia commonly occurs at watershed areas: the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid junction.
   - **F.** It is retroperitoneal — Wrong. Not relevant.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - hypotension during cardiac bypass surgery — Low-flow state.
     - crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea — Typical sequence.
     - splenic flexure — Watershed area.
   - **Reasoning:** Hypotension → low flow to watershed areas → splenic flexure ischemia → crampy pain then hematochezia.
   - **Teaching point:** Splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid (IMA/hypogastric) are watershed zones.
   - **Follow-up:** Why is this region especially vulnerable?
   - Page: 393

301. A 68-year-old thin woman has a tender, irreducible bulge in her right groin below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the pubic tubercle. She has vomiting and abdominal distension.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Femoral hernia
   - **A.** Esophageal hiatus — Wrong. Hiatal hernia.
   - **B.** Hesselbach triangle — Wrong. Direct hernia, above the ligament.
   - **C.** Femoral canal **(Correct)** — Correct. Femoral hernias pass below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein; more common in women and prone to incarceration.
   - **D.** Deep inguinal ring — Wrong. Indirect hernia.
   - **E.** Obturator foramen — Wrong. Obturator hernia.
   - **F.** Umbilical ring — Wrong. Umbilical hernia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - below the inguinal ligament — Femoral location.
     - thin woman — Typical patient.
     - irreducible — Femoral hernias commonly incarcerate.
     - vomiting and abdominal distension — Bowel obstruction.
   - **Reasoning:** Woman + groin bulge below the inguinal ligament + incarceration → femoral hernia through the femoral canal.
   - **Teaching point:** Femoral: below the ligament, medial to the femoral vein ("NAVEL": nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics).
   - **Follow-up:** Through which structure does this hernia pass?
   - Page: 377

302. A 70-year-old man has a bulge in his left groin that appears when he stands and strains. It does not enter the scrotum. At surgery, the hernia sac lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Direct inguinal hernia
   - **A.** It passes through the deep inguinal ring — Wrong. Indirect hernia.
   - **B.** It protrudes through Hesselbach triangle and is covered only by the external spermatic fascia **(Correct)** — Correct. Direct inguinal hernia: medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through a weak transversalis fascia, common in older men.
   - **C.** It is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels — Wrong. Indirect hernia.
   - **D.** It passes below the inguinal ligament — Wrong. Femoral hernia.
   - **E.** It occurs most often in infants — Wrong. Indirect hernia.
   - **F.** It results from a patent processus vaginalis — Wrong. Indirect hernia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 70-year-old man — Acquired weakness in older men.
     - does not enter the scrotum — Direct hernias rarely reach the scrotum.
     - medial to the inferior epigastric vessels — Defines a direct hernia.
   - **Reasoning:** Older man + groin bulge medial to the inferior epigastric vessels → direct hernia through Hesselbach triangle.
   - **Teaching point:** "MDs don't LIe": Medial = Direct, Lateral = Indirect.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best describes this hernia?
   - Page: 377

303. A 46-year-old man who drinks a pint of vodka daily has fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. The liver is enlarged and tender. His test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Alcohol-associated hepatitis
   - **A.** Ground-glass hepatocytes — Wrong. Hepatitis B.
   - **B.** Councilman bodies from viral injury alone — Wrong. Acute viral hepatitis.
   - **C.** Granulomatous destruction of bile ducts — Wrong. PBC.
   - **D.** Centrilobular congestion — Wrong. Budd-Chiari.
   - **E.** PAS-positive globules — Wrong. α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
   - **F.** Swollen, necrotic hepatocytes with Mallory bodies and neutrophils **(Correct)** — Correct. Alcohol-associated hepatitis: ballooning, Mallory bodies (damaged keratin) and neutrophil infiltration; AST:ALT ratio >2.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - drinks a pint of vodka daily — Heavy alcohol use.
     - fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice — Acute alcohol-associated hepatitis.
     - The liver is enlarged and tender — Hepatomegaly.
   - **Reasoning:** Heavy drinking + fever, RUQ pain, jaundice + AST:ALT >2 with AST <500, high GGT, macrocytosis (table) → alcohol-associated hepatitis → Mallory bodies.
   - **Teaching point:** "Make a toAST with alcohol": AST > ALT (ratio > 2).
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is most likely to be seen on liver biopsy?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       "head": [

       ],
       "rows": [

         ],
         [

         ],

         ],

         ],

         ],
         [
           "MCV",
           "104 fL",
           "80–100"
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Laboratory results
   - Page: 398

304. A 52-year-old woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridemia has mildly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 82 U/L, AST 54 U/L). She drinks alcohol only on special occasions. Hepatitis serologies are negative. Ultrasound shows a bright, echogenic liver.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** MASLD
   - **A.** Alcohol-associated fatty liver — Wrong. Minimal alcohol use; AST:ALT would be >2.
   - **B.** Hemochromatosis — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **C.** Wilson disease — Wrong. Young patients.
   - **D.** Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease **(Correct)** — Correct. MASLD: fatty infiltration associated with metabolic syndrome; ALT > AST.
   - **E.** Budd-Chiari syndrome — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **F.** Autoimmune hepatitis — Wrong. Autoantibodies and plasma cells.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - obesity, type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridemia — Metabolic syndrome.
     - ALT 82 U/L, AST 54 U/L — ALT > AST.
     - drinks alcohol only on special occasions — Excludes alcohol-associated disease.
     - bright, echogenic liver — Steatosis.
   - **Reasoning:** Metabolic syndrome + ALT > AST + minimal alcohol + echogenic liver → MASLD.
   - **Teaching point:** ALT > AST: "lipids" (MASLD); AST > ALT: alcohol.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 398

305. A 32-year-old woman who has taken oral contraceptive pills for 12 years has sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg. CT shows a 7-cm solitary liver mass with hemorrhage and free intraperitoneal blood. α-Fetoprotein is normal.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hepatic adenoma
   - **A.** Hepatic adenoma **(Correct)** — Correct. Benign tumor linked to oral contraceptives and anabolic steroids; can rupture and bleed.
   - **B.** Liver abscess — Wrong. Fever.
   - **C.** Focal nodular hyperplasia — Wrong. Central scar, rarely bleeds.
   - **D.** Hepatic hemangioma — Wrong. Biopsy risk, but rarely ruptures spontaneously.
   - **E.** Hepatocellular carcinoma — Wrong. AFP normal, no cirrhosis.
   - **F.** Angiosarcoma — Wrong. Vinyl chloride.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - oral contraceptive pills for 12 years — Main risk factor.
     - sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and lightheadedness — Rupture with hemorrhage.
     - solitary liver mass with hemorrhage — Adenoma bleeding.
     - α-Fetoprotein is normal — Argues against HCC.
   - **Reasoning:** Young woman on OCPs + solitary liver mass + rupture with hemoperitoneum → hepatic adenoma.
   - **Teaching point:** OCPs + liver mass that bleeds = hepatic adenoma.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 399

306. A 40-year-old woman has a 3-cm liver mass found incidentally on ultrasound for gallbladder evaluation. She is asymptomatic and liver enzymes are normal. Contrast CT shows peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in toward the center on delayed images.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hepatic hemangioma
   - **A.** Stop oral contraceptives — Wrong. Adenoma.
   - **B.** Surgical resection — Wrong. Not needed for an asymptomatic lesion.
   - **C.** Chemotherapy — Wrong. Benign.
   - **D.** Percutaneous biopsy — Wrong. Contraindicated because of hemorrhage risk.
   - **E.** Liver transplantation — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **F.** No treatment; reassurance **(Correct)** — Correct. Cavernous hemangioma, the most common benign liver tumor; biopsy is contraindicated and asymptomatic lesions need no treatment.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - found incidentally — Usually asymptomatic.
     - liver enzymes are normal — Benign.
     - peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in toward the center — Classic hemangioma imaging.
   - **Reasoning:** Incidental liver mass + peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill → hemangioma → no biopsy, observe.
   - **Teaching point:** Never biopsy a hemangioma.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
   - Page: 399

307. A 22-year-old college student notices that the whites of his eyes turn yellow during exam week, when he skips meals, and during colds. Examination is otherwise normal. Results before and after a 48-hour fast are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Gilbert syndrome
   - **A.** Splenectomy — Wrong. No hemolysis.
   - **B.** Liver biopsy — Wrong. Not needed.
   - **C.** Phototherapy — Wrong. Not needed.
   - **D.** ERCP — Wrong. No obstruction.
   - **E.** Reassurance **(Correct)** — Correct. Gilbert syndrome: mildly reduced UGT activity; benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with stress, fasting or illness.
   - **F.** Phenobarbital — Wrong. Used in Crigler-Najjar type II.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - during exam week, when he skips meals, and during colds — Stress, fasting and illness trigger jaundice.
     - Examination is otherwise normal — Benign condition.
     - whites of his eyes turn yellow — Scleral icterus appears at bilirubin around 2–3 mg/dL.
   - **Reasoning:** Intermittent jaundice with fasting/stress + isolated unconjugated rise + no hemolysis, normal enzymes (table) → Gilbert → reassurance.
   - **Teaching point:** Gilbert: unconjugated bilirubin rises with fasting; no hemolysis; no treatment.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
     {
       "type": "table",
       "head": [
         "Test",
         "Baseline",
         "After 48-hour fast"
       ],
       "rows": [
         [
           "Total bilirubin",
           "1.6 mg/dL",
           "3.4 mg/dL"
         ],
         [
           "Direct bilirubin",
           "0.2 mg/dL",
           "0.3 mg/dL"
         ],
         [
           "Hemoglobin",
           "15.2 g/dL",
           "15.1 g/dL"
         ],
         [
           "Reticulocytes",
           "1.0%",
           "1.0%"
         ],
         [
           "ALT / AST",
           "Normal",
           "Normal"
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Laboratory results
   - Page: 401

308. A 44-year-old woman with obesity has had constant right upper quadrant pain for 10 hours after a fatty meal, radiating to the right shoulder. Temperature is 38.3°C. She stops inhaling during deep palpation under the right costal margin. Bilirubin is normal. Results of a cholescintigraphy (HIDA) scan are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acute cholecystitis
   - **A.** Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **B.** Gallbladder cancer — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **C.** Obstruction of the cystic duct **(Correct)** — Correct. Acute cholecystitis: a stone blocks the cystic duct, so the gallbladder never fills.
   - **D.** Normal study — Wrong. Gallbladder should fill.
   - **E.** Common bile duct obstruction — Wrong. The duodenum fills.
   - **F.** Hepatocellular dysfunction — Wrong. The liver takes up tracer.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - constant right upper quadrant pain for 10 hours after a fatty meal — Persistent pain beyond simple biliary colic.
     - radiating to the right shoulder — Referred pain via the phrenic nerve.
     - stops inhaling during deep palpation — Murphy sign.
     - Bilirubin is normal — The common bile duct is not obstructed.
   - **Reasoning:** Fatty meal + prolonged RUQ pain + fever + Murphy sign + gallbladder never fills on HIDA (table) → cystic duct obstruction → acute cholecystitis.
   - **Teaching point:** HIDA: no gallbladder = cystic duct blocked; no duodenum = CBD blocked.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most likely cause of the scan findings?

     ```json
           "Visualized",
           "Not yet",
           "Not visualized",
           "Not yet"
         ],
         [

           "Visualized",
           "Not visualized",
           "Visualized"
         ],
         [
           "4 hours (after morphine)",
           "Fading",
           "Visualized",
           "Not visualized",
           "Visualized"
         ]
       ]

     ```

   - Page: 403

309. A 65-year-old woman with long-standing gallstones has an abdominal CT for back pain. It shows a gallbladder with a continuous rim of calcium in its wall. She has no abdominal symptoms.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Porcelain gallbladder
   - **A.** Observation only — Wrong. Malignancy risk.
   - **B.** Prophylactic cholecystectomy **(Correct)** — Correct. Porcelain gallbladder (calcified wall from chronic cholecystitis) is associated with gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
   - **C.** Repeat CT in 5 years — Wrong. Not appropriate.
   - **D.** Ursodiol therapy — Wrong. Not appropriate.
   - **E.** ERCP — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **F.** Shock wave lithotripsy — Wrong. Not appropriate.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - long-standing gallstones — Chronic cholecystitis.
     - continuous rim of calcium in its wall — Porcelain gallbladder.
     - no abdominal symptoms — Incidental finding.
   - **Reasoning:** Chronic gallstones → chronic cholecystitis → calcified wall (porcelain gallbladder) → cancer risk → cholecystectomy.
   - **Teaching point:** Porcelain gallbladder → think gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
   - Page: 403

310. A 50-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 25 years has chronic epigastric pain radiating to the back, bulky foul-smelling stools that float, and weight loss. He was recently diagnosed with diabetes. His test results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Chronic pancreatitis
   - **A.** Thiamine only — Wrong. Alcohol-related, but not from pancreatic insufficiency.
   - **B.** Biotin — Wrong. Not linked.
   - **C.** Folate only — Wrong. Not the main issue.
   - **D.** Vitamin A, D, E and K **(Correct)** — Correct. Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency causes fat malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.
   - **E.** Niacin only — Wrong. Not the main issue.
   - **F.** Vitamin C — Wrong. Water-soluble, not linked.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - drunk heavily for 25 years — Most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults.
     - bulky foul-smelling stools that float — Steatorrhea.
     - recently diagnosed with diabetes — Endocrine insufficiency.
     - epigastric pain radiating to the back — Pancreatic pain.
   - **Reasoning:** Alcohol + chronic pain + steatorrhea + diabetes + calcifications, low fecal elastase, normal lipase (table) → chronic pancreatitis → fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
   - **Teaching point:** In chronic pancreatitis, lipase may be normal; the pancreas has burned out.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely to develop?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       ],

         ],

         ],

           ""
         ],

         ],

         ]
       ]
     ```
