403. A 22-year-old African American man has had one episode of painless hematuria. He has never had pain crises. His hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL. Hemoglobin electrophoresis of his sample (lane 3) is shown with control lanes. In each lane, bands closer to the wells (origin, cathode) are, from top to bottom: HbC, HbS, HbF, HbA.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Sickle cell trait
   - **A.** Renal papillary necrosis from sickling in the hypoxic medulla **(Correct)** — Correct. Sickle cell trait (HbA and HbS bands); sickling in the low-Po2 renal medulla causes papillary necrosis.
   - **B.** Kidney stones from hypercalciuria — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **C.** Bladder cancer — Wrong. Unlikely at 22.
   - **D.** Renal cell carcinoma — Wrong. Not the classic association.
   - **E.** IgA nephropathy — Wrong. Not suggested by the findings.
   - **F.** Glomerular thrombotic microangiopathy — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - African American man — Population with high HbS prevalence.
     - never had pain crises — Trait, not disease.
     - hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL — No anemia.
     - painless hematuria — Papillary necrosis.
   - **Reasoning:** No crises, no anemia + HbA and HbS bands (figure) → sickle cell trait → medullary sickling → papillary necrosis → hematuria.
   - **Teaching point:** Electrophoresis order from origin: C, S, F, A ("A Fat Santa Claus" read from the anode).
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains his hematuria?

404. A 2-year-old girl living in an old rented apartment has irritability, constipation and abdominal pain. She chews on windowsills. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL and MCV is 68 fL. Peripheral smear shows fine blue dots throughout the red cells.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Lead poisoning
   - **A.** Porphobilinogen deaminase — Wrong. AIP.
   - **B.** Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase — Wrong. PCT.
   - **C.** Ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase **(Correct)** — Correct. Lead poisoning inhibits both, causing microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling.
   - **D.** Pyruvate kinase — Wrong. PK deficiency.
   - **E.** ALA synthase — Wrong. B6-dependent; X-linked sideroblastic anemia.
   - **F.** Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase — Wrong. G6PD deficiency.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - living in an old rented apartment — Lead paint in houses built before 1978.
     - chews on windowsills — Pica with paint chips.
     - fine blue dots throughout the red cells — Basophilic stippling.
     - constipation and abdominal pain — Lead colic.
   - **Reasoning:** Child in old housing + pica + colic + microcytic anemia + basophilic stippling → lead poisoning → inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase.
   - **Teaching point:** Lead: LLEEAAD — Lead lines, Encephalopathy, Erythrocyte stippling, Abdominal colic, Anemia, Drops.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following enzymes is inhibited in this patient?
   - Page: 425

405. A 45-year-old man started treatment for latent tuberculosis 4 months ago. He now has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.3 g/dL and MCV is 74 fL. Serum iron and ferritin are elevated. Bone marrow aspirate shows erythroid precursors with perinuclear blue granules on Prussian blue stain.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Sideroblastic anemia
   - **A.** Oral iron — Wrong. Iron is already high.
   - **B.** Vitamin B12 — Wrong. Not the cause.
   - **C.** Splenectomy — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **D.** Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) **(Correct)** — Correct. Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency; B6 is the cofactor for ALA synthase. This is sideroblastic anemia.
   - **E.** Succimer — Wrong. Lead.
   - **F.** Folate — Wrong. Not the cause.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - treatment for latent tuberculosis — Isoniazid.
     - Serum iron and ferritin are elevated — Iron loading.
     - perinuclear blue granules on Prussian blue stain — Ringed sideroblasts.
     - MCV is 74 fL — Microcytic anemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Isoniazid → B6 deficiency → ALA synthase cannot work → ringed sideroblasts, high iron → pyridoxine.
   - **Teaching point:** INH depletes B6 → neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
   - Page: 425

406. A 64-year-old woman with vitiligo has numbness of her feet and unsteadiness in the dark. She has decreased vibration and position sense in her legs, a positive Romberg sign and brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantar responses. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL with an MCV of 121 fL. Neutrophils have 6 nuclear lobes.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Vitamin B12 deficiency
   - **A.** Elevated orotic acid — Wrong. Orotic aciduria.
   - **B.** Low ferritin — Wrong. Iron deficiency.
   - **C.** Elevated homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid — Wrong. Folate deficiency.
   - **D.** Positive direct Coombs test — Wrong. AIHA.
   - **E.** Elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine **(Correct)** — Correct. Vitamin B12 deficiency (here likely pernicious anemia) raises both.
   - **F.** Low haptoglobin — Wrong. Hemolysis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - vitiligo — Associated autoimmune disease (pernicious anemia).
     - decreased vibration and position sense — Dorsal column involvement.
     - brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantar responses — Lateral corticospinal tract involvement.
     - MCV of 121 fL — Megaloblastic anemia.
     - 6 nuclear lobes — Hypersegmented neutrophils.
   - **Reasoning:** Autoimmune background + subacute combined degeneration + megaloblastic anemia → B12 deficiency → high MMA and homocysteine.
   - **Teaching point:** Neurologic signs + macrocytosis = B12, not folate.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following laboratory findings would confirm the underlying vitamin deficiency?
   - Page: 426

407. A 10-year-old boy has intermittent jaundice and an enlarged spleen. His father had his spleen removed as a teenager. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, MCHC is 37.5 g/dL and reticulocytes are 9%. The smear shows small round red cells without central pallor. The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hereditary spherocytosis
   - **A.** Flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 — Wrong. PNH.
   - **B.** Hemoglobin electrophoresis — Wrong. Hemoglobinopathies.
   - **C.** Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test **(Correct)** — Correct. Hereditary spherocytosis shows decreased EMA fluorescence (or increased osmotic fragility).
   - **D.** Serum ferritin — Wrong. Not diagnostic.
   - **E.** Bone marrow biopsy — Wrong. Not needed.
   - **F.** G6PD activity — Wrong. G6PD deficiency.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - His father had his spleen removed — Autosomal dominant inheritance; splenectomy is treatment.
     - MCHC is 37.5 g/dL — Increased MCHC.
     - small round red cells without central pallor — Spherocytes.
     - direct antiglobulin test is negative — Excludes AIHA.
   - **Reasoning:** Family history + splenomegaly + spherocytes + high MCHC + Coombs negative → hereditary spherocytosis → EMA binding test.
   - **Teaching point:** Spherocytes + Coombs negative = hereditary spherocytosis; Coombs positive = AIHA.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following tests would best confirm the diagnosis?
   - Page: 428

408. A 28-year-old man from Greece develops dark urine and back pain 3 days after starting primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Hemoglobin falls from 14.2 to 9.6 g/dL. The smear shows red cells with semicircular defects at the edge.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** G6PD deficiency
   - **A.** Heinz bodies **(Correct)** — Correct. G6PD deficiency: oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin; splenic removal leaves bite cells.
   - **B.** Basophilic stippling — Wrong. Lead, thalassemia.
   - **C.** Auer rods — Wrong. AML.
   - **D.** Howell-Jolly bodies — Wrong. Asplenia.
   - **E.** Pappenheimer bodies — Wrong. Sideroblastic anemia.
   - **F.** Ringed sideroblasts — Wrong. Bone marrow, sideroblastic anemia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - from Greece — Mediterranean ancestry.
     - 3 days after starting primaquine — Oxidant drug.
     - dark urine and back pain — Intravascular hemolysis.
     - semicircular defects at the edge — Bite cells.
   - **Reasoning:** Mediterranean man + oxidant drug → hemolysis with bite cells → G6PD deficiency → Heinz bodies.
   - **Teaching point:** "Stress makes me eat bites of fava beans with Heinz ketchup."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following inclusions would be seen with a supravital stain?
   - Page: 428

409. A 33-year-old woman has fatigue, dark morning urine and abdominal pain. She has hepatomegaly and ascites. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, WBC count is 2,900/mm³ and platelets are 88,000/mm³. LDH is high and haptoglobin is undetectable. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Doppler ultrasound shows hepatic vein thrombosis.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
   - **A.** Splenectomy — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **B.** Hydroxyurea — Wrong. Sickle cell disease.
   - **C.** Rituximab — Wrong. AIHA, TTP.
   - **D.** Eculizumab **(Correct)** — Correct. PNH: complement-mediated hemolysis from loss of CD55/CD59; eculizumab blocks C5.
   - **E.** Plasma exchange — Wrong. TTP.
   - **F.** Prednisone — Wrong. Not targeted.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - dark morning urine — Hemoglobinuria after nocturnal hemolysis.
     - WBC count is 2,900/mm³ and platelets are 88,000/mm³ — Pancytopenia.
     - direct antiglobulin test is negative — Not antibody-mediated.
     - hepatic vein thrombosis — Venous thrombosis (Budd-Chiari).
   - **Reasoning:** Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis + pancytopenia + Budd-Chiari → PNH (PIGA, CD55/59 loss) → eculizumab.
   - **Teaching point:** PNH triad: hemolysis, pancytopenia, thrombosis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate targeted treatment?
   - Page: 428

410. A 70-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia has worsening fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL with reticulocytes of 11%. The smear shows spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG and negative for complement.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
   - **A.** Plasma exchange — Wrong. TTP.
   - **B.** Folate alone — Wrong. Supportive only.
   - **C.** Iron supplements — Wrong. Not the cause.
   - **D.** Cold avoidance — Wrong. Cold AIHA.
   - **E.** Eculizumab — Wrong. PNH.
   - **F.** Glucocorticoids **(Correct)** — Correct. Warm AIHA (IgG, extravascular) is treated with steroids, then rituximab or splenectomy.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chronic lymphocytic leukemia — Associated with warm AIHA.
     - spherocytes — Partial phagocytosis in the spleen.
     - positive for IgG and negative for complement — Warm antibody.
     - reticulocytes of 11% — Marrow compensation.
   - **Reasoning:** CLL + spherocytes + IgG-positive Coombs → warm AIHA → glucocorticoids.
   - **Teaching point:** "Warm weather is Good" (IgG); cold is IgM + complement.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
   - Page: 429

411. A 19-year-old college student has a dry cough and low-grade fever for 2 weeks. Chest x-ray shows patchy interstitial infiltrates. When she goes outside in winter, her fingertips turn blue and painful. A blood sample clumps visibly when cooled.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia
   - **A.** IgE — Wrong. Allergy.
   - **B.** IgM with complement **(Correct)** — Correct. Cold agglutinin disease after Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection.
   - **C.** Anti-platelet factor 4 IgG — Wrong. HIT.
   - **D.** IgA — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Anti-D IgG — Wrong. Rh disease.
   - **F.** IgG — Wrong. Warm AIHA.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - dry cough and low-grade fever for 2 weeks — Atypical pneumonia.
     - patchy interstitial infiltrates — Mycoplasma pattern.
     - fingertips turn blue and painful — Cold agglutination in the extremities.
     - clumps visibly when cooled — Cold agglutinins.
   - **Reasoning:** Walking pneumonia + cold-induced acrocyanosis + agglutination when cooled → cold AIHA (IgM + complement) from Mycoplasma.
   - **Teaching point:** Cold AIHA: Mycoplasma, mono, CLL.
   - **Follow-up:** Which antibody type is most likely responsible for her hematologic findings?
   - Page: 429

412. A 26-year-old woman develops fatigue, gum bleeding and recurrent infections. She was treated with chloramphenicol for a severe infection 2 months ago. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, WBC count is 1,400/mm³, platelets are 18,000/mm³ and reticulocytes are 0.2%. No blasts are seen.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Aplastic anemia
   - **A.** Increased megakaryocytes — Wrong. ITP.
   - **B.** Hypercellular marrow with >20% blasts — Wrong. Acute leukemia.
   - **C.** Megaloblastic changes — Wrong. B12/folate deficiency.
   - **D.** Fibrosis with teardrop cells — Wrong. Myelofibrosis.
   - **E.** Hypocellular marrow replaced by fat **(Correct)** — Correct. Aplastic anemia from drug-induced stem cell injury.
   - **F.** Ringed sideroblasts — Wrong. Sideroblastic anemia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chloramphenicol — Classic drug cause.
     - Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, WBC count is 1,400/mm³, platelets are 18,000/mm³ — Pancytopenia.
     - reticulocytes are 0.2% — Marrow failure.
     - No blasts are seen — Argues against leukemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Drug exposure + pancytopenia + low reticulocytes, no blasts → aplastic anemia → fatty, hypocellular marrow.
   - **Teaching point:** Aplastic anemia: empty marrow, normal-looking cells.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is most likely to be seen on bone marrow biopsy?
   - Page: 427

413. A 58-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL with an MCV of 82 fL. Serum iron is low, TIBC is low and ferritin is elevated. CRP is high.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Anemia of chronic disease
   - **A.** Chronic blood loss from NSAIDs — Wrong. Would cause high TIBC and low ferritin.
   - **B.** Bone marrow infiltration — Wrong. Not suggested.
   - **C.** Autoimmune hemolysis — Wrong. Not consistent.
   - **D.** Methotrexate-induced folate deficiency — Wrong. Would be macrocytic.
   - **E.** Increased hepcidin blocking ferroportin **(Correct)** — Correct. Anemia of chronic disease: IL-6 raises hepcidin, trapping iron in macrophages.
   - **F.** Hemochromatosis — Wrong. Iron would be high.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - long-standing rheumatoid arthritis — Chronic inflammation.
     - TIBC is low and ferritin is elevated — Iron sequestration pattern.
     - CRP is high — Active inflammation (IL-6).
     - MCV of 82 fL — Normocytic.
   - **Reasoning:** Chronic inflammation + low iron, low TIBC, high ferritin → anemia of chronic disease → hepcidin.
   - **Teaching point:** Iron deficiency: TIBC up, ferritin down. Chronic disease: both reversed.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains her anemia?
   - Page: 427

414. A 6-year-old boy has a swollen, painful left knee after falling off his bicycle. He has had prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction. Platelet count, bleeding time and PT are normal; PTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing. His family pedigree is shown; the arrow marks the patient.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hemophilia A
   - **A.** Factor VIII **(Correct)** — Correct. Hemophilia A: X-linked recessive (affected males through carrier females), hemarthrosis, isolated prolonged PTT.
   - **B.** Fibrinogen — Wrong. Prolongs PT and PTT.
   - **C.** von Willebrand factor — Wrong. Mostly autosomal dominant; prolonged bleeding time.
   - **D.** Factor VII — Wrong. Prolongs PT.
   - **E.** Factor XIII — Wrong. Normal PT/PTT.
   - **F.** Factor XI — Wrong. Autosomal recessive (hemophilia C).
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - swollen, painful left knee — Hemarthrosis.
     - prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction — Bleeding after procedures.
     - PTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing — Intrinsic factor deficiency, not inhibitor.
     - bleeding time and PT are normal — Platelets and extrinsic pathway are normal.
   - **Reasoning:** Boy + hemarthrosis + isolated prolonged PTT that corrects + X-linked pedigree (affected uncle, carrier mother) → hemophilia A → factor VIII.
   - **Teaching point:** Hemophilia A "Ate" (eight); B = IX; both X-linked. C = XI, autosomal recessive.
   - **Follow-up:** Which factor is most likely deficient?

   - Page: 431

415. A 17-year-old girl has heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and frequent nosebleeds. Her father bruises easily. Platelet count and PT are normal. Bleeding time is prolonged and PTT is mildly prolonged. Platelet agglutination with ristocetin is reduced and corrects when normal plasma is added.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** von Willebrand disease
   - **A.** Platelet transfusion — Wrong. Platelets are normal.
   - **B.** Factor IX concentrate — Wrong. Hemophilia B.
   - **C.** Vitamin K — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Desmopressin **(Correct)** — Correct. von Willebrand disease: releases stored vWF and factor VIII from endothelial cells.
   - **E.** Aspirin — Wrong. Worsens bleeding.
   - **F.** Fresh frozen plasma only — Wrong. Not first line.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and frequent nosebleeds — Mucosal bleeding.
     - Her father bruises easily — Autosomal dominant.
     - PTT is mildly prolonged — vWF protects factor VIII.
     - corrects when normal plasma is added — vWF deficiency, unlike Bernard-Soulier.
   - **Reasoning:** Mucosal bleeding + AD inheritance + long bleeding time + mildly long PTT + ristocetin defect corrected by plasma → vWD → desmopressin.
   - **Teaching point:** Ristocetin defect that corrects with plasma = vWD; does not correct = Bernard-Soulier.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the best treatment before a planned dental extraction?
   - Page: 433

416. A 5-year-old boy has new petechiae and bruising 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. He is otherwise well, with no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Hemoglobin and WBC count are normal. Platelet count is 9,000/mm³. The smear shows large platelets and no other abnormal cells.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Immune thrombocytopenia
   - **A.** GpIb deficiency — Wrong. Bernard-Soulier.
   - **B.** Shiga toxin endothelial injury — Wrong. HUS.
   - **C.** Antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa leading to splenic destruction **(Correct)** — Correct. Immune thrombocytopenia, commonly after a viral illness in children.
   - **D.** Decreased platelet production from marrow infiltration — Wrong. Other lines are normal and no blasts are seen.
   - **E.** Deficiency of ADAMTS13 — Wrong. TTP.
   - **F.** Consumption of clotting factors — Wrong. DIC.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection — Postviral ITP in children.
     - no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly — Argues against leukemia.
     - Hemoglobin and WBC count are normal — Isolated thrombocytopenia.
     - large platelets — Young platelets from active marrow.
   - **Reasoning:** Child + recent virus + isolated severe thrombocytopenia + otherwise normal → ITP → anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies.
   - **Teaching point:** Isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child after a virus = ITP.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?
   - Page: 432

417. A 34-year-old woman is brought in confused with a fever of 38.6°C. She has petechiae on her legs. Her laboratory results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
   - **A.** Platelet transfusion — Wrong. May worsen thrombosis.
   - **B.** Cryoprecipitate — Wrong. Fibrinogen is normal.
   - **C.** Heparin — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **D.** IVIG — Wrong. ITP.
   - **E.** Supportive care only — Wrong. HUS in children.
   - **F.** Plasma exchange **(Correct)** — Correct. TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves large vWF multimers; plasma exchange (with steroids, rituximab).
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - confused — Neurologic symptoms.
     - fever of 38.6°C — Fever.
     - petechiae on her legs — Thrombocytopenia.
   - **Reasoning:** Fever + neurologic changes + MAHA (schistocytes, high LDH) + thrombocytopenia + AKI with normal PT/PTT (table) → TTP → plasma exchange.
   - **Teaching point:** Normal PT/PTT separates TTP/HUS from DIC.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
   - **Exhibit:**

         ],

         ],

           "Normal",
           ""
         ],
         [
           "Fibrinogen",
           "Normal",
           ""
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Laboratory results
   - Page: 432

418. A 3-year-old boy had bloody diarrhea after a petting zoo visit 6 days ago. He is now pale, lethargic and passing little urine. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, platelets are 42,000/mm³ and creatinine is 2.8 mg/dL. The smear shows helmet-shaped red cell fragments. PT and PTT are normal.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hemolytic-uremic syndrome
   - **A.** Splenectomy — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **B.** Supportive care, including dialysis if needed **(Correct)** — Correct. HUS from Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7.
   - **C.** Platelet transfusion routinely — Wrong. Not routine.
   - **D.** Rituximab — Wrong. TTP.
   - **E.** Plasma exchange — Wrong. TTP.
   - **F.** Antibiotics for E. coli — Wrong. May increase toxin release.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bloody diarrhea after a petting zoo visit — STEC exposure.
     - passing little urine — Acute kidney injury.
     - helmet-shaped red cell fragments — Schistocytes.
     - PT and PTT are normal — Not DIC.
   - **Reasoning:** Child + bloody diarrhea + MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI → HUS (Shiga toxin) → supportive care.
   - **Teaching point:** HUS = triad + bloody diarrhea; TTP = triad + fever + neurologic symptoms.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
   - Page: 432

419. A 41-year-old man has gum bleeding and easy bruising for 1 week. He is oozing from his venipuncture sites. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, WBC count is 32,000/mm³ and platelets are 21,000/mm³. PT and PTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is very high. Bone marrow shows many abnormal promyelocytes containing bundles of rod-shaped inclusions.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acute promyelocytic leukemia with DIC
   - **A.** Imatinib — Wrong. BCR-ABL.
   - **B.** Cladribine — Wrong. Hairy cell.
   - **C.** Rituximab — Wrong. CD20.
   - **D.** All-trans retinoic acid **(Correct)** — Correct. APL with t(15;17) PML-RARα; ATRA (and arsenic) induce differentiation. DIC is a common presentation.
   - **E.** Ruxolitinib — Wrong. JAK2.
   - **F.** Hydroxyurea — Wrong. Not targeted.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - oozing from his venipuncture sites — DIC.
     - fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is very high — Consumptive coagulopathy.
     - abnormal promyelocytes — APL.
     - bundles of rod-shaped inclusions — Multiple Auer rods (faggot cells).
   - **Reasoning:** DIC + abnormal promyelocytes with Auer rods → APL, t(15;17) → all-trans retinoic acid.
   - **Teaching point:** APL is the leukemia that presents with DIC and is treated with vitamin A.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following drugs targets the underlying molecular defect?
   - Page: 437

420. A 62-year-old man is started on unfractionated heparin after hip replacement. His platelet counts over the following days are shown. On day 8 his left leg becomes swollen; ultrasound shows a deep vein thrombosis.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
   - **A.** Stop heparin and start argatroban **(Correct)** — Correct. HIT type 2: a >50% fall 5–10 days after heparin with thrombosis; use a direct thrombin inhibitor (or fondaparinux).
   - **B.** Start warfarin alone immediately — Wrong. Risk of skin necrosis; not alone in acute HIT.
   - **C.** Switch to enoxaparin — Wrong. Cross-reacts with HIT antibodies.
   - **D.** Observe; this is HIT type 1 — Wrong. Type 1 is mild and in the first 2 days.
   - **E.** Give protamine — Wrong. Does not treat HIT.
   - **F.** Continue heparin and transfuse platelets — Wrong. Fuels thrombosis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - unfractionated heparin — Highest HIT risk.
     - On day 8 — Typical timing (5–10 days).
     - deep vein thrombosis — HIT causes thrombosis, not bleeding.
   - **Reasoning:** Heparin + platelets fall >50% after day 5 (figure) + new thrombosis → HIT type 2 (anti-PF4/heparin IgG) → stop heparin, start argatroban.
   - **Teaching point:** HIT: platelets go down, clots go up.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

   - Page: 440

421. A 29-year-old woman has her second deep vein thrombosis. Her first occurred while taking oral contraceptives. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 40. PT and PTT are normal. In a clotting assay, adding activated protein C fails to prolong her PTT normally.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Factor V Leiden
   - **A.** Antiphospholipid antibodies — Wrong. Prolonged PTT, not APC resistance.
   - **B.** Protein C deficiency — Wrong. APC added in the test would still work.
   - **C.** Mutation in the 3′ untranslated region of prothrombin — Wrong. Prothrombin G20210A; increases prothrombin levels.
   - **D.** JAK2 mutation — Wrong. Polycythemia vera.
   - **E.** Antithrombin deficiency — Wrong. Diminished heparin response.
   - **F.** Arg506Gln mutation in factor V **(Correct)** — Correct. Factor V Leiden resists inactivation by activated protein C.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - her second deep vein thrombosis — Recurrent venous thrombosis.
     - Her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 40 — Autosomal dominant family history.
     - adding activated protein C fails to prolong her PTT normally — APC resistance.
     - while taking oral contraceptives — An added estrogen trigger.
   - **Reasoning:** Recurrent VTE + family history + APC resistance → factor V Leiden (Arg506Gln).
   - **Teaching point:** APC resistance = factor V Leiden, the most common inherited thrombophilia.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely molecular defect?
   - Page: 433

422. A 50-year-old woman is started on warfarin alone for a new deep vein thrombosis. On day 3 she develops painful purple patches on her thighs and abdomen that become black and necrotic.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Warfarin skin necrosis
   - **A.** Warfarin-induced thrombocytopenia — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Allergic vasculitis — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **C.** Early depletion of protein C before procoagulant factors fall **(Correct)** — Correct. Protein C has a short half-life; a transient hypercoagulable state causes microthrombi and skin necrosis, especially with protein C deficiency.
   - **D.** Vitamin K excess — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Heparin-induced antibodies — Wrong. No heparin given.
   - **F.** Calcium deposition in vessels — Wrong. Calciphylaxis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - started on warfarin alone — No heparin bridge.
     - On day 3 — Early in therapy.
     - painful purple patches on her thighs and abdomen — Fatty areas typical of warfarin necrosis.
     - black and necrotic — Microthrombosis.
   - **Reasoning:** Warfarin without bridging → protein C falls first → transient hypercoagulability → skin necrosis.
   - **Teaching point:** Bridge with heparin until warfarin is therapeutic.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains this complication?
   - Page: 441

423. A 63-year-old woman receives a unit of fresh frozen plasma before a procedure. Within 3 hours she develops fever, severe dyspnea and hypotension. Oxygen saturation is 82%. Chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates. Jugular venous pressure is normal and BNP is not elevated.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Transfusion reactions
   - **A.** Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction — Wrong. Hemoglobinuria, back pain.
   - **B.** Transfusion-associated circulatory overload — Wrong. Hypertension, high JVP, high BNP.
   - **C.** Febrile nonhemolytic reaction — Wrong. No lung injury.
   - **D.** Bacterial sepsis from the unit — Wrong. Less consistent.
   - **E.** Transfusion-related acute lung injury **(Correct)** — Correct. TRALI: noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with hypotension within 6 hours.
   - **F.** Anaphylaxis from IgA deficiency — Wrong. Urticaria, bronchospasm, immediate.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Within 3 hours — TRALI occurs within 6 hours.
     - hypotension — TACO causes hypertension.
     - new bilateral infiltrates — Pulmonary edema.
     - Jugular venous pressure is normal and BNP is not elevated — Noncardiogenic.
   - **Reasoning:** Plasma transfusion → hypoxia + hypotension + bilateral infiltrates without volume overload → TRALI.
   - **Teaching point:** TRALI = hypotension, normal BNP; TACO = hypertension, high BNP.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
   - Page: 434

424. A 23-year-old woman has a painless neck mass and night sweats for 2 months. Chest x-ray shows a mediastinal mass. Biopsy of a cervical node shows bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules, with scattered large cells with bilobed nuclei and prominent nucleoli.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Hodgkin lymphoma
   - **A.** CD1a and S-100 — Wrong. Langerhans cells.
   - **B.** CD15 and CD30 **(Correct)** — Correct. Reed-Sternberg cells in nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma.
   - **C.** CD3 and CD4 — Wrong. Helper T cells.
   - **D.** CD16 and CD56 — Wrong. NK cells.
   - **E.** CD5 and CD23 — Wrong. CLL.
   - **F.** CD10 and TdT — Wrong. ALL.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 23-year-old woman — Young adult peak of the bimodal distribution.
     - night sweats — B symptoms.
     - mediastinal mass — Typical of nodular sclerosis.
     - bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules — Nodular sclerosis.
     - bilobed nuclei and prominent nucleoli — "Owl eye" Reed-Sternberg cells.
   - **Reasoning:** Young woman + B symptoms + mediastinal mass + collagen bands + RS cells → nodular sclerosis Hodgkin → CD15+/CD30+.
   - **Teaching point:** "2 owl eyes × 15 = 30."
   - **Follow-up:** The large cells are most likely positive for which markers?
   - Page: 434

425. A 14-year-old boy has a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass and bowel obstruction over 3 weeks. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized lymphocytes with a very high proliferation rate and scattered pale macrophages containing debris, giving a "starry sky" appearance.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Burkitt lymphoma
   - **A.** BCR-ABL — Wrong. CML.
   - **B.** c-myc **(Correct)** — Correct. Burkitt lymphoma, t(8;14).
   - **C.** PML-RARα — Wrong. APL.
   - **D.** Cyclin D1 — Wrong. Mantle cell.
   - **E.** BCL-2 — Wrong. Follicular lymphoma.
   - **F.** ALK — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - rapidly enlarging abdominal mass — Sporadic Burkitt affects the abdomen.
     - 14-year-old boy — Children and young adults.
     - very high proliferation rate — Extremely aggressive.
     - "starry sky" appearance — Tingible body macrophages.
   - **Reasoning:** Adolescent + fast-growing abdominal mass + starry sky → Burkitt → t(8;14) c-myc.
   - **Teaching point:** Endemic Burkitt (Africa) = jaw; sporadic = abdomen/pelvis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which gene is overexpressed due to a chromosomal translocation in this tumor?
   - Page: 435

426. A 61-year-old woman has had painless swelling of lymph nodes in her neck and groin that has come and gone for 3 years. She feels well. Node biopsy shows closely packed follicles of small cleaved cells throughout the node.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Follicular lymphoma
   - **A.** Overexpression of cyclin D1 — Wrong. Mantle cell lymphoma, aggressive.
   - **B.** HTLV-1 infection — Wrong. Adult T-cell lymphoma.
   - **C.** Overexpression of an inhibitor of apoptosis from t(14;18) **(Correct)** — Correct. Follicular lymphoma: BCL-2 blocks apoptosis, so cells accumulate slowly (indolent).
   - **D.** EBV infection of T cells — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Constitutive tyrosine kinase activity — Wrong. CML.
   - **F.** Overexpression of c-myc driving rapid proliferation — Wrong. Burkitt.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - has come and gone for 3 years — Waxing and waning lymphadenopathy.
     - She feels well — Indolent.
     - closely packed follicles — Follicular architecture.
   - **Reasoning:** Older adult + painless waxing and waning nodes + follicular pattern → follicular lymphoma → t(14;18) BCL-2.
   - **Teaching point:** BCL-2 = "Big Cell Lives 2 long" — cells don't die.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following best explains the behavior of this tumor?
   - Page: 435

427. A 71-year-old man has back pain and fatigue. His laboratory results are shown. A skull x-ray shows multiple round, punched-out lesions.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Multiple myeloma
   - **A.** Langerhans cells with Birbeck granules — Wrong. LCH.
   - **B.** Hairy cells with TRAP positivity — Wrong. Hairy cell leukemia.
   - **C.** Reed-Sternberg cells — Wrong. Hodgkin.
   - **D.** Hypocellular fatty marrow — Wrong. Aplastic anemia.
   - **E.** More than 10% monoclonal plasma cells **(Correct)** — Correct. Multiple myeloma with CRAB features; the dipstick misses light chains (Bence Jones protein).
   - **F.** Ringed sideroblasts — Wrong. Sideroblastic anemia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - back pain — Lytic bone lesions.
     - punched-out lesions — Lytic lesions on x-ray.
     - fatigue — Anemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Hypercalcemia + renal failure + anemia + bone lesions (CRAB) + high globulin gap + light chain proteinuria missed by dipstick (table) → multiple myeloma → >10% clonal plasma cells.
   - **Teaching point:** A negative dipstick with heavy urine protein = light chains.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is most likely to be found on bone marrow biopsy?
   - **Exhibit:**

         ],

         ],

         ],

         ],

           ""
         ]

   - Page: 436

428. A 69-year-old man has headaches, blurred vision, recurrent nosebleeds and numbness in his feet. He has lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Funduscopy shows dilated, segmented retinal veins. Calcium and creatinine are normal and skeletal survey shows no lytic lesions.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Waldenström macroglobulinemia
   - **A.** IgA — Wrong. Myeloma.
   - **B.** Free κ light chains only — Wrong. Light chain myeloma.
   - **C.** IgG — Wrong. Multiple myeloma.
   - **D.** IgM **(Correct)** — Correct. Waldenström macroglobulinemia: large IgM causes hyperviscosity.
   - **E.** IgE — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** IgD — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - headaches, blurred vision, recurrent nosebleeds — Hyperviscosity.
     - numbness in his feet — Peripheral neuropathy.
     - dilated, segmented retinal veins — Sausage-link veins.
     - no lytic lesions — Unlike myeloma.
   - **Reasoning:** Hyperviscosity + neuropathy + lymphadenopathy, HSM + no CRAB → Waldenström → IgM spike.
   - **Teaching point:** IgM is the largest Ig ("macro"), so it thickens the blood.
   - **Follow-up:** Serum protein electrophoresis is most likely to show a monoclonal spike of which immunoglobulin?
   - Page: 436

429. A 4-year-old boy with Down syndrome has fever, pallor, bone pain and bruising for 3 weeks. He has hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL, platelets are 22,000/mm³ and WBC count is 48,000/mm³ with many blasts. Blasts are myeloperoxidase-negative, TdT-positive and CD10-positive.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
   - **A.** Thyroid — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Kidneys — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Bone cortex — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Skin only — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Lungs and liver — Wrong. Not the classic sanctuary sites.
   - **F.** Central nervous system and testes **(Correct)** — Correct. ALL spreads to the CNS and testes; prophylaxis and evaluation are needed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Down syndrome — Increased ALL risk.
     - bone pain — Marrow expansion.
     - TdT-positive and CD10-positive — Pre-B lymphoblasts.
     - myeloperoxidase-negative — Not myeloid.
   - **Reasoning:** Child with Down syndrome + marrow failure + TdT+, CD10+ blasts → B-ALL → CNS and testicular involvement.
   - **Teaching point:** ALL: TdT+ ("To da T and B precursors"), most common childhood cancer.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following sites should be evaluated because the disease often spreads there?
   - Page: 437

430. A 74-year-old man has lymphocytosis of 62,000/mm³ found on routine blood testing. He feels well and has mild lymphadenopathy. The smear shows small mature lymphocytes and many crushed cells. Flow cytometry shows a B-cell population positive for CD5, CD20 and CD23.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
   - **A.** Autoimmune hemolytic anemia **(Correct)** — Correct. CLL is associated with warm AIHA (and cold AIHA), hypogammaglobulinemia and Richter transformation.
   - **B.** Tumor in the mediastinum — Wrong. T-ALL.
   - **C.** Blast crisis to AML — Wrong. CML.
   - **D.** Hyperviscosity from IgM — Wrong. Waldenström.
   - **E.** Gingival hyperplasia — Wrong. Monocytic AML.
   - **F.** Disseminated intravascular coagulation — Wrong. APL.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 74-year-old man — Most common adult leukemia in older adults.
     - He feels well — Often asymptomatic.
     - many crushed cells — Smudge cells.
     - CD5, CD20 and CD23 — CLL immunophenotype.
   - **Reasoning:** Older adult + lymphocytosis + smudge cells + CD5+/CD23+ B cells → CLL → autoimmune hemolysis.
   - **Teaching point:** CLL = Crushed Little Lymphocytes.
   - **Follow-up:** Which complication is this patient at increased risk for?
   - Page: 437

431. A 52-year-old man has fatigue, left upper quadrant fullness and recurrent infections. The spleen extends to the pelvis. There is no lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, WBC count is 2,100/mm³ and platelets are 64,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspiration yields no material. Circulating lymphocytes have fine cytoplasmic projections and stain for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Hairy cell leukemia
   - **A.** Imatinib — Wrong. CML.
   - **B.** All-trans retinoic acid — Wrong. APL.
   - **C.** Cladribine **(Correct)** — Correct. Hairy cell leukemia responds to purine analogs (cladribine, pentostatin).
   - **D.** Busulfan — Wrong. Marrow ablation.
   - **E.** Bortezomib — Wrong. Myeloma.
   - **F.** Ruxolitinib — Wrong. PV.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - The spleen extends to the pelvis — Massive splenomegaly.
     - There is no lymphadenopathy — Typical of hairy cell leukemia.
     - Bone marrow aspiration yields no material — Dry tap from marrow fibrosis.
     - tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase — TRAP positive.
   - **Reasoning:** Middle-aged man + massive spleen + pancytopenia + dry tap + TRAP+ hairy cells → hairy cell leukemia → cladribine.
   - **Teaching point:** "TRAPped in a hairy situation"; BRAF mutation.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following drugs is first-line therapy?
   - Page: 437

432. A 58-year-old woman has fatigue, early satiety and an enlarged spleen. Her laboratory results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Chronic myelogenous leukemia
   - **A.** All-trans retinoic acid — Wrong. APL.
   - **B.** Imatinib **(Correct)** — Correct. CML (BCR-ABL, t[9;22]); a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
   - **C.** Phlebotomy — Wrong. PV.
   - **D.** Antibiotics for infection — Wrong. A leukemoid reaction has a high LAP score and no basophilia.
   - **E.** Cladribine — Wrong. Hairy cell.
   - **F.** Rituximab — Wrong. B-cell lymphoma.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - early satiety and an enlarged spleen — Splenomegaly.
     - fatigue — Anemia.
     - 58-year-old woman — Median age of CML is in the 60s.
   - **Reasoning:** Very high WBC with all stages of granulocytes + basophilia + low LAP score (table) + splenomegaly → CML → imatinib.
   - **Teaching point:** Low LAP + basophils = CML; high LAP = leukemoid reaction.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

         ]

     ```
     Laboratory results
   - Page: 437

433. A 60-year-old man has headaches, itching after hot showers and episodes of burning pain and redness in his feet. His face is ruddy and the spleen is palpable. Hemoglobin is 19.8 g/dL, WBC count is 13,500/mm³ and platelets are 590,000/mm³. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Serum erythropoietin is low.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Polycythemia vera
   - **A.** KIT D816V — Wrong. Mastocytosis.
   - **B.** FLT3-ITD — Wrong. AML.
   - **C.** BCR-ABL fusion — Wrong. CML.
   - **D.** JAK2 V617F **(Correct)** — Correct. Polycythemia vera: increased RBCs, WBCs and platelets with low EPO.
   - **E.** VHL mutation causing EPO secretion — Wrong. EPO would be high.
   - **F.** PML-RARα — Wrong. APL.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - itching after hot showers — Aquagenic pruritus.
     - burning pain and redness in his feet — Erythromelalgia.
     - Oxygen saturation is 98% — Not secondary to hypoxia.
     - Serum erythropoietin is low — Primary polycythemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Panmyelosis + aquagenic pruritus + erythromelalgia + normal O2 + low EPO → polycythemia vera → JAK2 V617F.
   - **Teaching point:** PV: EPO low (feedback); secondary polycythemia: EPO high.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most likely mutation?
   - Page: 438

434. A 72-year-old man has fatigue, weight loss and a massively enlarged spleen. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL. The smear shows teardrop-shaped red cells and nucleated red cells with immature granulocytes. Bone marrow aspiration yields no material, and biopsy shows dense reticulin and collagen fibrosis.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Myelofibrosis
   - **A.** TGF-β from atypical megakaryocytes **(Correct)** — Correct. Primary myelofibrosis: TGF-β stimulates fibroblasts.
   - **B.** Erythropoietin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Thrombopoietin deficiency — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** IL-6 from macrophages — Wrong. Anemia of chronic disease.
   - **E.** Hepcidin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** IL-5 — Wrong. Eosinophils.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - massively enlarged spleen — Extramedullary hematopoiesis.
     - teardrop-shaped red cells — Dacrocytes.
     - nucleated red cells with immature granulocytes — Leukoerythroblastic smear.
     - aspiration yields no material — Dry tap.
   - **Reasoning:** Massive splenomegaly + teardrop cells + leukoerythroblastic smear + dry tap with fibrosis → myelofibrosis → megakaryocyte TGF-β.
   - **Teaching point:** "Bone marrow cries because it's fibrosed."
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following mediators drives the bone marrow changes?
   - Page: 438

435. A 2-year-old boy has a scaly, red rash on his scalp, recurrent ear discharge and a tender swelling over the skull. Skull x-ray shows a punched-out lytic lesion. Biopsy shows sheets of cells with folded, grooved nuclei that are positive for S-100 and CD1a. Electron microscopy shows rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Langerhans cell histiocytosis
   - **A.** Plasma cells — Wrong. Myeloma.
   - **B.** Osteoclasts — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Melanocytes — Wrong. S-100+ but CD1a−.
   - **D.** Neural crest neuroblasts — Wrong. Neuroblastoma.
   - **E.** Antigen-presenting cells of the skin **(Correct)** — Correct. Langerhans cell histiocytosis: Birbeck granules ("tennis rackets"); CD207+.
   - **F.** Mast cells — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - scaly, red rash on his scalp — Skin involvement.
     - recurrent ear discharge — Otitis media with mastoid involvement.
     - punched-out lytic lesion — Lytic bone lesion.
     - S-100 and CD1a — Langerhans cell markers.
     - rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules — Birbeck granules.
   - **Reasoning:** Child + lytic skull lesion + rash + otitis + S-100/CD1a+ cells with Birbeck granules → Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
   - **Teaching point:** LCH: CD1a, CD207 (langerin), Birbeck "tennis racket" granules.
   - **Follow-up:** Which normal cell type do these tumor cells most resemble?
   - Page: 439

436. A 30-year-old man with bulky diffuse large B-cell lymphoma starts chemotherapy. Twenty-four hours later he has muscle cramps and palpitations, and urine output falls. ECG shows peaked T waves. Potassium is 6.9 mEq/L, phosphate is 8.8 mg/dL, calcium is 6.8 mg/dL and uric acid is 14 mg/dL.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Tumor lysis syndrome
   - **A.** Probenecid — Wrong. Uricosuric; worsens renal precipitation.
   - **B.** Sodium bicarbonate — Wrong. Not recommended; can worsen calcium phosphate precipitation.
   - **C.** Colchicine — Wrong. Gout flares.
   - **D.** Allopurinol — Wrong. Prevents new uric acid formation; does not break down existing urate.
   - **E.** Febuxostat — Wrong. Xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
   - **F.** Rasburicase **(Correct)** — Correct. Recombinant uricase converts uric acid to allantoin in tumor lysis syndrome.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bulky diffuse large B-cell lymphoma — High tumor burden.
     - Twenty-four hours later — Shortly after starting chemotherapy.
     - peaked T waves — Hyperkalemia.
     - urine output falls — Acute kidney injury from urate and phosphate.
   - **Reasoning:** Chemo for bulky lymphoma → hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, AKI → TLS → rasburicase.
   - **Teaching point:** "BreaK the CUP": ↑K, ↓Ca, ↑Uric acid, ↑PO4.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following drugs would rapidly lower his uric acid by converting it to a soluble metabolite?
   - Page: 440

437. A 55-year-old woman completed chemotherapy for breast cancer 1 year ago. She now has progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea and leg edema. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. Her regimen included a drug that intercalates into DNA and generates free radicals.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Anthracycline cardiotoxicity
   - **A.** Mesna — Wrong. Cyclophosphamide cystitis.
   - **B.** Filgrastim — Wrong. Neutropenia.
   - **C.** Amifostine — Wrong. Platinum nephrotoxicity.
   - **D.** Dexrazoxane **(Correct)** — Correct. An iron chelator that protects against anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity.
   - **E.** Ondansetron — Wrong. Nausea.
   - **F.** Leucovorin — Wrong. Methotrexate rescue.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chemotherapy for breast cancer — Anthracycline-containing regimens.
     - dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30% — Dilated cardiomyopathy.
     - intercalates into DNA and generates free radicals — Anthracycline mechanism.
   - **Reasoning:** Anthracycline (doxorubicin) → free radical myocardial injury → dilated cardiomyopathy → dexrazoxane prevents.
   - **Teaching point:** Doxorubicin: irreversible; trastuzumab: often reversible.
   - **Follow-up:** Which agent, if given during chemotherapy, might have prevented this complication?
   - Page: 444

438. A 45-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is treated with an alkylating agent that requires activation in the liver. Three weeks later she has dysuria and gross hematuria. Urine culture is negative.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Cyclophosphamide
   - **A.** Mesna **(Correct)** — Correct. Binds acrolein, the bladder-toxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide.
   - **B.** Amifostine — Wrong. Platinum nephrotoxicity.
   - **C.** Dexrazoxane — Wrong. Anthracyclines.
   - **D.** Leucovorin — Wrong. Methotrexate.
   - **E.** Rasburicase — Wrong. TLS.
   - **F.** Allopurinol — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - granulomatosis with polyangiitis — Indication for cyclophosphamide.
     - requires activation in the liver — Nitrogen mustard prodrug.
     - gross hematuria — Hemorrhagic cystitis.
     - Urine culture is negative — Not infection.
   - **Reasoning:** Cyclophosphamide → acrolein in urine → hemorrhagic cystitis → mesna prevents.
   - **Teaching point:** Cyclophosphamide = CYstitis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug should have been given with the alkylating agent to prevent this?
   - Page: 445

439. A 27-year-old woman who is Rh-negative delivers her second child at home without prenatal care. Her first child, who is Rh-positive, was born 2 years ago, and she received no medications at that time. The newborn is pale and markedly edematous with ascites and hepatosplenomegaly. The direct antiglobulin test on the infant's red cells is positive.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
   - **A.** Exchange transfusion of the mother — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Phototherapy of the first child — Wrong. Treats jaundice, does not prevent sensitization.
   - **C.** Treating the father with anti-D — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Delivering the first child by cesarean section — Wrong. Does not prevent exposure.
   - **E.** Giving the mother iron supplements — Wrong. Not relevant.
   - **F.** Anti-D immune globulin to the mother during and after her first pregnancy **(Correct)** — Correct. It prevents maternal anti-D IgG formation that causes Rh hemolytic disease in later pregnancies.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Rh-negative — Can form anti-D.
     - her second child — Sensitization happens in the first pregnancy; disease appears in later ones.
     - received no medications at that time — No anti-D prophylaxis.
     - markedly edematous with ascites — Hydrops fetalis.
     - direct antiglobulin test on the infant's red cells is positive — Maternal antibody on fetal RBCs.
   - **Reasoning:** Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive first child without prophylaxis → maternal anti-D IgG → crosses placenta in the second pregnancy → hydrops fetalis.
   - **Teaching point:** Rh disease: second pregnancy, severe; ABO disease: first pregnancy, mild.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following would most likely have prevented this outcome?
   - Page: 411

440. A 66-year-old man has a serum protein electrophoresis done because of an elevated total protein on routine testing. It shows a monoclonal IgG spike of 1.1 g/dL. He has no symptoms. Hemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are normal, and a skeletal survey shows no lesions. Bone marrow biopsy shows 5% clonal plasma cells.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
   - **A.** Plasma exchange — Wrong. No hyperviscosity.
   - **B.** Start bortezomib-based chemotherapy — Wrong. Not myeloma.
   - **C.** Periodic monitoring **(Correct)** — Correct. MGUS: no CRAB, <10% plasma cells, M spike <3 g/dL; about 1–2% per year progress to myeloma.
   - **D.** Radiation therapy — Wrong. No lesion.
   - **E.** Reassure and discharge with no follow-up — Wrong. Needs monitoring.
   - **F.** Autologous stem cell transplant — Wrong. Not indicated.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - He has no symptoms — Asymptomatic.
     - monoclonal IgG spike of 1.1 g/dL — Small M spike (<3 g/dL).
     - Hemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are normal — No CRAB features.
     - 5% clonal plasma cells — <10%.
   - **Reasoning:** Small M spike + no CRAB + <10% plasma cells → MGUS → monitor for progression.
   - **Teaching point:** MGUS → myeloma at about 1% per year.
   - **Follow-up:** Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
   - Page: 436

## Hemeonc 2

Source: `mock-hemeonc-2.json`

441. A 10-month-old boy of Cypriot descent has pallor, poor feeding and an enlarging abdomen. He was well until 6 months of age. He has frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth, and the liver and spleen are enlarged. Skull x-ray shows a "hair-on-end" pattern. His laboratory results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** β-thalassemia major
   - **A.** Vitamin B12 deficiency — Wrong. Not related.
   - **B.** Acute myeloid leukemia — Wrong. Not typical.
   - **C.** Thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism only — Wrong. Not the main treatment complication.
   - **D.** Hereditary spherocytosis — Wrong. Not a complication.
   - **E.** Secondary hemochromatosis **(Correct)** — Correct. β-thalassemia major (β0/β0) needs regular transfusions, causing iron overload; chelation is required.
   - **F.** Iron deficiency — Wrong. Opposite problem.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - of Cypriot descent — Mediterranean ancestry.
     - He was well until 6 months of age — Symptoms begin as HbF declines.
     - frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth — Marrow expansion.
     - "hair-on-end" pattern — "Crew cut" skull.
     - the liver and spleen are enlarged — Extramedullary hematopoiesis.
   - **Reasoning:** Mediterranean infant + onset after 6 months + marrow expansion + absent HbA, high HbF (table) → β-thalassemia major → transfusions → iron overload.
   - **Teaching point:** β-thal major becomes symptomatic as γ chains switch off.
   - **Follow-up:** This child is at greatest long-term risk of which complication of his treatment?

         "Result",

       ],

           "10.5–13.5"
         ],

           "58 fL",
           "70–86"
         ],
         [

           "Target cells, marked anisopoikilocytosis, nucleated RBCs",

         ],

           "HbA2",
           "8%",

         ]
       ]

     Laboratory results
