   - Page: 552

744. A 14-month-old boy has a white reflex in his left eye in photographs. Exam shows a white retinal mass in both eyes. His family history is shown.
   - **Domain:** Genetics
   - **Topic:** Retinoblastoma
   - **A.** Medulloblastoma — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Osteosarcoma **(Correct)** — Correct. Germline RB1 mutation.
   - **C.** Hepatoblastoma — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Wilms tumor — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Neuroblastoma — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Meningioma — Wrong. NF2.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - white reflex in his left eye — Leukocoria.
     - white retinal mass in both eyes — Bilateral = familial.
     - His family history is shown — Autosomal dominant pattern.
   - **Reasoning:** Bilateral retinoblastoma + affected relatives → germline RB1 loss (two-hit) → later osteosarcoma.
   - **Teaching point:** Inherited as autosomal dominant though the gene acts recessively at the cell level.
   - **Follow-up:** Which tumor is this child at increased risk for later in life?
   - Page: 552

745. A 27-year-old man with chronic low back stiffness that improves with exercise has a painful red right eye with sensitivity to light. A thin layer of white cells is settled at the bottom of the front of the eye.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Uveitis
   - **A.** HLA-DQ2 — Wrong. Celiac.
   - **B.** HLA-DR4 — Wrong. Rheumatoid arthritis.
   - **C.** HLA-DR3 — Wrong. Lupus, type 1 diabetes.
   - **D.** HLA-B57 — Wrong. Abacavir.
   - **E.** HLA-B27 **(Correct)** — Correct. Anterior uveitis with hypopyon in ankylosing spondylitis.
   - **F.** HLA-B51 — Wrong. Behçet.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - low back stiffness that improves with exercise — Inflammatory back pain.
     - sensitivity to light — Photophobia.
     - settled at the bottom of the front of the eye — Hypopyon.
   - **Reasoning:** Inflammatory back pain + painful red eye + hypopyon → anterior uveitis → HLA-B27.
   - **Teaching point:** Sarcoidosis and Behçet syndrome also cause uveitis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which genetic marker is associated?
   - Page: 553

746. A 9-day-old girl born vaginally has swollen eyelids and watery discharge from both eyes. Her mother had no prenatal care. The infant also develops a staccato cough two weeks later.
   - **Domain:** Microbiology
   - **Topic:** Neonatal conjunctivitis
   - **A.** No treatment — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Topical steroids — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Oral erythromycin or azithromycin **(Correct)** — Correct. Chlamydia trachomatis D–K.
   - **D.** IV ceftriaxone — Wrong. Gonorrhea.
   - **E.** Topical acyclovir — Wrong. HSV.
   - **F.** Topical erythromycin alone — Wrong. Systemic therapy needed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 9-day-old — Onset 5–14 days.
     - no prenatal care — No screening.
     - staccato cough — Chlamydial pneumonia.
   - **Reasoning:** Conjunctivitis at day 5–14 + staccato cough → Chlamydia trachomatis → oral macrolide.
   - **Teaching point:** Gonococcal conjunctivitis begins at 2–5 days and needs ceftriaxone.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the appropriate treatment?
   - Page: 549

747. A 30-year-old woman has painful vision loss in her right eye. When a light is swung from her left eye to her right eye, both pupils dilate. When the light is moved back to the left eye, both pupils constrict.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Relative afferent pupillary defect
   - **A.** Left optic nerve — Wrong. Wrong side.
   - **B.** Right sympathetic chain — Wrong. Horner.
   - **C.** Right ciliary ganglion — Wrong. Efferent.
   - **D.** Right oculomotor nerve — Wrong. Efferent; right pupil would not constrict at all.
   - **E.** Right visual cortex — Wrong. Reflex intact.
   - **F.** Right optic nerve **(Correct)** — Correct. Relative afferent pupillary defect from optic neuritis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - painful vision loss in her right eye — Optic neuritis.
     - swung from her left eye to her right eye, both pupils dilate — Weak afferent input on the right.
     - both pupils constrict — Normal efferent pathway.
   - **Reasoning:** Swinging-flashlight dilation in the right eye → right afferent (optic nerve) lesion → Marcus Gunn pupil.
   - **Teaching point:** Both pupils always stay equal in size with a pure afferent lesion.
   - **Follow-up:** Which part of the reflex pathway is damaged?
   - Page: 554

748. A 24-year-old man was punched in the left eye. He has double vision when he looks up, his left eye appears sunken and his left cheek and upper lip are numb.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Blowout fracture
   - **A.** Levator palpebrae — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Inferior rectus **(Correct)** — Correct. Orbital floor (blowout) fracture.
   - **C.** Medial rectus — Wrong. Medial wall.
   - **D.** Superior rectus — Wrong. Roof fracture.
   - **E.** Lateral rectus — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Superior oblique — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - double vision when he looks up — Restricted upgaze.
     - his left eye appears sunken — Enophthalmos.
     - his left cheek and upper lip are numb — Infraorbital nerve.
   - **Reasoning:** Blunt eye trauma + diplopia on upgaze + enophthalmos + cheek numbness → orbital floor fracture → inferior rectus entrapment.
   - **Teaching point:** In children, a "white-eyed" trapdoor fracture can trigger the oculocardiac reflex.
   - **Follow-up:** Which muscle is trapped?
   - Page: 555

749. After a fall from a bicycle, a 16-year-old has double vision that is worse when he walks downstairs or reads. His right eye sits higher than the left. He tilts his head toward his left shoulder to make the double vision go away.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Cranial nerve IV palsy
   - **A.** Right trochlear nerve **(Correct)** — Correct. Superior oblique palsy.
   - **B.** Right medial longitudinal fasciculus — Wrong. INO.
   - **C.** Left oculomotor nerve — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Left trochlear nerve — Wrong. He would tilt right.
   - **E.** Right oculomotor nerve — Wrong. Down and out with ptosis.
   - **F.** Right abducens nerve — Wrong. Horizontal diplopia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - worse when he walks downstairs or reads — Down-and-in gaze.
     - His right eye sits higher than the left — Right hypertropia.
     - tilts his head toward his left shoulder — Compensates for lost intorsion.
   - **Reasoning:** Vertical diplopia on downgaze + right hypertropia + head tilt to left → right CN IV palsy.
   - **Teaching point:** CN IV is the thinnest and longest intracranial nerve, often injured by trauma.
   - **Follow-up:** Which nerve is injured?
   - Page: 556

750. A 40-year-old woman with recurrent ear infections has had foul-smelling drainage from her right ear for months without pain. Her hearing on the right has worsened. Otoscopy shows a pearly white mass behind a retracted eardrum.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Cholesteatoma
   - **A.** Mixed; Schwann cell tumor — Wrong. Schwannoma.
   - **B.** Conductive; ear canal occlusion by wax — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Sensorineural; destruction of hair cells — Wrong. Not the mechanism.
   - **D.** Conductive; erosion of the ossicles by keratinized squamous epithelium **(Correct)** — Correct. Cholesteatoma.
   - **E.** Central; auditory cortex lesion — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Sensorineural; endolymphatic hydrops — Wrong. Ménière.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - foul-smelling drainage from her right ear for months without pain — Painless otorrhea.
     - pearly white mass — Keratin debris.
     - behind a retracted eardrum — Retraction pocket origin.
   - **Reasoning:** Painless chronic otorrhea + pearly white retrotympanic mass → cholesteatoma → ossicular erosion → conductive loss.
   - **Teaching point:** "Skin in the wrong place."
   - **Follow-up:** What is the type of hearing loss and its mechanism?

751. A 74-year-old man says that people mumble and that he cannot follow conversations in restaurants. He has no ear pain or vertigo. Otoscopy is normal. His audiogram is shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Hearing loss
   - **A.** Tympanic membrane perforation — Wrong. Conductive.
   - **B.** Age-related loss of hair cells at the base of the cochlea **(Correct)** — Correct. Presbycusis.
   - **C.** Vestibular schwannoma — Wrong. Usually unilateral.
   - **D.** Endolymphatic hydrops — Wrong. Ménière.
   - **E.** Fixation of the stapes — Wrong. Conductive.
   - **F.** Loss of hair cells at the cochlear apex — Wrong. Low frequencies.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - cannot follow conversations in restaurants — High-frequency loss with background noise.
     - Otoscopy is normal — Not conductive.
     - His audiogram is shown — Bilateral symmetric high-frequency loss.
   - **Reasoning:** Elderly + bilateral symmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss → presbycusis → basal cochlear hair cell loss.
   - **Teaching point:** High frequencies are heard at the stiff, narrow base.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the cause of his hearing loss?
   - Page: 548

752. A 44-year-old woman has episodes of severe spinning lasting 2–4 hours, with nausea. Before each attack her left ear feels full, and she has a roaring sound in it. Over time, hearing in her left ear has worsened for low tones.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Vertigo
   - **A.** Schwann cell tumor — Wrong. Progressive, not episodic.
   - **B.** Debris in the semicircular canals — Wrong. BPPV.
   - **C.** Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve — Wrong. Single prolonged episode.
   - **D.** Middle ear effusion — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Brainstem ischemia — Wrong. Central.
   - **F.** Increased endolymph volume in the inner ear **(Correct)** — Correct. Ménière disease.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - severe spinning lasting 2–4 hours — Episodic vertigo.
     - her left ear feels full — Aural fullness.
     - a roaring sound in it — Tinnitus.
     - worsened for low tones — Low-frequency sensorineural loss.
   - **Reasoning:** Episodic vertigo for hours + aural fullness + tinnitus + fluctuating sensorineural loss → Ménière → endolymphatic hydrops.
   - **Teaching point:** "Men wear vests": vertigo, sensorineural loss, tinnitus.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the mechanism?
   - Page: 549

753. A 40-year-old man with 35% body surface area burns 10 days ago needs surgery. After induction with succinylcholine, his ECG shows tall peaked T waves followed by a wide-complex rhythm.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Neuromuscular blocking drugs
   - **A.** Release of potassium from muscle with upregulated extrajunctional nicotinic receptors **(Correct)** — Correct. Hyperkalemia.
   - **B.** Vagal stimulation — Wrong. Bradycardia.
   - **C.** Histamine release — Wrong. Hypotension.
   - **D.** Malignant hyperthermia — Wrong. Hypercapnia and rigidity.
   - **E.** Hypocalcemia — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Pseudocholinesterase deficiency — Wrong. Prolonged paralysis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 35% body surface area burns 10 days ago — Receptor upregulation.
     - induction with succinylcholine — Depolarizing blocker.
     - tall peaked T waves — Hyperkalemia.
   - **Reasoning:** Burns (or crush, denervation) + succinylcholine → depolarization of upregulated receptors → K+ efflux → hyperkalemia → arrhythmia.
   - **Teaching point:** Use a nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium instead.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the mechanism?
   - Page: 566

754. A 70-year-old man in septic shock with a BP of 78/40 mm Hg needs urgent intubation. The team chooses an induction agent that keeps his blood pressure stable. The next day he remains hypotensive despite fluids, and a random cortisol is low.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** General anesthetics
   - **A.** Ketamine — Wrong. Raises BP; no adrenal effect.
   - **B.** Propofol — Wrong. Lowers BP.
   - **C.** Etomidate **(Correct)** — Correct. Hemodynamically neutral; inhibits 11β-hydroxylase.
   - **D.** Midazolam — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Nitrous oxide — Wrong. Inhaled.
   - **F.** Thiopental — Wrong. Not listed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - keeps his blood pressure stable — Hemodynamically neutral.
     - remains hypotensive despite fluids — Adrenal insufficiency.
     - a random cortisol is low — Adrenal suppression.
   - **Reasoning:** Hemodynamically neutral induction + later low cortisol → etomidate → adrenal insufficiency.
   - **Teaching point:** Ketamine raises BP and HR; propofol drops BP.
   - **Follow-up:** Which induction agent was used?

755. Two sedative-hypnotics that both act on the GABA-A receptor are compared as shown. Drug P plateaus because it only enhances the effect of GABA that is already present.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Barbiturates
   - **A.** It inhibits CYP450 — Wrong. Induces.
   - **B.** Its overdose is reversed by flumazenil — Wrong. Benzodiazepine antidote.
   - **C.** It is safe in acute porphyria — Wrong. Contraindicated.
   - **D.** It increases the duration of chloride channel opening and can directly open the channel at high doses **(Correct)** — Correct. Barbiturate.
   - **E.** It increases the frequency of chloride channel opening — Wrong. Benzodiazepines (drug P).
   - **F.** It has no effect on respiration — Wrong. Fatal depression.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - both act on the GABA-A receptor — Shared target.
     - Drug P plateaus — Ceiling effect.
     - only enhances the effect of GABA that is already present — Benzodiazepine mechanism.
   - **Reasoning:** Ceiling effect = benzodiazepine (↑ frequency); no ceiling = barbiturate (↑ duration, direct opening) → coma and death.
   - **Teaching point:** "Frenzodiazepines" ↑ frequency; "barbidurates" ↑ duration.
   - **Follow-up:** Which statement about drug Q is correct?
   - Page: 561

756. A 67-year-old woman with Parkinson disease has stretches each day when her levodopa wears off before the next dose. A drug is added that blocks dopamine breakdown in the brain without affecting peripheral L-DOPA metabolism.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Parkinson disease therapy
   - **A.** Entacapone — Wrong. Peripheral COMT.
   - **B.** Carbidopa — Wrong. Peripheral DDC.
   - **C.** Benztropine — Wrong. Antimuscarinic.
   - **D.** Bromocriptine — Wrong. Ergot agonist.
   - **E.** Rasagiline **(Correct)** — Correct. Selective MAO-B inhibitor.
   - **F.** Amantadine — Wrong. Dyskinesias.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - wears off before the next dose — Wearing-off phenomenon.
     - blocks dopamine breakdown in the brain — Central action.
     - without affecting peripheral L-DOPA metabolism — Not COMT/DDC inhibitor.
   - **Reasoning:** Wearing-off + central dopamine breakdown blocker → MAO-B inhibitor (selegiline, rasagiline).
   - **Teaching point:** Tolcapone also blocks central COMT but is hepatotoxic.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug was added?
   - Page: 563

757. A 28-year-old woman with bipolar disorder and epilepsy was started on a new drug 3 weeks ago. Her dose was increased quickly because she was also taking valproate. She now has fever, painful mouth ulcers and a widespread rash with skin peeling.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Anticonvulsants
   - **A.** Lamotrigine **(Correct)** — Correct. SJS risk increases with rapid titration and valproate co-therapy.
   - **B.** Ethosuximide — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Levetiracetam — Wrong. Psychiatric effects.
   - **D.** Lithium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Topiramate — Wrong. Kidney stones.
   - **F.** Gabapentin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bipolar disorder and epilepsy — Both indications.
     - increased quickly because she was also taking valproate — Valproate raises lamotrigine levels.
     - widespread rash with skin peeling — Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
   - **Reasoning:** Mood stabilizer + anticonvulsant + rapid titration with valproate + mucocutaneous blistering → lamotrigine SJS.
   - **Teaching point:** Phenytoin and carbamazepine also cause SJS.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug was started?
   - Page: 560

758. A 5-year-old girl has a tonsillectomy and is given codeine for pain. That night she is very sleepy, her pupils are pinpoint and she is breathing slowly. Her mother had a similar reaction after a dental procedure.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Opioid analgesics
   - **A.** Pseudocholinesterase deficiency — Wrong. Succinylcholine.
   - **B.** Poor CYP2D6 metabolism — Wrong. No effect.
   - **C.** G6PD deficiency — Wrong. Hemolysis.
   - **D.** Allergy to opioids — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolism converting codeine to morphine **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Slow acetylation — Wrong. Isoniazid, hydralazine.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - given codeine — Prodrug.
     - her pupils are pinpoint and she is breathing slowly — Opioid toxicity.
     - Her mother had a similar reaction — Inherited variant.
   - **Reasoning:** Codeine prodrug + toxicity in child and parent → ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolism → excess morphine.
   - **Teaching point:** Poor metabolizers get no pain relief from codeine.
   - **Follow-up:** What explains her reaction?
   - Page: 567

759. A 58-year-old man with chronic knee pain who takes sertraline is started on a pain reliever. A week later he is agitated and sweating, with tremor, diarrhea and jerking muscles. His temperature is 39°C, and reflexes are brisk with clonus.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Tramadol
   - **A.** Capsaicin — Wrong. Topical.
   - **B.** Tramadol **(Correct)** — Correct. Weak opioid that inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake.
   - **C.** Acetaminophen — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Morphine — Wrong. Does not inhibit serotonin reuptake.
   - **E.** Buprenorphine — Wrong. Not serotonergic.
   - **F.** Celecoxib — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - takes sertraline — SSRI.
     - agitated and sweating, with tremor, diarrhea — Serotonin syndrome.
     - reflexes are brisk with clonus — Neuromuscular hyperactivity.
   - **Reasoning:** SSRI + tramadol → serotonin syndrome (autonomic, mental status, clonus).
   - **Teaching point:** Tramadol also lowers seizure threshold.
   - **Follow-up:** Which pain drug was started?
   - Page: 567

760. A 70-year-old woman with open-angle glaucoma uses eye drops every night. Over months, her treated green eye turns brown, and her eyelashes on that side grow longer and darker.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Glaucoma therapy
   - **A.** Contracts the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork — Wrong. Pilocarpine.
   - **B.** Decreases aqueous production via α2 agonism — Wrong. Brimonidine.
   - **C.** Increases uveoscleral outflow as a prostaglandin F2α analog **(Correct)** — Correct. Latanoprost.
   - **D.** Decreases aqueous production via β-blockade — Wrong. Timolol.
   - **E.** Dilates the pupil via α1 agonism — Wrong. Epinephrine.
   - **F.** Decreases aqueous production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase — Wrong. Acetazolamide.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - open-angle glaucoma — Indication.
     - uses eye drops every night — Once-daily prostaglandin.
     - her treated green eye turns brown — Iris darkening.
     - eyelashes on that side grow longer and darker — Hypertrichosis.
   - **Reasoning:** Glaucoma drop + iris browning + eyelash growth → latanoprost → ↑ uveoscleral outflow.
   - **Teaching point:** β-blockers and acetazolamide cause no pupil or vision change.
   - **Follow-up:** How does her drug lower intraocular pressure?
   - Page: 568

## Psychiatry 1

Source: `mock-psychiatry-1.json`

761. A 34-year-old woman with cancer refuses to talk about her prognosis. Instead she lectures the nurses about the molecular pathways of her tumor and the response rates of different drugs. She shows no visible emotion while discussing them.
   - **Domain:** Psychology
   - **Topic:** Ego defenses
   - **A.** Repression — Wrong. Not unconscious forgetting.
   - **B.** Sublimation — Wrong. Not channeling an impulse.
   - **C.** Displacement — Wrong. Not redirecting emotion.
   - **D.** Denial — Wrong. She acknowledges the cancer.
   - **E.** Intellectualization **(Correct)** — Correct. Using facts and logic to distance herself from distress.
   - **F.** Rationalization — Wrong. Not explaining away events.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - refuses to talk about her prognosis — Avoiding emotional content.
     - lectures the nurses about the molecular pathways — Retreat into facts.
     - shows no visible emotion — Emotional distance.
   - **Reasoning:** Serious diagnosis + focus on technical details + no emotion → intellectualization.
   - **Teaching point:** Isolation of affect separates feelings from events; intellectualization uses facts to do it.
   - **Follow-up:** Which defense mechanism is she using?
   - Page: 571

762. A 45-year-old man is passed over for a promotion that goes to a younger colleague. He tells his friends that he never wanted the job because the hours would have ruined his golf game. His performance reviews had been poor for 2 years.
   - **Domain:** Psychology
   - **Topic:** Ego defenses
   - **A.** Reaction formation — Wrong. Not the opposite feeling.
   - **B.** Humor — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Acting out — Wrong. Not an action.
   - **D.** Rationalization **(Correct)** — Correct. A plausible explanation that avoids self-blame.
   - **E.** Denial — Wrong. He acknowledges the outcome.
   - **F.** Projection — Wrong. Not attributing his feelings to others.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - passed over for a promotion — Disappointing event.
     - he never wanted the job — Explaining away.
     - His performance reviews had been poor — Real reason avoided.
   - **Reasoning:** Disappointment + acceptable-sounding explanation that hides the true reason → rationalization.
   - **Teaching point:** "Sour grapes" is the classic example.
   - **Follow-up:** Which defense mechanism is he using?
   - Page: 571

763. A 6-year-old boy who was toilet trained at 3 begins wetting his pants during the day and asking to drink from a bottle after his parents bring home a new baby. He is otherwise healthy, and urinalysis is normal.
   - **Domain:** Psychology
   - **Topic:** Ego defenses
   - **A.** Identification — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Regression **(Correct)** — Correct. Returning to earlier behaviors under stress.
   - **C.** Acting out — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Fixation — Wrong. He had progressed beyond this stage.
   - **E.** Displacement — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Dissociation — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - toilet trained at 3 — Previously achieved milestone.
     - begins wetting his pants — Loss of milestone.
     - new baby — Stressor.
     - urinalysis is normal — No medical cause.
   - **Reasoning:** Stressor + return to earlier behavior after mastering it → regression.
   - **Teaching point:** Fixation means never fully leaving the earlier stage.
   - **Follow-up:** Which defense mechanism explains his behavior?
   - Page: 571

764. A healthy infant is brought for a well-child visit. She sits without support, transfers a block from one hand to the other and babbles. She cries and clings to her mother when the physician approaches. She cannot yet crawl or wave bye-bye.
   - **Domain:** Psychology
   - **Topic:** Normal infant and child development
   - **A.** 6 months **(Correct)** — Correct. Sits, transfers objects, stranger anxiety.
   - **B.** 2 months — Wrong. Too young to sit.
   - **C.** 18 months — Wrong. Much later.
   - **D.** 9 months — Wrong. Would crawl.
   - **E.** 12 months — Wrong. Would walk and say words.
   - **F.** 4 months — Wrong. Not sitting yet.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - sits without support — By 6 months.
     - transfers a block from one hand to the other — By 6–9 months.
     - cries and clings to her mother when the physician approaches — Stranger anxiety by 6 months.
     - cannot yet crawl — Before 8 months.
   - **Reasoning:** Sitting + hand-to-hand transfer + stranger anxiety, no crawling → about 6 months.
   - **Teaching point:** Separation anxiety and object permanence come at about 9 months.
   - **Follow-up:** What is her most likely age?
   - Page: 572

765. A 9-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a swollen right thigh. His father says he fell while walking. X-rays show a spiral femur fracture and healing fractures of several posterior ribs. Retinal exam is normal.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Child abuse
   - **A.** Discharge with orthopedic follow-up — Wrong. Unsafe.
   - **B.** Order a vitamin D level only — Wrong. Not sufficient.
   - **C.** Report suspected abuse to child protective services **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Obtain parental consent to involve social services — Wrong. Not needed.
   - **E.** Confront the father about the inconsistency — Wrong. Not required.
   - **F.** Test for osteogenesis imperfecta before taking any action — Wrong. Do not delay reporting.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - he fell while walking — Developmentally implausible at 9 months.
     - spiral femur fracture — Twisting injury.
     - healing fractures of several posterior ribs — Injuries at different stages.
   - **Reasoning:** History inconsistent with development + fractures in different stages → suspected physical abuse → mandatory report.
   - **Teaching point:** Suspicion alone requires a report; confirmation is not needed.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate next step?
   - Page: 573

766. A 9-year-old boy is referred because he cannot finish his schoolwork. His teacher says he blurts out answers, leaves his seat and loses his materials. His parents describe the same behavior at home and at church since age 5. His IQ is normal.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
   - **A.** Lithium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Fluoxetine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Risperidone — Wrong. Not first-line.
   - **D.** Haloperidol — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Guanfacine — Wrong. Alternative, not first-line.
   - **F.** Methylphenidate **(Correct)** — Correct. Stimulant for ADHD.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - blurts out answers, leaves his seat — Impulsivity, hyperactivity.
     - loses his materials — Inattention.
     - at home and at church — ≥2 settings.
     - His IQ is normal — Not intellectual disability.
   - **Reasoning:** Hyperactivity + impulsivity + inattention in ≥2 settings before age 12 → ADHD → stimulant.
   - **Teaching point:** Atomoxetine and α2-agonists are alternatives.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is first-line?
   - Page: 574

767. A 2-year-old boy does not respond to his name and has not started using words. He avoids eye contact and spends hours spinning the wheels of a toy car. He becomes very upset when his daily routine changes. Hearing testing is normal. His head circumference is at the 97th percentile.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Autism spectrum disorder
   - **A.** It is more common in males and associated with increased head size **(Correct)** — Correct. Autism spectrum disorder.
   - **B.** Onset is typically after age 10 — Wrong. Early childhood.
   - **C.** Intellectual disability is required for diagnosis — Wrong. Not required.
   - **D.** It is caused by childhood vaccines — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** It is more common in females — Wrong. Males.
   - **F.** Stimulants are first-line treatment — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - does not respond to his name — Social deficit.
     - spends hours spinning the wheels — Repetitive behavior.
     - very upset when his daily routine changes — Insistence on sameness.
     - Hearing testing is normal — Not deafness.
   - **Reasoning:** Social and communication deficits + repetitive behaviors + restricted interests in early childhood → autism spectrum disorder.
   - **Teaching point:** Rule out hearing loss first.
   - **Follow-up:** Which statement about his condition is correct?
   - Page: 574

768. An 11-year-old boy has blinked his eyes forcefully and jerked his shoulders for 2 years. Over the past year he has also started grunting and clearing his throat many times a day. He can suppress the movements briefly but feels an urge to do them. He also washes his hands repeatedly.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Tourette syndrome
   - **A.** Conduct disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** ADHD **(Correct)** — Correct. Tourette syndrome is associated with ADHD and OCD.
   - **C.** Autism — Wrong. Not the classic association.
   - **D.** Bipolar disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Absence epilepsy — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Schizophrenia — Wrong. Not the association.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - blinked his eyes forcefully and jerked his shoulders — Motor tics.
     - grunting and clearing his throat — Vocal tics.
     - can suppress the movements briefly — Premonitory urge.
     - washes his hands repeatedly — OCD features.
   - **Reasoning:** Motor + vocal tics >1 year before age 18 → Tourette syndrome → associated OCD and ADHD.
   - **Teaching point:** For distressing tics: tetrabenazine, antipsychotics or α2-agonists.
   - **Follow-up:** Which other condition is most commonly associated?
   - Page: 574

769. An 85-year-old man had hip surgery 2 days ago. Tonight he pulled out his IV, is shouting that there are snakes on the floor and does not know where he is. This morning he was calm and oriented. He received diphenhydramine for sleep last night. His temperature is 38.3°C.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Delirium
   - **A.** Increase diphenhydramine — Wrong. Anticholinergics worsen delirium.
   - **B.** Start lorazepam — Wrong. May worsen delirium.
   - **C.** Start donepezil — Wrong. Not dementia.
   - **D.** Apply four-point restraints — Wrong. Avoid unnecessary restraints.
   - **E.** Search for and treat the underlying cause and stop deliriogenic drugs **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Start long-term risperidone — Wrong. As needed only.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - had hip surgery 2 days ago — Postoperative.
     - there are snakes on the floor — Visual hallucinations.
     - This morning he was calm and oriented — Waxing and waning.
     - received diphenhydramine — Anticholinergic.
     - His temperature is 38.3°C — Possible infection.
   - **Reasoning:** Acute fluctuating confusion + visual hallucinations + anticholinergic + fever → delirium → treat cause, remove offending drugs.
   - **Teaching point:** Delirium is reversible; dementia is chronic with preserved attention early.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate next step?
   - Page: 575

770. A 30-year-old man is found in a bus station 300 km from home. He does not know his name or how he got there. Ten days ago, his wife and son died in a house fire. Neurologic exam, CT and toxicology are normal. He is not seeking any benefit.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Dissociative disorders
   - **A.** Malingering — Wrong. No external gain.
   - **B.** Korsakoff syndrome — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Dissociative identity disorder — Wrong. No separate identities.
   - **D.** Dissociative amnesia with fugue **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Conversion disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Transient global amnesia — Wrong. Not listed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - does not know his name — Loss of personal information.
     - 300 km from home — Unexpected travel (fugue).
     - died in a house fire — Severe trauma.
     - He is not seeking any benefit — Not malingering.
   - **Reasoning:** Severe trauma + loss of autobiographical memory + unplanned travel → dissociative amnesia with fugue.
   - **Teaching point:** Organic causes must be ruled out first.
   - **Follow-up:** Which diagnosis is most likely?
   - Page: 575

771. A 22-year-old college student has become withdrawn over the past 9 months. He says his roommate is broadcasting his thoughts on the radio and he hears two voices arguing about him. He stopped going to class and rarely showers. His speech is hard to follow. Urine drug screen is negative.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Schizophrenia
   - **A.** Clozapine — Wrong. Treatment-resistant only.
   - **B.** Lorazepam — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Lithium — Wrong. Bipolar.
   - **D.** Sertraline — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Electroconvulsive therapy — Wrong. Not first-line.
   - **F.** Risperidone **(Correct)** — Correct. Atypical antipsychotic for schizophrenia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - over the past 9 months — ≥6 months.
     - broadcasting his thoughts on the radio — Delusion.
     - hears two voices arguing about him — Auditory hallucinations.
     - rarely showers — Negative symptoms.
   - **Reasoning:** >6 months of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech and negative symptoms → schizophrenia → atypical antipsychotic.
   - **Teaching point:** Brief psychotic <1 month; schizophreniform 1–6 months.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
   - Page: 577

772. A 58-year-old retired teacher has believed for 3 years that her husband is having an affair with their neighbor. There is no evidence. She hires a private investigator and checks his phone daily. She has no hallucinations, keeps her house well, volunteers at church and her speech is organized.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Delusional disorder
   - **A.** Brief psychotic disorder — Wrong. Too long.
   - **B.** Schizotypal personality disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Delusional disorder **(Correct)** — Correct. Jealous type.
   - **D.** Schizophrenia — Wrong. Functioning preserved, no other symptoms.
   - **E.** Major depression with psychotic features — Wrong. No mood episode.
   - **F.** Paranoid personality disorder — Wrong. Not a fixed delusion.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - believed for 3 years that her husband is having an affair — Fixed false belief >1 month.
     - She has no hallucinations — No other psychotic symptoms.
     - volunteers at church and her speech is organized — Functioning preserved.
   - **Reasoning:** Single non-bizarre delusion >1 month + otherwise normal functioning → delusional disorder.
   - **Teaching point:** Delusional disorder can be shared (folie à deux).
   - **Follow-up:** Which diagnosis is most likely?

773. A 31-year-old woman comes for depression. Her mood chart is shown. During the elevated periods she slept 4 hours a night, felt creative and talked fast for about 5 days, but kept working and was never hospitalized. Her depressed periods lasted about 3 weeks each, with anhedonia, guilt and poor sleep.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Bipolar disorder
   - **A.** Bipolar I disorder — Wrong. Requires a manic episode.
   - **B.** Borderline personality disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Major depressive disorder — Wrong. Hypomania present.
   - **D.** Bipolar II disorder **(Correct)** — Correct. Hypomania + major depressive episodes.
   - **E.** Cyclothymic disorder — Wrong. Full depressive episodes present.
   - **F.** Schizoaffective disorder — Wrong. No psychosis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - about 5 days — ≥4 days, hypomania.
     - kept working and was never hospitalized — No marked impairment.
     - lasted about 3 weeks each — ≥2 weeks, major depressive episode.
   - **Reasoning:** Hypomanic episodes (≥4 days, no impairment) + major depressive episodes → bipolar II.
   - **Teaching point:** Antidepressant monotherapy can trigger mania; screen for hypomania before starting.
   - **Follow-up:** Which diagnosis is most likely?
   - Page: 578

774. A 27-year-old man is brought by police after trying to buy three sports cars with no money. For 10 days he has slept 2 hours a night, talks so fast that he cannot be interrupted and says he has been chosen to end world hunger. He is easily distracted by noises in the hallway.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Bipolar disorder
   - **A.** Methylphenidate — Wrong. Worsens mania.
   - **B.** Lithium **(Correct)** — Correct. Mood stabilizer for bipolar I.
   - **C.** Buspirone — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Clonazepam alone — Wrong. Not adequate.
   - **E.** Bupropion — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Sertraline — Wrong. May worsen mania.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - trying to buy three sports cars with no money — Impulsivity.
     - slept 2 hours a night — Decreased need for sleep.
     - talks so fast that he cannot be interrupted — Pressured speech.
     - chosen to end world hunger — Grandiosity.
     - easily distracted — Distractibility.
   - **Reasoning:** ≥1 week of elevated mood with DIG FAST features → manic episode → bipolar I → lithium.
   - **Teaching point:** Atypical antipsychotics, valproate and carbamazepine are also used.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug would be most appropriate for long-term relapse prevention?
   - Page: 578

775. A 70-year-old man has lost 9 kg over 3 months, wakes at 3 AM and cannot get back to sleep, and no longer enjoys his garden. He believes his intestines have rotted away and that he is being punished for his sins. He has not eaten or drunk for 2 days and is getting weak.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** MDD with psychotic features
   - **A.** Electroconvulsive therapy **(Correct)** — Correct. Psychotic depression with refusal to eat or drink.
   - **B.** Lithium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Haloperidol alone — Wrong. Not adequate.
   - **D.** Lorazepam — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Psychotherapy alone — Wrong. Not adequate.
   - **F.** Sertraline alone — Wrong. Too slow and incomplete.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - no longer enjoys his garden — Anhedonia.
     - his intestines have rotted away — Nihilistic, mood-congruent delusion.
     - being punished for his sins — Guilt delusion.
     - has not eaten or drunk for 2 days — Life-threatening.
   - **Reasoning:** MDD with mood-congruent psychotic features + refusal of food/fluids → urgent ECT.
   - **Teaching point:** Otherwise, antidepressant plus atypical antipsychotic.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate treatment?
   - Page: 579

776. Ten days after the delivery of her first baby, a 26-year-old woman tells her husband that the baby is the devil and that God has told her to drown him. She has not slept for 3 days. Her mother has bipolar disorder.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Postpartum psychosis
   - **A.** Start sertraline and follow up in 2 weeks — Wrong. Unsafe.
   - **B.** Refer for outpatient CBT — Wrong. Unsafe.
   - **C.** Reassure her that this is postpartum blues — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Advise her to stop breastfeeding only — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Hospitalize her and start an atypical antipsychotic **(Correct)** — Correct. Postpartum psychosis.
   - **F.** Prescribe zolpidem for sleep — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - the baby is the devil — Delusion.
     - God has told her to drown him — Command hallucination, infanticide risk.
     - She has not slept for 3 days — Possible mania.
     - Her mother has bipolar disorder — Risk factor.
   - **Reasoning:** Postpartum delusions + thoughts of harming baby + family bipolar history → postpartum psychosis → emergency hospitalization.
   - **Teaching point:** Postpartum blues: 2–3 days after delivery, resolves within 2 weeks.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate next step?
   - Page: 579

777. A 29-year-old woman has had four episodes over 2 months of sudden pounding heartbeat, sweating, shaking, chest tightness and fear that she is dying. Each episode peaks within 10 minutes. She now avoids driving in case it happens again. ECG, TSH and toxicology are normal.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Panic disorder
   - **A.** Bupropion — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Haloperidol — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Propranolol before driving — Wrong. Performance anxiety.
   - **D.** Buspirone — Wrong. Not first-line for panic.
   - **E.** Daily alprazolam alone — Wrong. Not first-line long term.
   - **F.** An SSRI with CBT **(Correct)** — Correct. Panic disorder.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - sudden pounding heartbeat, sweating, shaking — Autonomic surge.
     - peaks within 10 minutes — Panic attack.
     - avoids driving in case it happens again — Behavioral change from attacks.
     - ECG, TSH and toxicology are normal — Medical causes excluded.
   - **Reasoning:** Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + ≥1 month of worry/behavior change → panic disorder → SSRI + CBT.
   - **Teaching point:** Benzodiazepines are for short-term acute relief only.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the best long-term treatment?
   - Page: 580

778. A 24-year-old law student has worried for a year that she will fail, that her parents will get sick and that she cannot pay her loans. She has trouble sleeping, cannot concentrate, feels tense in her shoulders and is irritable with her friends. She has no panic attacks.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Generalized anxiety disorder
   - **A.** Buspirone — Wrong. Second-line.
   - **B.** Propranolol — Wrong. Performance anxiety.
   - **C.** Escitalopram **(Correct)** — Correct. SSRI for generalized anxiety disorder.
   - **D.** Alprazolam — Wrong. Second-line.
   - **E.** Hydroxyzine — Wrong. Not listed.
   - **F.** Quetiapine — Wrong. Not first-line.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - worried for a year — ≥6 months.
     - that she will fail, that her parents will get sick and that she cannot pay her loans — Multiple domains.
     - cannot concentrate, feels tense in her shoulders and is irritable — CRIMES symptoms.
   - **Reasoning:** Excessive worry about many things ≥6 months + ≥3 CRIMES symptoms → GAD → SSRI/SNRI + CBT.
   - **Teaching point:** Buspirone, TCAs and benzodiazepines are second-line.
   - **Follow-up:** What is a first-line medication?
   - Page: 580

779. A 35-year-old man spends 3 hours each morning checking that the doors are locked and the stove is off because he fears his family will die in a fire or robbery. He knows the fears are excessive and wishes he could stop. He is late to work most days.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Obsessive-compulsive disorders
   - **A.** Delusional belief without insight — Wrong. Insight present.
   - **B.** A dissociative disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Egosyntonic perfectionism — Wrong. OCPD.
   - **D.** Egodystonic obsessions and compulsions **(Correct)** — Correct. OCD.
   - **E.** A cluster C personality disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Psychosis requiring antipsychotics first — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - spends 3 hours each morning checking — Time-consuming compulsions.
     - fears his family will die in a fire or robbery — Intrusive obsessions.
     - He knows the fears are excessive and wishes he could stop — Egodystonic, insight.
   - **Reasoning:** Intrusive obsessions + compulsions that relieve distress + insight → OCD (egodystonic) → SSRI + CBT.
   - **Teaching point:** OCPD is egosyntonic: the person sees nothing wrong.
   - **Follow-up:** Which statement best describes his condition?
   - Page: 580

780. A 32-year-old firefighter pulled a child's body from a burning building 6 weeks ago. Since then he has nightmares, sudden vivid memories of the scene and jumps at small noises. He avoids driving past the street and feels numb with his family. He has started drinking to sleep.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Post-traumatic stress disorder
   - **A.** Prazosin **(Correct)** — Correct. α1-blocker for PTSD nightmares.
   - **B.** Lithium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Lorazepam — Wrong. Not recommended.
   - **D.** Haloperidol — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Bupropion — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Zolpidem — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 6 weeks ago — >1 month.
     - sudden vivid memories of the scene — Re-experiencing.
     - jumps at small noises — Hyperarousal.
     - avoids driving past the street — Avoidance.
   - **Reasoning:** Trauma + re-experiencing + avoidance + hyperarousal + negative mood >1 month → PTSD → SSRI/venlafaxine + CBT; prazosin for nightmares.
   - **Teaching point:** Symptoms for 3 days to 1 month = acute stress disorder.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug specifically helps his nightmares?
   - Page: 581

781. A 26-year-old woman has had a series of intense relationships that end in rage when she feels abandoned. She has cut her wrists several times when upset, spends impulsively and says she feels "empty inside." She tells you that you are the only doctor who understands her and that the previous doctor was evil.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Personality disorders
   - **A.** Psychoanalysis — Wrong. Not the best evidence.
   - **B.** Electroconvulsive therapy — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Lithium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Clozapine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Long-term benzodiazepines — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Dialectical behavior therapy **(Correct)** — Correct. Borderline personality disorder.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - end in rage when she feels abandoned — Fear of abandonment.
     - cut her wrists several times — Self-harm.
     - empty inside — Chronic emptiness.
     - you are the only doctor who understands her and that the previous doctor was evil — Splitting.
   - **Reasoning:** Unstable relationships + abandonment fear + self-harm + emptiness + splitting → borderline personality disorder → DBT.
   - **Teaching point:** Females > males; high suicide risk.
   - **Follow-up:** Which treatment has the best evidence?
   - Page: 582

782. A 40-year-old man has no close friends and works alone as a night-shift lighthouse keeper. He has never wanted a romantic relationship and seems indifferent when coworkers praise or criticize him. He has no odd beliefs, and his speech is normal.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Personality disorders
   - **A.** Antisocial — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Schizotypal — Wrong. Odd beliefs and eccentricity.
   - **C.** Dependent — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Avoidant — Wrong. Wants relationships but fears rejection.
   - **E.** Schizoid **(Correct)** — Correct. Detached, indifferent, prefers solitude.
   - **F.** Paranoid — Wrong. Distrust.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - has never wanted a romantic relationship — Lack of desire for relationships.
     - indifferent when coworkers praise or criticize him — Aloof.
     - He has no odd beliefs — Not schizotypal.
   - **Reasoning:** Social withdrawal by choice + emotional indifference without odd thinking → schizoid personality disorder.
   - **Teaching point:** Avoidant patients want connection but fear rejection.
   - **Follow-up:** Which personality disorder is most likely?
   - Page: 582

783. A 30-year-old woman wants friends and a partner but turns down every invitation because she is sure people will think she is boring. She switched to a job with no customer contact to avoid criticism. She feels lonely and inadequate.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Personality disorders
   - **A.** Borderline — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Avoidant **(Correct)** — Correct. Cluster C.
   - **C.** Histrionic — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Dependent — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Schizotypal — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Schizoid — Wrong. Does not want relationships.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - wants friends and a partner — Desires relationships.
     - sure people will think she is boring — Fear of rejection.
     - She feels lonely and inadequate — Feelings of inadequacy.
   - **Reasoning:** Desire for relationships + hypersensitivity to rejection + inhibition → avoidant personality disorder.
   - **Teaching point:** Social anxiety disorder often coexists.
   - **Follow-up:** Which personality disorder is most likely?

784. A 32-year-old nurse has had six hospital admissions this year for confusion and sweating from low blood sugar. She does not have diabetes. She asks for more tests and seems eager to have a pancreatic biopsy. She is not seeking time off work or money. Her results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Factitious disorders
   - **A.** Illness anxiety disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Sulfonylurea overdose — Wrong. Screen negative; C-peptide would be high.
   - **C.** Factitious disorder imposed on self **(Correct)** — Correct. Secret insulin injection to assume the sick role.
   - **D.** Somatic symptom disorder — Wrong. Symptoms are produced intentionally.
   - **E.** Insulinoma — Wrong. C-peptide would be high.
   - **F.** Malingering — Wrong. No external gain.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - six hospital admissions this year — Multiple admissions.
     - seems eager to have a pancreatic biopsy — Willingness for invasive procedures.
     - She is not seeking time off work or money — No external gain.
     - A 32-year-old nurse — Healthcare worker.
   - **Reasoning:** Hypoglycemia with high insulin + low C-peptide + healthcare worker + no external gain → exogenous insulin → factitious disorder.
   - **Teaching point:** Symptoms intentional, motivation unconscious (primary gain).
   - **Follow-up:** Which diagnosis is most likely?
   - Page: 583

785. Three days after watching her father die suddenly of a heart attack, a 19-year-old woman cannot move her right arm. Her reflexes, tone and imaging are normal. When her arm is dropped over her face, it falls to the side and misses. She seems calm and unconcerned about the weakness.
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Conversion disorder
   - **A.** Malingering — Wrong. No external gain.
   - **B.** Factitious disorder — Wrong. Not intentionally produced.
   - **C.** Stroke — Wrong. Normal exam and imaging.
   - **D.** Multiple sclerosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Somatic symptom disorder — Wrong. Not a loss of neurologic function.
   - **F.** Conversion (functional neurologic symptom) disorder **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - watching her father die suddenly — Acute stressor.
     - cannot move her right arm — Loss of motor function.
     - falls to the side and misses — Inconsistent exam.
     - calm and unconcerned — La belle indifférence.
   - **Reasoning:** Acute stressor + neurologic deficit inconsistent with disease + indifference → conversion disorder.
   - **Teaching point:** Symptoms and motivation are both unconscious.
   - **Follow-up:** Which diagnosis is most likely?

786. A 20-year-old dancer has swollen cheeks below her ears, eroded tooth enamel and small calluses on the backs of her fingers. She admits eating large amounts of food in secret several times a week and then feeling out of control. Her results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Bulimia nervosa
   - **A.** Escitalopram — Wrong. Not contraindicated.
   - **B.** Ondansetron — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Fluoxetine — Wrong. Approved treatment.
   - **D.** Bupropion **(Correct)** — Correct. Seizure risk in bulimia.
   - **E.** Mirtazapine — Wrong. Not the listed contraindication.
   - **F.** Sertraline — Wrong. Not contraindicated.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - swollen cheeks below her ears — Parotid hypertrophy.
     - eroded tooth enamel — Acid exposure from vomiting.
     - small calluses on the backs of her fingers — Russell sign.
     - eating large amounts of food in secret — Binge eating.
   - **Reasoning:** Binge-purge + normal BMI + parotid swelling + Russell sign + hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis → bulimia nervosa → avoid bupropion.
   - **Teaching point:** Fluoxetine is the approved drug.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is contraindicated in her treatment?

787. A 17-year-old girl with a BMI of 13.9 kg/m² is admitted with bradycardia and hypotension. She is started on high-calorie feeding. On day 3 she develops muscle weakness, confusion and an irregular heartbeat. Her phosphate levels are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Anorexia nervosa
   - **A.** Excess cortisol from stress — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Hyperthyroidism from feeding — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Vomiting causing alkalosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Thiamine excess — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Insulin release drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells **(Correct)** — Correct. Refeeding syndrome.
   - **F.** Fluid overload alone — Wrong. Not the main mechanism.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - BMI of 13.9 kg/m² — Severe malnutrition.
     - started on high-calorie feeding — Sudden calorie increase.
     - muscle weakness, confusion and an irregular heartbeat — Hypophosphatemia effects.
   - **Reasoning:** Severe malnutrition + rapid feeding → ↑ insulin → intracellular shift of PO4, K+, Mg2+ → refeeding syndrome.
   - **Teaching point:** Start feeding slowly and monitor electrolytes closely.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the mechanism of her deterioration?
   - Page: 584

788. A 45-year-old man drinks heavily. At a clinic visit he says, "I know drinking is hurting my liver and my marriage, but I'm not sure I can give it up right now. It's how I relax."
   - **Domain:** Psychiatry
   - **Topic:** Transtheoretical model of change
   - **A.** Tell him he must stop or be discharged — Wrong. Not appropriate.
   - **B.** Praise his progress and discuss relapse prevention — Wrong. Maintenance.
   - **C.** Discuss the pros of changing and the cons of continuing to drink **(Correct)** — Correct. Contemplation stage.
   - **D.** Refer him to inpatient detoxification immediately — Wrong. Not ready.
   - **E.** Avoid discussing alcohol until he raises it — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Set a quit date and prescribe naltrexone today — Wrong. Preparation.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - I know drinking is hurting my liver and my marriage — Acknowledges the problem.
     - I'm not sure I can give it up right now — Ambivalence.
     - It's how I relax — Perceived benefit.
   - **Reasoning:** Acknowledges problem but ambivalent → contemplation → explore pros and cons.
   - **Teaching point:** Precontemplation patients deny there is a problem.
   - **Follow-up:** Which approach best matches his stage of change?
   - Page: 586

789. A 30-year-old woman with depression takes fluoxetine. She is given a drug for a migraine and another for nausea in the emergency department. An hour later she is agitated, sweating and shivering, with diarrhea, a temperature of 39.2°C and rhythmic jerking of her ankles when they are flexed.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Psychiatric emergencies
   - **A.** Cyproheptadine **(Correct)** — Correct. 5-HT2 antagonist for serotonin syndrome.
   - **B.** Dantrolene — Wrong. NMS, malignant hyperthermia.
   - **C.** Bromocriptine — Wrong. NMS.
   - **D.** Phentolamine — Wrong. Hypertensive crisis.
   - **E.** Physostigmine — Wrong. Anticholinergic toxicity.
   - **F.** Acetaminophen — Wrong. Not effective.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - takes fluoxetine — SSRI.
     - a drug for a migraine and another for nausea — Triptan and ondansetron.
     - agitated, sweating and shivering, with diarrhea — Autonomic and mental status changes.
     - rhythmic jerking of her ankles — Clonus.
   - **Reasoning:** SSRI + triptan + ondansetron → serotonin syndrome (3 A's) → benzodiazepines, then cyproheptadine.
   - **Teaching point:** Clonus and hyperreflexia distinguish it from NMS.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug should be given if benzodiazepines and supportive care fail?

790. A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia was given several doses of haloperidol over 3 days for agitation. He is now confused and stiff. His findings are shown.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Psychiatric emergencies
   - **A.** Benztropine alone — Wrong. Dystonia.
   - **B.** Dantrolene and bromocriptine **(Correct)** — Correct. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
   - **C.** Haloperidol at a lower dose — Wrong. Stop the drug.
   - **D.** Cyproheptadine — Wrong. Serotonin syndrome.
   - **E.** Phentolamine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Physostigmine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - given several doses of haloperidol over 3 days — Typical antipsychotic, onset over days.
     - He is now confused and stiff — Encephalopathy and rigidity.
     - A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia — Patient on antipsychotics.

791. A 52-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has been stable on lithium for 6 years. Her primary care physician started a new drug for high blood pressure. Her lithium levels are shown. She now has vomiting, slurred speech, a coarse tremor and an unsteady gait.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Lithium
   - **A.** Theophylline — Wrong. Lowers lithium.
   - **B.** Clonidine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Doxazosin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Hydrochlorothiazide **(Correct)** — Correct. Increases proximal lithium reabsorption.
   - **E.** Amlodipine — Wrong. Does not raise lithium.
   - **F.** Furosemide — Wrong. Less effect than thiazides.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - stable on lithium for 6 years — Previously therapeutic.
     - new drug for high blood pressure — Antihypertensive.
     - vomiting, slurred speech, a coarse tremor and an unsteady gait — Lithium toxicity.
   - **Reasoning:** New thiazide → volume contraction → ↑ PCT Na+ and lithium reabsorption → lithium toxicity.
   - **Teaching point:** ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs also raise lithium levels.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug was most likely started?

792. A 19-year-old woman is brought in drowsy 2 hours after taking a full bottle of her mother's amitriptyline. Her findings are shown. Shortly after arrival she has a generalized seizure.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
   - **A.** Naloxone — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Physostigmine — Wrong. Not standard; may cause arrhythmia.
   - **C.** IV sodium bicarbonate **(Correct)** — Correct. Reverses Na+ channel blockade.
   - **D.** Dantrolene — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Haloperidol — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Flumazenil — Wrong. Can provoke seizures.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - a full bottle of her mother's amitriptyline — TCA overdose.
     - drowsy — CNS depression.
     - generalized seizure — Convulsions.
   - **Reasoning:** TCA overdose + anticholinergic signs + wide QRS + seizure → Na+ channel blockade → sodium bicarbonate.
   - **Teaching point:** "Tri-C-cyclics": Convulsions, Coma, Cardiotoxicity.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most important next treatment?
   - Page: 587

793. A 48-year-old man is admitted for a broken leg. Three days after admission he becomes agitated, sweaty and tremulous. He is picking at the bedsheets, says spiders are crawling on the wall and does not know where he is. His heart rate is 134/min and BP 172/100 mm Hg. His wife says he drinks a bottle of vodka daily.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Delirium tremens
   - **A.** Haloperidol alone — Wrong. Lowers seizure threshold.
   - **B.** Clonidine alone — Wrong. Not adequate.
   - **C.** Naltrexone — Wrong. Not for acute withdrawal.
   - **D.** Disulfiram — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Physical restraint without medication — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Long-acting benzodiazepine, such as diazepam or chlordiazepoxide **(Correct)** — Correct. Delirium tremens.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Three days after admission — 2–4 days after last drink.
     - says spiders are crawling on the wall — Hallucinations.
     - does not know where he is — Disorientation.
     - His heart rate is 134/min — Autonomic hyperactivity.
     - drinks a bottle of vodka daily — Heavy alcohol use.
   - **Reasoning:** Heavy drinker hospitalized + 2–4 days without alcohol + delirium + autonomic hyperactivity → DTs → long-acting benzodiazepine.
   - **Teaching point:** Give thiamine before glucose.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate treatment?

794. Police bring in a 23-year-old man who was fighting several officers at once. He is extremely agitated and shouting nonsense. His findings are shown. Urine screen is negative for opioids, cocaine and amphetamines.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Psychoactive drug intoxication
   - **A.** μ-opioid agonist — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** NMDA receptor antagonist **(Correct)** — Correct. Phencyclidine.
   - **C.** GABA-A modulator — Wrong. Depressant.
   - **D.** CB1 agonist — Wrong. Cannabis.
   - **E.** Dopamine reuptake blocker — Wrong. Cocaine; screen negative.
   - **F.** 5-HT2A agonist — Wrong. LSD; no nystagmus or violence.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - fighting several officers at once — Violence.
     - extremely agitated — Psychomotor agitation.
     - negative for opioids, cocaine and amphetamines — Not common stimulants.
   - **Reasoning:** Violence + nystagmus + hypertension + analgesia → PCP → NMDA antagonist.
   - **Teaching point:** Vertical nystagmus is a strong clue to PCP.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the mechanism of the drug he most likely used?
   - Page: 589

795. A 21-year-old woman is brought from a music festival with confusion, clenched jaw and teeth grinding. Her temperature is 40.1°C. She drank many liters of water during the night. Her sodium is 119 mEq/L.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Psychoactive drug intoxication
   - **A.** Benzodiazepines — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Heroin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** LSD — Wrong. No hyponatremia.
   - **D.** Cannabis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** MDMA (ecstasy) **(Correct)** — Correct. Hyperthermia, bruxism and hyponatremia.
   - **F.** Alcohol — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - music festival — Typical setting.
     - clenched jaw and teeth grinding — Bruxism.
     - Her temperature is 40.1°C — Hyperthermia.
     - Her sodium is 119 mEq/L — Hyponatremia.
   - **Reasoning:** Party + bruxism + hyperthermia + hyponatremia (water intake, ADH) → MDMA.
   - **Teaching point:** MDMA reverses SERT > DAT, NET and can cause serotonin syndrome.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug did she most likely take?
   - Page: 589

796. A 38-year-old man with depression has not responded to two SSRIs. He has gained weight on them and is unhappy about their sexual side effects. He also wants to stop smoking a pack a day. He has no history of seizures or eating disorders.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Atypical antidepressants
   - **A.** Bupropion **(Correct)** — Correct. NE/DA reuptake inhibitor; less sexual dysfunction and weight gain, aids smoking cessation.
   - **B.** Amitriptyline — Wrong. Weight gain, anticholinergic.
   - **C.** Paroxetine — Wrong. Sexual dysfunction, weight gain.
   - **D.** Mirtazapine — Wrong. Weight gain.
   - **E.** Phenelzine — Wrong. Not first choice.
   - **F.** Trazodone — Wrong. Sedation, priapism.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - gained weight on them — Avoid weight gain.
     - unhappy about their sexual side effects — Avoid sexual dysfunction.
     - stop smoking a pack a day — Smoking cessation.
     - no history of seizures or eating disorders — No contraindication.
   - **Reasoning:** Depression + SSRI side effects + smoker without seizure risk → bupropion.
   - **Teaching point:** Bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia and anorexia nervosa.
   - **Follow-up:** Which antidepressant is most appropriate?
   - Page: 594

797. A 36-year-old woman with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is started on clozapine. Six weeks later she has a sore throat and fever of 39°C.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Antipsychotics
   - **A.** Fasting lipids — Wrong. Not urgent.
   - **B.** Absolute neutrophil count **(Correct)** — Correct. Agranulocytosis risk.
   - **C.** Serum prolactin — Wrong. Not urgent.
   - **D.** Serum sodium — Wrong. Not the priority.
   - **E.** ECG only — Wrong. Not the priority.
   - **F.** Thyroid-stimulating hormone — Wrong. Lithium.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - treatment-resistant schizophrenia — Clozapine indication.
     - started on clozapine — Agranulocytosis risk.
     - sore throat and fever of 39°C — Possible neutropenic infection.
   - **Reasoning:** Clozapine + fever and sore throat → check ANC for agranulocytosis.
   - **Teaching point:** Clozapine also causes seizures, myocarditis and hypersalivation.
   - **Follow-up:** Which test is the most important to order now?
   - Page: 591

798. A 64-year-old man has taken fluphenazine for schizophrenia for 15 years. His family notices that he constantly smacks his lips, pokes his tongue out and makes chewing movements. The movements worsen when he is anxious.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Antipsychotics
   - **A.** Levodopa — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Increase fluphenazine — Wrong. Masks temporarily, worsens long term.
   - **C.** Propranolol — Wrong. Akathisia.
   - **D.** Benztropine — Wrong. May worsen.
   - **E.** Valbenazine **(Correct)** — Correct. VMAT2 inhibitor for tardive dyskinesia.
   - **F.** Dantrolene — Wrong. NMS.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - taken fluphenazine for schizophrenia for 15 years — Long-term typical antipsychotic.
     - smacks his lips, pokes his tongue out — Orofacial dyskinesia.
     - makes chewing movements — Choreiform movements.
   - **Reasoning:** Years of D2 blockade + orofacial chorea → tardive dyskinesia → valbenazine or deutetrabenazine.
   - **Teaching point:** Order of EPS: ADAPT — Acute Dystonia, Akathisia, Parkinsonism, Tardive dyskinesia.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is most appropriate?
   - Page: 591

799. A 41-year-old woman has depression with prominent anxiety and insomnia. She has lost 8 kg because she has no appetite. She wants something to take at night.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Atypical antidepressants
   - **A.** Trazodone; 5-HT2 antagonist — Wrong. Sedating but not used as antidepressant at low dose.
   - **B.** Bupropion; NE and DA reuptake inhibitor — Wrong. Activating and appetite-suppressing.
   - **C.** Venlafaxine; SNRI — Wrong. Not the best fit.
   - **D.** Fluoxetine; SSRI — Wrong. Activating, may reduce appetite.
   - **E.** Lithium; mood stabilizer — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Mirtazapine; α2 antagonist that increases NE and 5-HT release, with H1 blockade causing sedation and appetite **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - prominent anxiety and insomnia — Wants sedation.
     - lost 8 kg because she has no appetite — Benefits from weight gain.
     - something to take at night — Sedating drug.
   - **Reasoning:** Depression + insomnia + weight loss → mirtazapine ("munch more and move less").
   - **Teaching point:** Mirtazapine's sedation is stronger at low doses.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is most appropriate, and how does it work?
   - Page: 594

800. A 26-year-old man has used heroin daily for 3 years and wants treatment. He last injected 4 hours ago. He is given his first dose of sublingual buprenorphine in the clinic. Within an hour he has yawning, a runny nose, abdominal cramps, diarrhea and goosebumps.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Medically supervised opioid withdrawal
   - **A.** He had a delayed heroin overdose — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Buprenorphine is a full agonist overdose — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist that displaced heroin from μ receptors **(Correct)** — Correct. Precipitated withdrawal.
   - **D.** He is allergic to buprenorphine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** The naloxone component was absorbed sublingually — Wrong. Not the main mechanism.
   - **F.** He developed serotonin syndrome — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - last injected 4 hours ago — Full agonist on board.
     - first dose of sublingual buprenorphine — Partial agonist.
     - yawning, a runny nose, abdominal cramps, diarrhea and goosebumps — Opioid withdrawal.
   - **Reasoning:** Recent full agonist + buprenorphine → displacement at μ receptors → precipitated withdrawal.
   - **Teaching point:** Wait until mild withdrawal begins before starting buprenorphine.
   - **Follow-up:** Why did this happen?
   - Page: 594

## Public Health 1

Source: `mock-public-health-1.json`

801. An investigator enrolls 500 adults with newly diagnosed pancreatic cancer and 500 adults without cancer, then asks both groups about past occupational solvent exposure. Exposure was reported by 90 of the patients with cancer and 30 of those without.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Observational studies
   - **A.** A randomized trial, reporting absolute risk reduction — Wrong. No intervention was assigned.
   - **B.** A case-control study, reporting an odds ratio **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** A cross-sectional study, reporting prevalence — Wrong. Two defined groups were compared for prior exposure.
   - **D.** A case series, reporting no measure of association — Wrong. There is a comparison group.
   - **E.** An ecological study, reporting population correlation — Wrong. Individuals were studied.
   - **F.** A cohort study, reporting relative risk — Wrong. Groups were chosen by disease, not exposure.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 500 adults with newly diagnosed pancreatic cancer and 500 adults without cancer — Groups defined by disease status.
     - asks both groups about past occupational solvent exposure — Exposure assessed retrospectively.
     - Exposure was reported by 90 of the patients with cancer and 30 of those without — Odds of exposure compared between groups.
   - **Reasoning:** Selecting on disease and looking backward at exposure defines a case-control study, whose measure is the odds ratio.
   - **Teaching point:** Had the investigator instead followed exposed and unexposed solvent workers forward, the design would be a cohort study with relative risk.
   - **Follow-up:** Which study design is this, and which measure of association should the investigator report?
   - Page: 256

802. In a trial of a new anticoagulant, 300 patients were randomized to the drug and 300 to placebo. Forty patients assigned to the drug stopped taking it and switched to placebo, and the investigators analyzed every patient in the group to which they were originally assigned.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Clinical trials
   - **A.** Meta-analysis, which pools summary data — Wrong. Only one trial is described.
   - **B.** Per-protocol analysis, which raises internal validity — Wrong. That excludes noncompleters.
   - **C.** Subgroup analysis, which identifies effect modification — Wrong. No stratifying factor was used.
   - **D.** As-treated analysis, which removes confounding — Wrong. That groups patients by treatment received.
   - **E.** Intention-to-treat analysis, which avoids bias from attrition, crossover and nonrandom noncompliance **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Crossover analysis, which lets patients serve as their own controls — Wrong. No washout or sequence was described.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - randomized to the drug and 300 to placebo — Random allocation.
     - Forty patients assigned to the drug stopped taking it and switched to placebo — Crossover and noncompliance.
     - analyzed every patient in the group to which they were originally assigned — Analysis by original assignment.
   - **Reasoning:** Analyzing patients by original random assignment is intention-to-treat, which protects against bias introduced by dropouts and crossover, though it may dilute the measured effect.
   - **Teaching point:** Excluding the 40 who stopped treatment would be a per-protocol analysis and would raise the risk of bias.
   - **Follow-up:** Which analysis was used, and what is its main advantage?
   - Page: 257

803. A new drug is given to 30 healthy volunteers in escalating doses, with no control group, to find the highest dose that can be tolerated without severe adverse effects.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Clinical trials
   - **A.** Preclinical testing — Wrong. That is in animals and in vitro.
   - **B.** Phase 4 — Wrong. That is postmarketing surveillance.
   - **C.** Phase 1 **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Phase 2 — Wrong. That assesses whether the drug works, in patients.
   - **E.** Phase 3 — Wrong. That compares with standard of care in large numbers.
   - **F.** Phase 0 — Wrong. That is microdosing for pharmacokinetics.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - given to 30 healthy volunteers in escalating doses — Small number, dose escalation.
     - with no control group — Open label.
     - to find the highest dose that can be tolerated — Maximum tolerable dose.
   - **Reasoning:** Phase 1 assesses safety by dose escalation in a small number of healthy volunteers or patients to define the maximum tolerable dose.
   - **Teaching point:** Rare adverse effects discovered after approval come from phase 4 postmarketing surveillance.
   - **Follow-up:** Which phase of clinical testing is this?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
     {
       "type": "table",
       "head": [
         "",
         "Disease present",
         "Disease absent"
       ],
       "rows": [
         [
           "Test positive",
           "80",
           "60"
         ],
         [
           "Test negative",
           "20",
           "840"
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Results of a screening test applied to 1000 people
   - Page: 257

804. A screening test for a liver condition is applied to 1000 people whose true disease status is known by biopsy. The results are shown in the table.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Diagnostic tests
   - **A.** Sensitivity 80%, positive predictive value 57% **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** Sensitivity 57%, positive predictive value 80% — Wrong. The two values are transposed.
   - **C.** Sensitivity 20%, positive predictive value 43% — Wrong. These are the error rates.
   - **D.** Sensitivity 93%, positive predictive value 80% — Wrong. 93% is the specificity.
   - **E.** Sensitivity 93%, positive predictive value 57% — Wrong. Sensitivity is not 93%.
   - **F.** Sensitivity 80%, positive predictive value 98% — Wrong. 98% is the negative predictive value.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - applied to 1000 people whose true disease status is known by biopsy — A reference standard defines disease.
     - A screening test for a liver condition — A single test under evaluation.
     - The results are shown in the table — Counts of true and false results.
   - **Reasoning:** Sensitivity is 80 of 100 with disease, or 80%; positive predictive value is 80 of the 140 positive tests, or 57%.
   - **Teaching point:** Specificity here is 840 of 900 without disease, or 93%, and negative predictive value is 840 of 860, or 98%.
   - **Follow-up:** What are the sensitivity and the positive predictive value of this test?
   - Page: 260

805. A clinic serves a population in which the prevalence of a condition is 2%. The same test is then used in a referral center where prevalence is 40%. Sensitivity and specificity of the test are unchanged.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Diagnostic tests
   - **A.** Positive predictive value is lower and negative predictive value higher in the referral center — Wrong. The relationship is reversed.
   - **B.** Both predictive values are higher in the referral center — Wrong. Negative predictive value falls as prevalence rises.
   - **C.** Only sensitivity changes — Wrong. Sensitivity is a fixed property.
   - **D.** Positive predictive value is higher and negative predictive value lower in the referral center **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Both predictive values are unchanged — Wrong. Predictive values depend on prevalence.
   - **F.** Only specificity changes — Wrong. Specificity is a fixed property.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - prevalence of a condition is 2% — Low pretest probability.
     - a referral center where prevalence is 40% — High pretest probability.
     - Sensitivity and specificity of the test are unchanged — Fixed test properties.
   - **Reasoning:** Positive predictive value varies directly with prevalence and negative predictive value inversely, while sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself.
   - **Teaching point:** Prevalence is approximately equivalent to pretest probability in this reasoning.
   - **Follow-up:** How do the predictive values differ between the two settings?
   - Page: 260

806. A laboratory lowers the cutoff value of a tumor marker used for screening, so that more results are called positive.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Diagnostic tests
   - **A.** Only the false-negative rate rises — Wrong. False negatives fall.
   - **B.** All four measures fall — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Nothing changes, since cutoffs do not affect test performance — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Sensitivity falls and specificity rises — Wrong. That follows raising the cutoff.
   - **E.** All four measures rise — Wrong. The trade-off is unavoidable.
   - **F.** Sensitivity and negative predictive value rise, while specificity and positive predictive value fall **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - lowers the cutoff value of a tumor marker used for screening — Threshold moved down.
     - so that more results are called positive — More true and false positives.
     - tumor marker used for screening — Screening favors sensitivity.
   - **Reasoning:** Lowering a cutoff captures more true positives and more false positives, raising sensitivity and negative predictive value while lowering specificity and positive predictive value.
   - **Teaching point:** Raising the cutoff does the opposite and is appropriate for a confirmatory test.
   - **Follow-up:** What happens to the test characteristics?
