807. Two candidate diagnostic tests, A and B, are compared in the same group of patients with known disease status, and their receiver operating characteristic curves are plotted.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Receiver operating characteristic curve
   - **A.** Test B, because a lower curve means fewer false positives — Wrong. Not how the plot is read.
   - **B.** They perform identically, since both reach the top right corner — Wrong. All such curves do.
   - **C.** Test B, because its curve is closer to the diagonal — Wrong. The diagonal means no discrimination.
   - **D.** It cannot be judged without the prevalence — Wrong. These curves are independent of prevalence.
   - **E.** Test A, because its curve lies closer to the upper left corner and so has the greater area under the curve **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Neither, because both curves start at the origin — Wrong. All such curves do.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Two candidate diagnostic tests, A and B — Head-to-head comparison.
     - the same group of patients with known disease status — One population, one reference standard.
     - their receiver operating characteristic curves are plotted — Sensitivity against the false-positive rate.
   - **Reasoning:** A receiver operating characteristic curve plots sensitivity against 1 minus specificity; the better test has the larger area under the curve and hugs the upper left corner.
   - **Teaching point:** A curve lying along the diagonal has an area of 0.5 and no predictive value.
   - **Follow-up:** Which test performs better, and on what basis?
   - Page: 261

808. A home blood pressure monitor gives readings that differ by no more than 1 mm Hg on repeated measurement of the same arm, but every reading is 18 mm Hg higher than a calibrated mercury device.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Precision and accuracy
   - **A.** Precision low, accuracy high, with random error — Wrong. The readings are highly reproducible.
   - **B.** Precision and accuracy cannot be distinguished — Wrong. They are separate properties.
   - **C.** Precision high, accuracy low, with systematic error **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Precision low, accuracy high, with systematic error — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Precision low, accuracy low, with random error — Wrong. Readings are reproducible.
   - **F.** Precision high, accuracy high, with no error — Wrong. The readings are consistently wrong.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - differ by no more than 1 mm Hg on repeated measurement — High reproducibility.
     - every reading is 18 mm Hg higher than a calibrated mercury device — Consistent deviation from truth.
     - A home blood pressure monitor gives readings — A measuring instrument.
   - **Reasoning:** Reproducible readings mean high precision, while a constant offset from the true value means low accuracy from systematic error.
   - **Teaching point:** Random error lowers precision and raises the standard deviation, which in turn lowers statistical power.
   - **Follow-up:** How are the precision and accuracy of this monitor best described, and what kind of error is present?
   - Page: 261

809. A new treatment shortens the average duration of a chronic skin disease from 10 years to 4 years. The number of new cases each year in the community is unchanged.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Incidence and prevalence
   - **A.** Incidence falls and prevalence is unchanged — Wrong. The reverse is true.
   - **B.** Both fall — Wrong. Incidence is unchanged.
   - **C.** Incidence rises and prevalence falls — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Neither changes — Wrong. Prevalence depends on duration.
   - **E.** Both rise — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Incidence is unchanged and prevalence falls **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - shortens the average duration of a chronic skin disease from 10 years to 4 years — Duration falls.
     - The number of new cases each year in the community is unchanged — Incidence constant.
     - A new treatment — An intervention affecting disease course, not onset.
   - **Reasoning:** Prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by duration, so shortening duration lowers prevalence while leaving incidence untouched.
   - **Teaching point:** An effective vaccine would instead lower both incidence and prevalence.
   - **Follow-up:** What happens to the incidence and the prevalence of the disease?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       ],

         ],

           "Falls"
         ],

           "Rises",
           "Rises"
         ],

           "Falls",
           "Falls"
         ]
       ]

     ```
     Effect of various situations on incidence and prevalence
   - Page: 262

810. A public health officer reviews the table while planning a program for a chronic airborne infectious disease in a city.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Incidence and prevalence
   - **A.** Extensive vaccination of the susceptible population **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** Shortening the duration of illness only — Wrong. Incidence is unchanged.
   - **C.** Introducing a drug that lengthens survival — Wrong. Prevalence would rise.
   - **D.** Opening more specialist clinics — Wrong. No stated effect on either measure.
   - **E.** Lengthening hospital stays — Wrong. No stated effect on either measure.
   - **F.** Improving diagnostic sensitivity — Wrong. Both would rise.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - reviews the table while planning a program — The table gives the direction of each effect.
     - a chronic airborne infectious disease in a city — Transmission can be interrupted.
     - A public health officer — Planning at population level.
   - **Reasoning:** Measures that prevent new cases, such as vaccination or reducing contact, lower incidence, and lower incidence in turn lowers prevalence.
   - **Teaching point:** Treatments that only shorten illness lower prevalence alone, and better survival raises prevalence.
   - **Follow-up:** Which intervention would lower both incidence and prevalence?
   - Page: 262

811. Investigators recruit cases of a liver disease from the inpatient wards of a tertiary hospital and controls from the same wards. The exposure histories of both groups turn out to be unlike those of the surrounding community.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Bias and study errors
   - **A.** Measurement bias, reduced by standardized instruments — Wrong. No distorted measurement is described.
   - **B.** Selection bias, specifically Berkson bias, reduced by choosing an appropriate comparison group drawn from the target population **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** Procedure bias, reduced by blinding — Wrong. Groups were not treated differently.
   - **D.** Recall bias, reduced by shortening the interval from exposure to follow-up — Wrong. The problem is who was enrolled.
   - **E.** Lead-time bias, reduced by measuring back-end survival — Wrong. No screening or survival claim is made.
   - **F.** Length-time bias, reduced by a randomized screening trial — Wrong. No screening test is described.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - recruit cases of a liver disease from the inpatient wards of a tertiary hospital — Hospital-based sampling.
     - controls from the same wards — Controls are also hospitalized.
     - unlike those of the surrounding community — The sample is unrepresentative.
   - **Reasoning:** Hospitalized cases and controls are less healthy and carry different exposures, which is Berkson bias, a form of selection bias remedied by proper sampling and randomization.
   - **Teaching point:** Participants lost to follow-up with a different prognosis would instead be attrition bias.
   - **Follow-up:** Which bias is this, and how could it have been reduced?
   - Page: 263

812. In a trial of a physical therapy program, patients in the treatment arm are seen in a specialized rehabilitation unit with more staff time, while the control arm is seen in the general clinic.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Bias and study errors
   - **A.** Selection bias, reduced by randomization — Wrong. Allocation itself is not at issue.
   - **B.** Measurement bias, reduced by objective instruments — Wrong. The difference lies in the care given.
   - **C.** Recall bias, reduced by using medical records — Wrong. No recall of exposure is involved.
   - **D.** Procedure bias, reduced by blinding and the use of placebo **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Lead-time bias, reduced by adjusting for severity — Wrong. No early detection is described.
   - **F.** Length-time bias, reduced by randomized screening — Wrong. No screening is described.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - patients in the treatment arm are seen in a specialized rehabilitation unit with more staff time — Groups treated unequally.
     - the control arm is seen in the general clinic — Different setting for controls.
     - a trial of a physical therapy program — An interventional study.
   - **Reasoning:** When subjects in different groups are not treated the same, procedure bias arises, and blinding with placebo limits the influence of participants and researchers.
   - **Teaching point:** A researcher who records better outcomes because they expect them shows observer-expectancy bias, addressed by the same measures.
   - **Follow-up:** Which bias does this introduce, and what reduces it?
   - Page: 263

813. A screening program detects a cancer 3 years earlier than it would otherwise have been found. Patients detected by screening live, on average, 3 years longer from diagnosis, but they die at the same ages as unscreened patients.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Bias and study errors
   - **A.** Effect modification, addressed by stratification — Wrong. No subgroup difference is described.
   - **B.** Length-time bias, addressed by a randomized screening trial — Wrong. The issue is the earlier starting point, not which tumors are found.
   - **C.** Attrition bias, addressed by intention-to-treat analysis — Wrong. No differential loss is described.
   - **D.** Recall bias, addressed by using records — Wrong. No recall is involved.
   - **E.** Lead-time bias, addressed by measuring back-end survival with adjustment for disease severity at diagnosis **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Confounding, addressed by regression — Wrong. No third factor is described.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - detects a cancer 3 years earlier than it would otherwise have been found — Diagnosis moved earlier.
     - live, on average, 3 years longer from diagnosis — Survival measured from diagnosis.
     - they die at the same ages as unscreened patients — No change in disease course.
   - **Reasoning:** Lead-time bias arises when earlier detection lengthens survival measured from diagnosis without changing the course of disease; adjusting for severity at diagnosis exposes it.
   - **Teaching point:** A caveat of adjusting for severity is that it may mask causality.
   - **Follow-up:** Which bias explains the apparent survival benefit, and how is it addressed?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
     {
       "type": "table",
       "head": [
         "Analysis",
         "Coffee and lung cancer",
         "Oral contraceptives and venous thrombosis"
       ],
       "rows": [
         [
           "Crude",
           "Significant",
           "Significant"
         ],
         [
           "Smokers only",
           "None",
           "Strong"
         ],
         [
           "Nonsmokers only",
           "None",
           "None"
         ],
         [
           "Interpretation",
           "?",
           "?"
         ]
       ]
     }
     ```
     Crude and stratified results of two studies
   - Page: 263

814. Two studies are summarized in the table, each showing a significant crude association that changes after stratification by smoking.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Confounding and effect modification
   - **A.** Effect modification and confounding — Wrong. The findings are reversed.
   - **B.** Lead-time bias and length-time bias — Wrong. Neither involves screening.
   - **C.** Confounding in both — Wrong. One association persists strongly in a subgroup.
   - **D.** Confounding and effect modification **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Selection bias and recall bias — Wrong. Neither is a bias of sampling or recall.
   - **F.** Effect modification in both — Wrong. One association disappears entirely.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Two studies are summarized in the table — Two separate associations.
     - a significant crude association — Both look real before stratification.
     - changes after stratification by smoking — Smoking is the stratifying factor.
   - **Reasoning:** An association that disappears on stratification was confounded, while one that is strong in one stratum and absent in another shows effect modification, a true interaction.
   - **Teaching point:** Confounding is handled by matching or regression; effect modification is reported by stratum.
   - **Follow-up:** Which phenomena do the coffee study and the oral contraceptive study illustrate, respectively?
   - Page: 264

815. A set of 11 laboratory values is 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 94. The last value came from a mislabeled specimen that cannot be removed from the record.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Measures of central tendency
   - **A.** The mean, because it uses all the data — Wrong. It is most distorted by the outlier.
   - **B.** The median, because it is far less affected by the extreme value **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** The mode, because it is the most common value — Wrong. It ignores most of the distribution.
   - **D.** The standard deviation, because it summarizes spread — Wrong. That is not a measure of central tendency.
   - **E.** The standard error, because it narrows with sample size — Wrong. That is not a measure of central tendency.
   - **F.** The variance, because it is the squared deviation — Wrong. That is not a measure of central tendency.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 94 — One extreme value.
     - The last value came from a mislabeled specimen — The outlier is spurious.
     - cannot be removed from the record — The data must be summarized as they stand.
   - **Reasoning:** The mean is most affected by outliers, so for skewed data the median is the better measure of central tendency; the mode is least affected but least informative here.
   - **Teaching point:** In a normal distribution the mean, median and mode coincide and the mean is preferred.
   - **Follow-up:** Which measure of central tendency best represents the typical value, and why?
   - Page: 265

816. A trial comparing two antihypertensives finds a mean difference in systolic pressure of 4 mm Hg, with a 95% confidence interval of −1 to 9 mm Hg.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Confidence interval
   - **A.** The result is significant, because the interval is narrow — Wrong. Width alone does not decide.
   - **B.** The null hypothesis has been proven true — Wrong. A null hypothesis is never proven.
   - **C.** A type I error has certainly occurred — Wrong. No error can be identified from this alone.
   - **D.** The confidence interval is invalid without the p value — Wrong. The interval is interpretable on its own.
   - **E.** The result is significant, because the point estimate favors one drug — Wrong. The interval decides.
   - **F.** The result is not statistically significant, because the confidence interval for the mean difference includes 0 **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - a mean difference in systolic pressure of 4 mm Hg — A point estimate.
     - with a 95% confidence interval of −1 to 9 mm Hg — The interval spans zero.
     - A trial comparing two antihypertensives — Two groups compared on a numerical outcome.
   - **Reasoning:** The null hypothesis is not rejected when a 95% confidence interval for a mean difference includes 0, or when an interval for an odds ratio or relative risk includes 1.
   - **Teaching point:** Had the interval been 1 to 9 mm Hg, the result would have been significant.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the correct conclusion?
   - Page: 267

817. A study is designed with alpha set at 0.05 and a power of 0.80, but recruitment falls short and only half the planned participants enroll. The true treatment effect is real but modest.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Testing errors
   - **A.** An increased risk of a type II error, because power falls with a smaller sample **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** No consequence, since alpha is unchanged — Wrong. Power depends on sample size.
   - **C.** Greater precision of measurement — Wrong. Not a consequence of fewer subjects.
   - **D.** A larger measured effect size — Wrong. Sample size does not change the true effect.
   - **E.** A narrower confidence interval — Wrong. Smaller samples widen the interval.
   - **F.** An increased risk of a type I error — Wrong. Alpha was unchanged.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - alpha set at 0.05 and a power of 0.80 — Planned error rates.
     - only half the planned participants enroll — Sample size halved.
     - The true treatment effect is real but modest — A real effect may be missed.
   - **Reasoning:** Power is 1 minus beta and rises with sample size, effect size, precision and alpha, so an undersized study is prone to a false-negative type II error.
   - **Teaching point:** Statistical significance is not the same as clinical significance, so even a significant small effect may not matter to patients.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most likely consequence?

818. Survival after randomization to two chemotherapy regimens is plotted, and the log rank test gives a p value of 0.002.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Kaplan-Meier curve
   - **A.** The steeper curve indicates a lower hazard — Wrong. A steeper curve means a higher hazard.
   - **B.** The two regimens are equivalent — Wrong. The curves separate and the p value is small.
   - **C.** Death occurred less often with the new regimen, and the difference is statistically significant **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Death occurred more often with the new regimen — Wrong. Its curve is higher throughout.
   - **E.** The plot shows sensitivity against the false-positive rate — Wrong. That is a receiver operating characteristic curve.
   - **F.** No conclusion can be drawn without the prevalence — Wrong. Prevalence is irrelevant here.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Survival after randomization to two chemotherapy regimens is plotted — A Kaplan-Meier survival plot.
     - the log rank test gives a p value of 0.002 — The difference is significant.
     - two chemotherapy regimens — Two treatment arms compared.
   - **Reasoning:** A Kaplan-Meier curve plots survival probability against time; the flatter curve has the lower hazard, and the log rank test or Cox regression gives the p value for the difference.
   - **Teaching point:** The hazard ratio is derived from the relative slopes of the curves, and separation over time reflects its magnitude.
   - **Follow-up:** What do the curves and the test result indicate?
   - Page: 259

819. A systematic review pools the relative risks from 14 randomized trials of a lipid-lowering drug to produce a single summary estimate and also reports how much the effect sizes vary between trials.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Meta-analysis
   - **A.** A case-control study, limited by recall bias — Wrong. No cases and controls are selected.
   - **B.** Root cause analysis, limited by retrospective recall — Wrong. That analyzes medical errors.
   - **C.** A cohort study, limited by loss to follow-up — Wrong. No new cohort was followed.
   - **D.** An ecological study, limited by the ecological fallacy — Wrong. Populations are not being compared.
   - **E.** A crossover trial, limited by carryover between periods — Wrong. No sequence of treatments is described.
   - **F.** Meta-analysis, limited by the quality of the individual studies and bias in study selection **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - pools the relative risks from 14 randomized trials — Summary data combined.
     - produce a single summary estimate — A more precise estimate of effect size.
     - reports how much the effect sizes vary between trials — Heterogeneity estimated.
   - **Reasoning:** Meta-analysis pools summary data for a more precise effect estimate and improves power, strength of evidence and external validity, but it inherits the flaws of its component studies.
   - **Teaching point:** Pooling studies cannot fix bias in which studies were chosen for inclusion.
   - **Follow-up:** Which method is this, and what chiefly limits it?
   - Page: 267

820. An investigator wishes to compare the mean serum sodium among patients in four different treatment groups, all values being numerical.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Common statistical tests
   - **A.** ANOVA, because the means of three or more groups are compared **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** A log rank test, because groups are compared over time — Wrong. That compares survival curves.
   - **C.** Fisher exact test, because the sample may be small — Wrong. That compares proportions.
   - **D.** A t-test, because means are compared — Wrong. A t-test handles only two groups.
   - **E.** Pearson correlation, because two variables are related — Wrong. No two continuous variables are being correlated.
   - **F.** Chi-square, because several groups are involved — Wrong. That compares proportions.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - compare the mean serum sodium among patients in four different treatment groups — Means across four groups.
     - all values being numerical — Numerical outcome.
     - An investigator wishes to compare — A comparison of groups is planned.
   - **Reasoning:** Numerical means in two groups call for a t-test and in three or more for analysis of variance, while categorical proportions call for chi-square, or the Fisher exact test in small samples.
   - **Teaching point:** Comparing the proportion of hypertensive patients across three age groups would instead call for chi-square.
   - **Follow-up:** Which statistical test is appropriate, and why?

821. In a vaccine trial, 8% of placebo recipients and 2% of vaccine recipients developed influenza by the end of the season.
   - **Domain:** Biostatistics
   - **Topic:** Quantifying risk
   - **A.** Absolute risk reduction 0.08 and number needed to treat 12.5 — Wrong. That uses the placebo risk alone.
   - **B.** Absolute risk reduction 0.75 and number needed to treat 1.3 — Wrong. 0.75 is the relative risk reduction.
   - **C.** Absolute risk reduction 0.25 and number needed to treat 4 — Wrong. 0.25 is the relative risk.
   - **D.** Absolute risk reduction 4 and number needed to treat 0.25 — Wrong. These are not risks.
   - **E.** Absolute risk reduction 0.06 and number needed to treat about 17 **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Absolute risk reduction 0.02 and number needed to treat 50 — Wrong. That uses the vaccine risk alone.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 8% of placebo recipients — Risk without the intervention.
     - 2% of vaccine recipients developed influenza — Risk with the intervention.
     - In a vaccine trial — An intervention is being compared with placebo.
   - **Reasoning:** Absolute risk reduction is the difference in risk, 8% minus 2%, or 0.06, and the number needed to treat is its reciprocal, about 17.
   - **Teaching point:** The relative risk here is 0.25 and the relative risk reduction 0.75.
   - **Follow-up:** What are the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat?
   - Page: 258

822. In a cohort of chemical workers, bladder cancer developed in 21 per 1000 exposed workers and in 1 per 1000 unexposed workers over the same period.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Quantifying risk
   - **A.** Relative risk 22 and number needed to harm 45 — Wrong. Risks are not added.
   - **B.** Relative risk 0.05 and number needed to harm 1000 — Wrong. The ratio is inverted.
   - **C.** Relative risk 20 and number needed to harm 21 — Wrong. 20 per 1000 is the attributable risk.
   - **D.** Relative risk 21 and number needed to harm 50 **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Relative risk 21 and number needed to harm 1000 — Wrong. That ignores attributable risk.
   - **F.** Relative risk 21 and number needed to harm 21 — Wrong. The reciprocal of attributable risk is 50.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bladder cancer developed in 21 per 1000 exposed workers — Risk among the exposed.
     - 1 per 1000 unexposed workers — Risk among the unexposed.
     - In a cohort of chemical workers — Groups defined by exposure and followed forward.
   - **Reasoning:** Relative risk is 21 divided by 1, and the number needed to harm is the reciprocal of the attributable risk of 20 per 1000, which is 50.
   - **Teaching point:** In a case-control study the corresponding measure would be the odds ratio, which approximates relative risk only for rare disease.
   - **Follow-up:** What are the relative risk and the number needed to harm?
   - Page: 258

823. During an outbreak at a wedding, 60 of 80 guests who ate the shellfish became ill, and 6 of the 60 ill guests died.
   - **Domain:** Epidemiology
   - **Topic:** Quantifying risk
   - **A.** Attack rate 60%, case fatality rate 10% — Wrong. The attack rate uses the number exposed.
   - **B.** Attack rate 75%, case fatality rate 10% **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** Attack rate 6 per 1000 per year, case fatality rate 10% — Wrong. That is a mortality rate format.
   - **D.** Attack rate 80%, case fatality rate 6% — Wrong. Neither calculation is correct.
   - **E.** Attack rate 75%, case fatality rate 7.5% — Wrong. Deaths are divided by cases, not by those exposed.
   - **F.** Attack rate 10%, case fatality rate 75% — Wrong. The two are transposed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - 60 of 80 guests who ate the shellfish became ill — Ill divided by exposed.
     - 6 of the 60 ill guests died — Deaths divided by cases.
     - During an outbreak at a wedding — A point-source exposure.
   - **Reasoning:** Attack rate is those who became ill divided by those exposed, 60 of 80 or 75%, and case fatality rate is deaths divided by cases, 6 of 60 or 10%.
   - **Teaching point:** A mortality rate instead expresses deaths per 1000 people in a population per year.
   - **Follow-up:** What are the attack rate and the case fatality rate?
   - Page: 259

824. A 34-year-old woman with a stable, well-controlled psychotic illness refuses an elective hernia repair. She explains what the operation involves, why her surgeon recommends it, how she is weighing the risks against her own priorities, and states clearly that she declines.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Decision-making capacity
   - **A.** Obtain consent from her nearest relative, because of her psychiatric diagnosis — Wrong. Diagnosis alone does not remove capacity.
   - **B.** Invoke therapeutic privilege and withhold the risks — Wrong. Disclosure is not harming her.
   - **C.** Respect the refusal, because she demonstrates understanding, appreciation, reasoning and the ability to express a choice **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Seek a court ruling on competency before proceeding — Wrong. A judge decides competency, which is not in question here.
   - **E.** Proceed under implied consent, since surgery is beneficial — Wrong. This is not an emergency.
   - **F.** Treat her refusal as invalid until a psychiatrist agrees — Wrong. Capacity is determined by the treating physician for this decision.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - a stable, well-controlled psychotic illness refuses an elective hernia repair — Mental illness is not an exclusion criterion.
     - She explains what the operation involves, why her surgeon recommends it — Understanding and appreciation.
     - how she is weighing the risks against her own priorities, and states clearly that she declines — Reasoning and expressing a choice.
   - **Reasoning:** Capacity is decision-specific and is present when the patient shows understanding, appreciation, reasoning and expression of a choice, regardless of a psychiatric diagnosis.
   - **Teaching point:** Competency is a global legal determination made by a judge, not by the treating team.
   - **Follow-up:** How should the team proceed?
   - Page: 268

825. A man is brought in unconscious after a crash and needs immediate surgery to stop internal bleeding. No family can be reached and he has no advance directive on file.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Informed consent
   - **A.** Therapeutic privilege, since disclosure would harm him — Wrong. He cannot receive disclosure at all.
   - **B.** A waiver, since he has not objected — Wrong. A waiver requires an explicit act by the patient.
   - **C.** A court order obtained before incision — Wrong. Delay would be harmful and is not required.
   - **D.** Implied consent, because this is an emergency **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** No treatment until a relative is located — Wrong. Emergency care should not be withheld.
   - **F.** Surrogate consent from the hospital administrator — Wrong. An administrator is not a surrogate.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - brought in unconscious after a crash and needs immediate surgery — No capacity and no time.
     - No family can be reached — No surrogate is available.
     - he has no advance directive on file — No prior instructions exist.
   - **Reasoning:** In an emergency where the patient cannot consent and no surrogate is available, implied consent permits life-saving treatment.
   - **Teaching point:** Outside an emergency, consent for an incapacitated patient comes from a legal surrogate.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the correct basis for proceeding?
   - Page: 269

826. A 16-year-old asks to be treated for a sexually transmitted infection and for contraception, and asks that her parents not be told. She lives at home and is not married.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Consent for minors
   - **A.** Treat the infection but refuse contraception without consent — Wrong. Both fall under the same exception.
   - **B.** Treat only if she is declared emancipated — Wrong. Emancipation is a separate exception.
   - **C.** Notify her parents first and then treat — Wrong. That disregards the exception.
   - **D.** Refer her to a court for an emancipation ruling — Wrong. Not required for these services.
   - **E.** Provide the care, since parental consent is usually not required for sexually transmitted infections or contraception, while encouraging her to talk with her guardian **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Refuse until a parent consents, since she is a minor — Wrong. These services are an exception in general.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - A 16-year-old asks to be treated for a sexually transmitted infection and for contraception — Services within the usual exception.
     - asks that her parents not be told — Confidentiality concern.
     - She lives at home and is not married — She is not emancipated.
   - **Reasoning:** Parental consent is usually not required for contraception, sexually transmitted infections and prenatal care, for substance use disorder treatment, or for emergency care, and healthy minor-guardian communication should still be encouraged.
   - **Teaching point:** Abortion is the usual exception within this group, since many states require parental notification or consent.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the correct approach?
   - **Exhibit:**

     ```json
       ],

         ],
     ```

     The four parts of Medicare
   - Page: 269

827. A 70-year-old man is admitted for pneumonia, sees his physician in the clinic two weeks later, and fills a prescription for an inhaler. He asks which parts of his coverage apply to each of the three.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Medicare and Medicaid
   - **A.** Part B, Part A and Part D — Wrong. The first two are transposed.
   - **B.** Part D, Part B and Part A — Wrong. The order is reversed.
   - **C.** Part A, Part D and Part B — Wrong. The last two are transposed.
   - **D.** Medicaid covers all three — Wrong. Medicaid serves people with limited income or resources.
   - **E.** Part C, Part C and Part D — Wrong. Part C is an optional private combination of A and B.
   - **F.** Part A, Part B and Part D **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - A 70-year-old man is admitted for pneumonia — A hospital admission.
     - sees his physician in the clinic two weeks later — An outpatient physician fee.
     - fills a prescription for an inhaler — A prescription drug.
   - **Reasoning:** Part A covers hospital admissions including hospice and skilled nursing, Part B covers basic medical bills, Part C delivers A and B through private companies, and Part D covers prescription drugs.
   - **Teaching point:** Medicare is for the elderly and the disabled, while Medicaid is joint federal and state assistance for the disadvantaged.
   - **Follow-up:** Which parts cover the admission, the clinic visit and the inhaler, in that order?
   - Page: 277

828. A healthy 44-year-old man has no symptoms. His physician counsels him on diet and exercise, orders a fasting glucose, and reviews his hemoglobin A1c target because he was found last year to have diabetes.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Disease prevention
   - **A.** All three are tertiary prevention — Wrong. They target different stages.
   - **B.** Primary, secondary and tertiary **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** Quaternary, primary and secondary — Wrong. No intervention is being withdrawn.
   - **D.** Tertiary, secondary and primary — Wrong. The order is reversed.
   - **E.** Primary, tertiary and quaternary — Wrong. Screening is secondary prevention.
   - **F.** Secondary, primary and tertiary — Wrong. The first two are transposed.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - counsels him on diet and exercise — Reducing risk before disease begins.
     - orders a fasting glucose — Screening for presymptomatic disease.
     - reviews his hemoglobin A1c target — Guiding treatment to prevent complications.
   - **Reasoning:** Primary prevention stops disease onset, secondary screens for presymptomatic disease, tertiary limits progression in symptomatic disease, and quaternary avoids overtreatment.
   - **Teaching point:** Stopping a sulfonylurea after repeated hypoglycemia would be quaternary prevention.
   - **Follow-up:** Which levels of prevention do the diet counseling, the fasting glucose and the A1c target represent, in that order?
   - Page: 276

829. An 81-year-old woman on a sulfonylurea has had four episodes of hypoglycemia requiring help in two months. Her physician stops the drug and sets a less strict glucose target.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Disease prevention
   - **A.** Quaternary prevention **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** Hospice care — Wrong. No prognosis of 6 months or less is described.
   - **C.** Secondary prevention — Wrong. No screening for presymptomatic disease is involved.
   - **D.** Palliative care — Wrong. The aim is not comfort in life-threatening illness.
   - **E.** Tertiary prevention — Wrong. The aim is not to limit disease progression.
   - **F.** Primary prevention — Wrong. She already has the disease.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - has had four episodes of hypoglycemia requiring help in two months — Harm from treatment.
     - Her physician stops the drug — An unnecessary or harmful intervention is withdrawn.
     - sets a less strict glucose target — Reducing overmedicalization.
   - **Reasoning:** Quaternary prevention aims to prevent overtreatment and iatrogenic harm by quitting unnecessary medical interventions in overmedicalized patients.
   - **Teaching point:** Monitoring hemoglobin A1c to prevent complications in the same patient would be tertiary prevention.
   - **Follow-up:** Which level of prevention does this represent?
   - Page: 276

830. A nurse sustains a needlestick from a patient known to have untreated HIV infection. She presents 6 hours after the injury.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Chemoprophylaxis
   - **A.** Observe and repeat testing at one year only — Wrong. Prophylaxis and earlier testing are indicated.
   - **B.** Test now and start treatment only if the baseline test is positive — Wrong. Prophylaxis should not be delayed.
   - **C.** Start tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, emtricitabine and an integrase inhibitor for 28 days, with HIV testing at baseline and at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Start doxycycline within 72 hours — Wrong. That prevents bacterial sexually transmitted infections.
   - **E.** Give HIV immune globulin alone — Wrong. No such prophylaxis is used.
   - **F.** Give a single dose of a protease inhibitor — Wrong. A 28-day combination regimen is used.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - A nurse sustains a needlestick from a patient known to have untreated HIV infection — Occupational exposure.
     - She presents 6 hours after the injury — Within the 72-hour window.
     - a patient known to have untreated HIV infection — A high-risk source.
   - **Reasoning:** Postexposure prophylaxis for HIV is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate with emtricitabine plus raltegravir or dolutegravir for 28 days, started within 72 hours, with serial testing.
   - **Teaching point:** A household contact of meningococcal disease would instead receive rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the correct management?
   - Page: 276

831. A college student shared a dormitory room with a classmate who has just been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Chemoprophylaxis
   - **A.** Doxycycline within 72 hours — Wrong. That targets bacterial sexually transmitted infections.
   - **B.** No prophylaxis, since he has no symptoms — Wrong. Close contacts require prophylaxis.
   - **C.** Immune globulin and a vaccine on a 0, 3, 7 and 14 day schedule — Wrong. That is rabies prophylaxis.
   - **D.** Rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Atovaquone-proguanil before and after travel — Wrong. That is malaria prophylaxis.
   - **F.** Tenofovir, emtricitabine and dolutegravir for 28 days — Wrong. That is HIV prophylaxis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - shared a dormitory room with a classmate — Close contact.
     - just been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis — The index case.
     - A college student — A household-equivalent exposure.
   - **Reasoning:** Household or close contacts of Neisseria meningitidis receive rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone.
   - **Teaching point:** An unimmunized person bitten by a rabid animal needs wound cleaning, vaccine and rabies immune globulin on a 0, 3, 7 and 14 day schedule.
   - **Follow-up:** What should the student receive?

   - Page: 276

832. A pharmacist notices that a newly ordered antibiotic would interact dangerously with a patient's existing medication and cancels the order before any dose is given.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Medical errors
   - **A.** An active error, with immediate impact on the patient — Wrong. No dose reached the patient.
   - **B.** Not an error at all, so no analysis is warranted — Wrong. Near misses are instructive.
   - **C.** A sentinel event, since permanent harm was possible — Wrong. No harm occurred.
   - **D.** A never event, which should never occur — Wrong. No serious adverse event took place.
   - **E.** A near miss, which exposes dangers through the narrow prevention of harm **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** A latent error, waiting to cause harm — Wrong. The problem was an individual order, not a system design.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - A pharmacist notices that a newly ordered antibiotic would interact dangerously — The hazard was recognized.
     - cancels the order before any dose is given — No harm reached the patient.
     - a patient's existing medication — The interaction had real potential for harm.
   - **Reasoning:** A near miss is an unplanned event that does not cause harm but had the potential to do so, and it exposes dangers that should be addressed.
   - **Teaching point:** Had the dose been given and caused permanent harm, the event would be a sentinel event.
   - **Follow-up:** How is this event classified, and what does it reveal?
   - Page: 278

833. After a patient receives a tenfold overdose from an infusion pump, the hospital convenes a team that reviews records, interviews staff, and builds a cause-and-effect diagram to identify every process, equipment and staffing problem that contributed.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Medical error analysis
   - **A.** Failure mode and effects analysis, a forward-looking approach — Wrong. That is applied before implementation.
   - **B.** Root cause analysis, a retrospective approach applied after a failure to prevent recurrence **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** A randomized trial of pump models — Wrong. No allocation is described.
   - **D.** A sentinel event report, which requires no analysis — Wrong. Analysis is precisely what is described.
   - **E.** A near-miss review, since no harm occurred — Wrong. Harm did occur.
   - **F.** A meta-analysis of prior incidents — Wrong. No summary data from studies are pooled.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - After a patient receives a tenfold overdose from an infusion pump — The failure has already happened.
     - reviews records, interviews staff, and builds a cause-and-effect diagram — Characteristic methods.
     - identify every process, equipment and staffing problem that contributed — Multiple underlying domains.
   - **Reasoning:** Root cause analysis is retrospective, using records, interviews, the 5 whys, fishbone diagrams and process maps to find all the problems behind an error.
   - **Teaching point:** Mapping how a new process might fail, and ranking those failures by probability and impact before launch, is failure mode and effects analysis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which analysis is this, and what is its orientation?
   - Page: 278

834. Before introducing a new electronic prescribing system, a committee lists every way the ordering process might go wrong and ranks each possibility by how likely it is and how badly it would affect patients.
   - **Domain:** Healthcare delivery
   - **Topic:** Medical error analysis
   - **A.** Root cause analysis — Wrong. That follows a failure that has already occurred.
   - **B.** A randomized controlled trial — Wrong. No allocation is described.
   - **C.** Failure mode and effects analysis **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** A sentinel event investigation — Wrong. No harm has occurred.
   - **E.** A cross-sectional survey — Wrong. No prevalence is measured.
   - **F.** A near-miss review — Wrong. No event has occurred.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Before introducing a new electronic prescribing system — Applied in advance.
     - lists every way the ordering process might go wrong — Inductive identification of failure modes.
     - ranks each possibility by how likely it is and how badly it would affect patients — Prioritization by probability and impact.
   - **Reasoning:** Failure mode and effects analysis is forward-looking, using inductive reasoning to find possible failures before implementation and prioritizing them by probability and patient impact.
   - **Teaching point:** Reviewing an overdose that has already happened would call for root cause analysis instead.
   - **Follow-up:** Which method is being used?
   - Page: 278

835. A surgical team realizes that an invasive biopsy intended for another patient was performed on a man who did not need it. The pathology is benign and he appears unharmed.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Medical errors
   - **A.** Inform his family rather than the patient — Wrong. The patient holds the right to the information.
   - **B.** Report it to the institution alone — Wrong. The patient must also be told.
   - **C.** Document the error internally without telling him, since he was not harmed — Wrong. Disclosure does not depend on harm.
   - **D.** Disclose only if he asks about the procedure — Wrong. Disclosure is not conditional on a question.
   - **E.** Wait for the root cause analysis before disclosing — Wrong. Disclosure should not be delayed.
   - **F.** Inform the patient that a mistake has been made, regardless of the outcome **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - an invasive biopsy intended for another patient was performed on a man who did not need it — Patient identification error.
     - The pathology is benign and he appears unharmed — No apparent harm resulted.
     - A surgical team realizes — The error is known to the team.
   - **Reasoning:** Medical errors should be disclosed to patients independent of the immediate outcome, whether harmful or not.
   - **Teaching point:** Analyzing how the identification failure happened is a separate obligation, met by root cause analysis.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the physician obligated to do?
   - Page: 275

836. A mother and her 15-year-old daughter are brought in after a crash, both unresponsive and bleeding heavily. The father states that the family are Jehovah's Witnesses and refuses transfusion for both.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Challenging scenarios
   - **A.** Transfuse the daughter but not the mother **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** Transfuse neither, respecting the family's beliefs — Wrong. A minor's emergency care cannot be refused on faith alone.
   - **C.** Transfuse both, since the situation is emergent — Wrong. An adult's known preferences can be honored through a proxy.
   - **D.** Transfuse only if the father changes his mind — Wrong. The minor should be transfused regardless.
   - **E.** Transfuse the mother but not the daughter — Wrong. The reasoning is reversed.
   - **F.** Delay both transfusions until a court order is obtained — Wrong. Delay would be harmful for the minor.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - A mother and her 15-year-old daughter are brought in after a crash — One adult and one minor.
     - both unresponsive and bleeding heavily — An emergency with no capacity.
     - The father states that the family are Jehovah's Witnesses and refuses transfusion for both — A proxy refusal on faith.
   - **Reasoning:** Emergent care can be refused by the healthcare proxy for an adult, particularly where preferences are known or reasonably inferred, but not for a minor based solely on faith.
   - **Teaching point:** A legally emancipated minor would be treated as an adult for consent purposes.
   - **Follow-up:** How should the team proceed?
   - Page: 275

837. A man with advanced dementia loses the ability to make decisions and left no advance directive. His wife, his adult son and his brother each give a different account of what he would have wanted.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Surrogate decision-maker
   - **A.** His adult son, since children know the patient best — Wrong. Children follow the spouse in priority.
   - **B.** His wife, since a spouse has priority among surrogates, deciding what the patient would have done **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **C.** A judge, in all such cases — Wrong. Judicial involvement is not routinely required.
   - **D.** The treating physician, since no directive exists — Wrong. A surrogate hierarchy applies.
   - **E.** His brother, since siblings are neutral — Wrong. Siblings come after parents.
   - **F.** Whichever relative is available first — Wrong. There is a defined order.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - loses the ability to make decisions and left no advance directive — Surrogate decision-making applies.
     - His wife, his adult son and his brother each give a different account — The surrogates disagree.
     - A man with advanced dementia — Capacity is absent and will not return.
   - **Reasoning:** The priority of surrogates is spouse, then adult children, then parents, then adult siblings, then other relatives, and the surrogate must decide what the patient would have done.
   - **Teaching point:** Had he named an agent through a medical power of attorney, that agent would take precedence.
   - **Follow-up:** Who should make the decision, and on what basis?
   - Page: 270

838. A woman tells you she is being hurt at home by her partner. She has bruises in several stages of healing and asks you not to call the police. Her state does not require reporting of intimate partner violence in competent adults.
   - **Domain:** Ethics
   - **Topic:** Challenging scenarios
   - **A.** Discharge her with a referral and no further discussion — Wrong. Safety assessment is needed.
   - **B.** Insist that she leave her partner before she goes home — Wrong. Pressure is not appropriate.
   - **C.** Tell her partner that you know, so he can be counseled — Wrong. That would endanger her.
   - **D.** Report to the police immediately despite her wishes — Wrong. State law does not require it here.
   - **E.** Ask whether she is safe, help devise an emergency plan, ask direct open-ended questions about the findings, summarize her answers back to her, and respect her decision about reporting **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **F.** Avoid asking about the bruises to spare her distress — Wrong. Direct questions about findings are appropriate.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - She has bruises in several stages of healing — Repeated injury over time.
     - asks you not to call the police — Her stated preference about reporting.
     - Her state does not require reporting of intimate partner violence in competent adults — No legal reporting duty applies.
   - **Reasoning:** Ask about safety, help build an emergency plan, use direct open-ended questions and summarize the answers, without pressuring the patient to leave or to disclose unless state law requires it.
   - **Teaching point:** Reasonable suspicion of abuse of a child or a dependent adult must be reported by law.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most appropriate response?
   - Page: 275

839. A patient with limited English is seen for abdominal pain. Her adult son offers to interpret, and a trained medical interpreter is available by video within a few minutes. The situation is not an emergency.
   - **Domain:** Communication
   - **Topic:** Use of interpreters
   - **A.** Ask the patient to write her symptoms down instead — Wrong. That does not address the language barrier.
   - **B.** Postpone the visit until an in-person interpreter is available — Wrong. Telephone or video interpretation is acceptable.
   - **C.** Use the trained medical interpreter, speak directly to the patient with eye contact, allow extra time and ask one question at a time **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **D.** Proceed in English and use gestures — Wrong. That is only acceptable in an emergency.
   - **E.** Use the son, since he knows her history — Wrong. A trained interpreter is preferred outside emergencies.
   - **F.** Speak to the interpreter in the third person for clarity — Wrong. Address the patient directly.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - A patient with limited English is seen for abdominal pain — Language assistance is needed.
     - a trained medical interpreter is available by video within a few minutes — A professional option exists.
     - The situation is not an emergency — Standard procedure applies.
   - **Reasoning:** A professionally trained medical interpreter should be used unless the physician is conversationally fluent, with direct speech and eye contact, extra time and one question at a time.
   - **Teaching point:** If the patient prefers a family member, that preference should be recorded in the chart.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the best approach?
   - Page: 273

840. You must tell a patient that her biopsy shows a metastatic cancer. You arrange a private room, offer in advance for her to bring someone, and sit down with her.
   - **Domain:** Communication
   - **Topic:** Delivering bad news
   - **A.** Determine her understanding and expectations, then obtain her permission to disclose the news and how much detail she wants **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** Ask her family to deliver the news instead — Wrong. That is not appropriate.
   - **C.** Acknowledge her emotions before any information is exchanged — Wrong. Emotions are addressed as the news is received.
   - **D.** Discuss treatment options and the next appointment — Wrong. That is the final step.
   - **E.** Share the full pathology report in detail — Wrong. That comes after permission and in small pieces.
   - **F.** Withhold the result under therapeutic privilege — Wrong. Nothing suggests severe harm from disclosure.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - You arrange a private room — Setting.
     - offer in advance for her to bring someone — Support is arranged.
     - sit down with her — The setting step is complete.
   - **Reasoning:** In the SPIKES approach, setting is followed by perception and invitation, then knowledge in small pieces without jargon, then emotions, then strategy.
   - **Teaching point:** Giving control to the patient in the final step, by asking how she would like to proceed, may be empowering.
   - **Follow-up:** What should you do next, before giving the result?
   - Page: 273

## Renal 1

Source: `mock-renal-1.json`

841. A 36-week fetus has bilateral hydronephrosis, a distended thick-walled bladder and severe oligohydramnios on ultrasound. The fetus is male. After birth, he has a weak urinary stream, flattened facial features and respiratory distress.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Posterior urethral valves
   - **A.** Prune belly syndrome — Wrong. Not listed.
   - **B.** Bilateral renal agenesis — Wrong. No kidneys or bladder distension.
   - **C.** Posterior urethral valves **(Correct)** — Correct. Most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants.
   - **D.** Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease — Wrong. Enlarged echogenic kidneys, no bladder distension.
   - **E.** Bilateral ureteropelvic junction obstruction — Wrong. Bladder would be normal.
   - **F.** Vesicoureteral reflux alone — Wrong. Not the cause of oligohydramnios here.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - bilateral hydronephrosis — Obstruction below both ureters.
     - distended thick-walled bladder — Bladder outlet obstruction.
     - severe oligohydramnios — Low fetal urine output reaching amniotic fluid.
     - The fetus is male — Prostatic urethra.
   - **Reasoning:** Male fetus + bilateral hydronephrosis + thick bladder + oligohydramnios → posterior urethral valves → Potter features.
   - **Teaching point:** Pulmonary hypoplasia is the main cause of death in Potter sequence.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the most likely cause?
   - Page: 597

842. A 15-year-old girl with short stature and a webbed neck has recurrent urinary tract infections. CT shows both kidneys joined at their lower poles, lying lower than normal in front of the aorta.
   - **Domain:** Embryology
   - **Topic:** Horseshoe kidney
   - **A.** Celiac trunk — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Inferior mesenteric artery **(Correct)** — Correct. Horseshoe kidney.
   - **C.** Superior mesenteric artery — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Gonadal artery — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Common iliac artery — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Renal artery — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - short stature and a webbed neck — Turner syndrome.
     - joined at their lower poles — Fused inferior poles.
     - lying lower than normal — Arrested ascent.
   - **Reasoning:** Turner syndrome + fused inferior poles + low kidneys → horseshoe kidney trapped by IMA.
   - **Teaching point:** Associated with UPJ obstruction, stones, infection and renal cancer.
   - **Follow-up:** Which vessel prevented the kidneys from ascending?
   - Page: 597

843. A 30-year-old woman has a hysterectomy for fibroids. Two days later she has flank pain and fever. CT shows hydronephrosis on the left with a dilated ureter down to the level of the uterine artery ligation.
   - **Domain:** Anatomy
   - **Topic:** Course of ureters
   - **A.** It runs with the round ligament — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** It passes over the common iliac artery — Wrong. True but not the injury site here.
   - **C.** It passes over the uterine artery — Wrong. It passes under.
   - **D.** It lies inside the bladder wall — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** It passes through the broad ligament above the ovary — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** It passes under the uterine artery near the cervix **(Correct)** — Correct. "Water under the bridge."
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - has a hysterectomy — Pelvic surgery.
     - hydronephrosis on the left — Ureteral obstruction.
     - down to the level of the uterine artery ligation — Ligated with the artery.
   - **Reasoning:** Hysterectomy + hydronephrosis to uterine artery level → ureter ligated where it passes under the uterine artery.
   - **Teaching point:** In men, the ureter passes under the vas deferens.
   - **Follow-up:** Why was this structure injured?

844. A healthy volunteer has a renal clearance study. The results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Filtration
   - **A.** 16% — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** 50% — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** 30% — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** 25% — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** 20% **(Correct)** — Correct. GFR = (40 × 1.2)/0.4 = 120; RPF = (300 × 1.2)/0.6 = 600; FF = 120/600.
   - **F.** 10% — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - healthy volunteer — Normal values expected.
     - renal clearance study — Inulin and PAH clearance.
     - The results are shown — Data in the table.
   - **Reasoning:** Inulin clearance = GFR (120 mL/min); PAH clearance = eRPF (600 mL/min) → FF = 20%.
   - **Teaching point:** RBF = RPF/(1 − Hct) = 1000 mL/min.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the filtration fraction?
   - Page: 601

845. A 78-year-old woman with heart failure takes lisinopril and furosemide. She starts taking naproxen for knee pain. A week later her creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Filtration
   - **A.** Ureteral obstruction — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Afferent and efferent dilation — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** No arteriolar change; tubular toxicity only — Wrong. Not the main mechanism.
   - **D.** Afferent constriction (NSAID) and efferent dilation (ACE inhibitor) **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **E.** Efferent constriction alone — Wrong. Would raise GFR.
   - **F.** Afferent dilation and efferent constriction — Wrong. Would raise GFR.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - takes lisinopril and furosemide — ACE inhibitor + diuretic.
     - starts taking naproxen — Prostaglandin inhibition.
     - creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL — AKI.
   - **Reasoning:** NSAID blocks prostaglandin afferent dilation + ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction + diuretic volume loss → falling glomerular pressure → AKI ("triple whammy").
   - **Teaching point:** Prostaglandins dilate afferent (PDA); angiotensin II constricts efferent (ACE).
   - **Follow-up:** What happened to her glomerular arterioles?

846. A medical student studies the curves shown, which describe glucose handling in a healthy adult. Glucose first appears in the urine at about 200 mg/dL, yet the reabsorption curve does not reach its plateau until about 375 mg/min.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Glucose clearance
   - **A.** Nephrons have different transport maxima (splay) **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** Glucose is filtered less at high concentrations — Wrong. Filtered linearly.
   - **C.** SGLT2 is inhibited by glucose — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** GFR falls as glucose rises — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Insulin increases tubular reabsorption — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Glucose is secreted at high levels — Wrong. Not secreted.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - first appears in the urine at about 200 mg/dL — Renal threshold.
     - does not reach its plateau until about 375 mg/min — Tm.
     - glucose handling in a healthy adult — Normal physiology.
   - **Reasoning:** Threshold (~200 mg/dL) to Tm (~375 mg/min) region = splay from nephron heterogeneity.
   - **Teaching point:** Pregnancy and SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria below the normal threshold.
   - **Follow-up:** What explains the gradual rather than sharp transition?
   - Page: 602

847. A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes starts a new oral drug. His HbA1c falls, he loses 2 kg and his urine dipstick is strongly positive for glucose even when his blood glucose is 130 mg/dL. He also develops balanitis.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Glucose clearance
   - **A.** Pancreatic β cells — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Small intestine — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Distal convoluted tubule — Wrong. Thiazides.
   - **D.** Thick ascending limb — Wrong. Loop diuretics.
   - **E.** Proximal convoluted tubule **(Correct)** — Correct. SGLT2 inhibitor.
   - **F.** Collecting duct — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - urine dipstick is strongly positive for glucose — Glucosuria.
     - blood glucose is 130 mg/dL — Below normal threshold.
     - balanitis — Genital infection from glucosuria.
   - **Reasoning:** Glucosuria at normal glucose + weight loss + genital infection → SGLT2 inhibitor → PCT.
   - **Teaching point:** SGLT2 reabsorbs most filtered glucose in the early PCT.
   - **Follow-up:** Where does the drug act?

848. A physiologist measures three substances along the proximal tubule. The results are shown. Substance X is freely filtered and its total amount in the tubule does not change.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Relative concentrations along proximal tubule
   - **A.** X = inulin, Y = sodium, Z = glucose **(Correct)** — Correct.
   - **B.** X = bicarbonate, Y = urea, Z = PAH — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** X = PAH, Y = glucose, Z = sodium — Wrong. Glucose falls.
   - **D.** X = sodium, Y = glucose, Z = inulin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** X = glucose, Y = inulin, Z = sodium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** X = glucose, Y = sodium, Z = inulin — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - freely filtered and its total amount in the tubule does not change — Neither reabsorbed nor secreted.
     - three substances along the proximal tubule — TF/P analysis.
     - A physiologist measures — Experimental measurement.
   - **Reasoning:** Concentration rises as water leaves (inulin); stays at 1 with isotonic reabsorption (Na+); falls toward 0 when reabsorbed faster than water (glucose).
   - **Teaching point:** PAH rises even more than inulin because it is secreted.
   - **Follow-up:** Which substances are X, Y and Z?

849. Two young adults are evaluated for weakness and muscle cramps. Neither uses diuretics or laxatives. Their findings are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Renal tubular defects
   - **A.** Generalized proximal tubule transport — Wrong. Fanconi; acidosis.
   - **B.** 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase — Wrong. AME; hypertension.
   - **C.** Na+/Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule **(Correct)** — Correct. Gitelman syndrome.
   - **D.** Epithelial Na+ channel in the collecting tubule — Wrong. Liddle; hypertension.
   - **E.** Carbonic anhydrase — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb — Wrong. Patient 1 (Bartter).
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Neither uses diuretics or laxatives — Excludes acquired causes.
     - weakness and muscle cramps — Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia.
     - Two young adults — Inherited disorders.
   - **Reasoning:** Normotensive hypokalemic alkalosis + low Mg2+ + low urine Ca2+ → Gitelman (thiazide-like DCT defect); high urine Ca2+ → Bartter (loop-like).
   - **Teaching point:** Gitelman is milder than Bartter.
   - **Follow-up:** Which transporter is defective in patient 2?
   - Page: 604

850. A 19-year-old man has a BP of 172/104 mm Hg. Serum K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and HCO3− is 31 mEq/L. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both very low. His mother and brother also have hypertension starting in adolescence. He does not eat licorice.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Renal tubular defects
   - **A.** Furosemide — Wrong. Worsens hypokalemia.
   - **B.** Lisinopril — Wrong. RAAS already suppressed.
   - **C.** Spironolactone — Wrong. Aldosterone is not elevated.
   - **D.** Dexamethasone — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Hydrochlorothiazide — Wrong. Worsens hypokalemia.
   - **F.** Amiloride **(Correct)** — Correct. Liddle syndrome: overactive ENaC.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - BP of 172/104 mm Hg — Hypertension.
     - Serum K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and HCO3− is 31 mEq/L — Hypokalemic alkalosis.
     - renin and aldosterone are both very low — Mineralocorticoid-like state without aldosterone.
     - His mother and brother — Autosomal dominant.
     - He does not eat licorice — Excludes acquired AME.
   - **Reasoning:** Young hypertensive + hypokalemic alkalosis + low renin/aldosterone + AD inheritance → Liddle syndrome → amiloride.
   - **Teaching point:** AME also has low renin and aldosterone but is recessive or from licorice.
   - **Follow-up:** Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
   - Page: 604

851. A 70-year-old woman with heart failure takes high doses of furosemide. Her ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. She reports leg cramps.
   - **Domain:** Pharmacology
   - **Topic:** Loop diuretics
   - **A.** Hyperuricemia only — Wrong. Not the best answer.
   - **B.** Hypomagnesemia **(Correct)** — Correct. Loop diuretics waste Mg2+ and K+.
   - **C.** Hyperkalemia — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Metabolic acidosis — Wrong. Loop diuretics cause alkalosis.
   - **E.** Hypercalcemia — Wrong. Loop diuretics lower calcium.
   - **F.** Hypermagnesemia — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - high doses of furosemide — Loop diuretic.
     - flattened T waves and prominent U waves — Hypokalemia.
     - leg cramps — Electrolyte loss.
   - **Reasoning:** Loop diuretic → loss of K+ and Mg2+ (OHH DAANG) → hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.
   - **Teaching point:** Correct magnesium first, or potassium will not stay up.
   - **Follow-up:** Which other finding is most likely?
   - **Exhibit:**

852. A 17-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep, rapid breathing after missing insulin doses. Her results are shown.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Acid-base physiology
   - **A.** Normal anion gap acidosis with respiratory acidosis — Wrong. Gap is high.
   - **B.** Mixed metabolic alkalosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** Metabolic acidosis with concomitant respiratory acidosis — Wrong. PCO2 within predicted.
   - **D.** Elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation **(Correct)** — Correct. Gap = 28; Winters: 1.5(8) + 8 = 20 ± 2.
   - **E.** Normal anion gap acidosis from diarrhea — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation — Wrong. pH low.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - type 1 diabetes — DKA risk.
     - deep, rapid breathing — Kussmaul respiration.
     - missing insulin doses — Precipitant.
   - **Reasoning:** DKA → anion gap 134 − (98 + 8) = 28 → AG metabolic acidosis; Winters predicts PCO2 18–22 → appropriately compensated.
   - **Teaching point:** Ketones are the K in GOLDMARK.
   - **Follow-up:** Which statement best describes her acid-base status?
   - Page: 610

853. A 45-year-old man is found confused after a party. He has an elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, an elevated osmolal gap and envelope-shaped crystals in his urine. Creatinine is rising.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Acidosis and alkalosis
   - **A.** Isopropyl alcohol — Wrong. No acidosis.
   - **B.** Ethylene glycol **(Correct)** — Correct. Calcium oxalate crystals.
   - **C.** Lithium — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **D.** Methanol — Wrong. Visual loss, no oxalate crystals.
   - **E.** Salicylates — Wrong. Not oxalate crystals.
   - **F.** Acetaminophen — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis — GOLDMARK.
     - elevated osmolal gap — Toxic alcohol.
     - envelope-shaped crystals — Calcium oxalate.
   - **Reasoning:** AG acidosis + osmolal gap + oxalate crystals + AKI → ethylene glycol (antifreeze).
   - **Teaching point:** Treat with fomepizole.
   - **Follow-up:** What did he ingest?
   - Page: 610

854. A 24-year-old woman has had severe watery diarrhea for 5 days from a cholera-like illness. Arterial pH is 7.30, HCO3− is 15 mEq/L, Na+ is 138 mEq/L and Cl− is 113 mEq/L.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Acidosis and alkalosis
   - **A.** 25 mEq/L; elevated anion gap acidosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** 40 mEq/L; elevated anion gap acidosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **C.** 10 mEq/L; metabolic alkalosis — Wrong. pH is low.
   - **D.** 18 mEq/L; mixed disorder — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** 0 mEq/L; respiratory acidosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **F.** 10 mEq/L; normal anion gap metabolic acidosis **(Correct)** — Correct. 138 − (113 + 15).
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - severe watery diarrhea — HCO3− loss.
     - Cl− is 113 mEq/L — Hyperchloremia.
     - HCO3− is 15 mEq/L — Metabolic acidosis.
   - **Reasoning:** Diarrhea → HCO3− loss with Cl− retention → normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis (SHARDS).
   - **Teaching point:** Normal anion gap is about 8–12 mEq/L.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the anion gap and its category?
   - Page: 610

855. A 27-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome has recurrent kidney stones. She has a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia and a urine pH of 6.5. The stones are radiopaque and composed of calcium phosphate.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Renal tubular acidosis
   - **A.** Defective HCO3− reabsorption in the PCT — Wrong. Type 2; urine pH can drop below 5.5.
   - **B.** Urease-producing bacteria — Wrong. Struvite.
   - **C.** Hypoaldosteronism with low NH3 synthesis — Wrong. Type 4; hyperkalemia.
   - **D.** α-Intercalated cells cannot secrete H+ **(Correct)** — Correct. Distal (type 1) RTA.
   - **E.** Defective NaCl transport in the DCT — Wrong. Gitelman.
   - **F.** Overactive ENaC — Wrong. Liddle.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - Sjögren syndrome — Autoimmune cause of type 1 RTA.
     - non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia — RTA type 1 or 2.
     - urine pH of 6.5 — Cannot acidify urine.
     - calcium phosphate — Stones form in alkaline urine.
   - **Reasoning:** Autoimmune disease + NAGMA + hypokalemia + urine pH > 5.5 + CaP stones → distal RTA.
   - **Teaching point:** Amphotericin B also causes type 1 RTA.
   - **Follow-up:** Which defect is present?
   - Page: 611

856. A 62-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and CKD has a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Serum K+ is 6.1 mEq/L. Renin and aldosterone are low. He takes lisinopril.
   - **Domain:** Physiology
   - **Topic:** Renal tubular acidosis
   - **A.** Contraction alkalosis — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **B.** Uremic acidosis with high anion gap — Wrong. Gap normal.
   - **C.** Type 2 (proximal) — Wrong. Hypokalemia.
   - **D.** Fanconi syndrome — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **E.** Type 4 (hyperkalemic) **(Correct)** — Correct. Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism worsened by ACE inhibitor.
   - **F.** Type 1 (distal) — Wrong. Hypokalemia.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - long-standing type 2 diabetes — Hyporeninism.
     - Serum K+ is 6.1 mEq/L — Hyperkalemia.
     - Renin and aldosterone are low — Hypoaldosteronism.
     - He takes lisinopril — Worsens hypoaldosteronism.
   - **Reasoning:** Diabetes + NAGMA + hyperkalemia + low aldosterone → type 4 RTA (↓ NH3 synthesis).
   - **Teaching point:** Hyperkalemia itself suppresses ammoniagenesis.
   - **Follow-up:** Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present?
   - Page: 611

857. An 8-year-old boy has smoky brown urine and puffy eyes. Three weeks ago he had impetigo on his legs. His BP is 142/92 mm Hg. Urine shows RBC casts and mild proteinuria. Serum C3 is low.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Nephritic syndrome
   - **A.** Linear deposits along the GBM — Wrong. Goodpasture.
   - **B.** Mesangial IgA deposits — Wrong. IgA nephropathy.
   - **C.** Subepithelial immune complex humps **(Correct)** — Correct. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
   - **D.** Basket-weave GBM splitting — Wrong. Alport.
   - **E.** Effacement of foot processes only — Wrong. Minimal change.
   - **F.** Spike-and-dome subepithelial deposits — Wrong. Membranous.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - smoky brown urine and puffy eyes — Nephritic syndrome.
     - Three weeks ago he had impetigo — Latent period after streptococcal skin infection.
     - RBC casts — Glomerular bleeding.
     - Serum C3 is low — Complement consumption.
   - **Reasoning:** Strep infection 2–4 weeks earlier + nephritic syndrome + low C3 → PSGN → subepithelial humps.
   - **Teaching point:** IgA nephropathy occurs during the infection, with normal complement.
   - **Follow-up:** What would electron microscopy of a kidney biopsy show?
   - Page: 614

858. A 23-year-old man coughs up blood and has rapidly rising creatinine over 2 weeks. Urine has RBC casts. Kidney biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli with smooth linear IgG along the basement membrane.
   - **Domain:** Immunology
   - **Topic:** Nephritic syndrome
   - **A.** Autoantibodies against type IV collagen in basement membranes (type II hypersensitivity) **(Correct)** — Correct. Goodpasture syndrome.
   - **B.** Type IV collagen gene mutation — Wrong. Alport.
   - **C.** ANCA-mediated vasculitis — Wrong. Pauci-immune, no deposits.
   - **D.** Immune complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) — Wrong. Granular pattern.
   - **E.** IgA immune complexes — Wrong. Mesangial.
   - **F.** T-cell mediated injury (type IV hypersensitivity) — Wrong. Not correct.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - coughs up blood — Pulmonary hemorrhage.
     - rapidly rising creatinine over 2 weeks — RPGN.
     - crescents in most glomeruli — Crescentic GN.
     - smooth linear IgG — Anti-GBM antibodies.
   - **Reasoning:** Hemoptysis + RPGN + linear IgG → anti-GBM (Goodpasture) → type II hypersensitivity.
   - **Teaching point:** Treat urgently with plasmapheresis, steroids and cyclophosphamide.
   - **Follow-up:** What is the mechanism of his disease?
   - Page: 614

859. A 47-year-old man has chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge, cough with lung nodules on CT and hematuria with RBC casts. Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with no immune deposits on immunofluorescence.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Nephritic syndrome
   - **A.** Anti-PLA2R — Wrong. Membranous.
   - **B.** PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) **(Correct)** — Correct. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
   - **C.** Anti-dsDNA — Wrong. Lupus; granular deposits.
   - **D.** Anti-GBM — Wrong. Linear IF.
   - **E.** Anti-streptolysin O — Wrong. PSGN.
   - **F.** MPO-ANCA — Wrong. Microscopic polyangiitis.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge — Upper airway involvement.
     - lung nodules — Granulomatous inflammation.
     - no immune deposits — Pauci-immune.
   - **Reasoning:** Upper airway + lung nodules + pauci-immune crescentic GN → GPA → PR3-ANCA.
   - **Teaching point:** MPA has p-ANCA and no granulomas; EGPA adds asthma and eosinophilia.
   - **Follow-up:** Which antibody is most likely positive?
   - Page: 614

860. A 16-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria. He wears hearing aids for sensorineural hearing loss. Eye exam shows a cone-shaped bulging of the lens. His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30.
   - **Domain:** Pathology
   - **Topic:** Alport syndrome
   - **A.** Effaced foot processes only — Wrong. Minimal change.
   - **B.** Mesangial IgA deposits — Wrong. IgA nephropathy.
   - **C.** Linear IgG — Wrong. Goodpasture (IF, not EM).
   - **D.** Subepithelial humps — Wrong. PSGN.
   - **E.** Tram-track GBM duplication — Wrong. MPGN.
   - **F.** Irregular thickening and splitting of the GBM with a basket-weave pattern **(Correct)** — Correct. Alport syndrome.
   - **Clinical clues:**
     - persistent microscopic hematuria — Nephritic picture.
     - sensorineural hearing loss — Can't hear.
     - cone-shaped bulging of the lens — Anterior lenticonus.
     - His maternal uncle — X-linked inheritance.
   - **Reasoning:** Hematuria + hearing loss + lens abnormality + X-linked → Alport (type IV collagen) → basket-weave GBM.
   - **Teaching point:** "Can't see, can't pee, can't hear a bee."
   - **Follow-up:** What would electron microscopy of the kidney show?
